*Figure UC.1. Panel A separates the normal, top-cube and reverse-parameter signs. Panel B plots only the exact generating weights on the real section \(w=(1,q)\), \(N=2\). Panel C is the parameter simplex of UC.11. Panel D retains the distinct spatial parameters in the two incidence orders. The complete current and complement identities are UC.6–UC.15.*

#### The source kernels and the diagonal shift

Let \(P,P^*\) be the two complex projective bases, each of
complex dimension \(N\ge1\). Use ordinary kernel convolution
over the compact middle projective space, as in LI.32.
Write \(S\) for the closed incidence and \(\Omega\) for its
open complement. With \(j:\Omega\hookrightarrow P\times P^*\)
and its transposed embedding, put
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 L=\mathbf C_S[-1],\\
 A=j_!\mathbf C_\Omega,\\
 L^{\rm op}=\mathbf C_{S^{\rm op}}[-1],\\
 B=Rj^{\rm op}_*\mathbf C_{\Omega^{\rm op}}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{SN.1}
\]
The unit-normalized topological inverse of LI.D is
\(B[2N]\), so its two oriented convolution identifications
are \(A*B[2N]\simeq\mathbf C_{\Delta_P}\) and
\(B*A[2N]\simeq\mathbf C_{\Delta_{P^*}}\).
These are the complete compact-fibre and boundary
identifications LI.34–LI.41, with positive complex
orientation, not a fibre Euler-characteristic equality.

##### SN.0. Both open/closed arrows

The ordinary open/closed exact sequence gives the triangle
\[
 L\xrightarrow{u}A\longrightarrow
             \mathbf C_{P\times P^*}\xrightarrow{+1}.
 \tag{SN.2}
\]
Here \(u\) is the shifted connecting arrow. OCM.3–OCM.5
constructs its actual cone map, using the lifted
restriction and its differential homotopy. Thus it has
the signs of that full relative model.

For the transposed open, the closed-support triangle is
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathbf C_{S^{\rm op}}[-2]\longrightarrow
 \mathbf C_{P^*\times P}\longrightarrow B\\
 \xrightarrow{v}L^{\rm op}\xrightarrow{+1}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{SN.3}
\]
To identify the first term, straighten the hypersurface
to a complex normal disc and use its positively oriented
real codimension-two Thom class, with arbitrary tangential
coefficients. HI.A proves this full supported comparison
including the collapsed fibre. The normal orientations
glue, since a holomorphic change of normal frame has
positive real Jacobian. The source of the first map is
therefore precisely the displayed shifted constant sheaf.
The triangle itself is the actual closed-support/open
restriction triangle from the relative cone.
It also specifies the boundary map \(v\).

The one-normal circle in \(B\) is sent by \(v\) to its
positive generator. A representative for its compact
boundary is
\(-d\chi\wedge d\theta/(2\pi)\), with \(\chi\) equal to
one near zero and zero outside an inner disc. Its integral
is one, as proved in LI.38–LI.39. This checks the
normal orientation in SN.3, rather than inferring it
from the shift alone.

For any bounded holomorphic coefficient complex \(F\),
application of the actual microlocal Hom gives
isomorphisms on every nonzero incidence conormal:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 u^*:\mu\operatorname{hom}(A,F)\\
          \xrightarrow{\sim}\mu\operatorname{hom}(L,F),\\
 v^*:\mu\operatorname{hom}(L^{\rm op},F)\\
          \xrightarrow{\sim}\mu\operatorname{hom}(B,F).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{SN.4}
\]
Indeed the cone of either map is a shift of microlocal
Hom from the ambient constant sheaf. OCM.A proves its
off-zero vanishing by the actual pulled-coefficient
homotopy, not by an assumed symbol realization. All
operations in the definition of microlocal Hom are
derived additive operations and preserve the displayed
triangles. The source arrows and their comparisons are
therefore the same derived arrows as in SN.2–SN.3.

##### SN.1. The two convolution comparisons

There is a useful common source for the first order:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 L*L^{\rm op}[2N]\ \xleftarrow{\ 1*v\ }\ 
 L*B[2N]\\
 \xrightarrow{\ u*1\ }A*B[2N]
                    \xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbf C_{\Delta_P}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{SN.5}
\]
After applying microlocal Hom with any fixed bounded coefficient
complex, both left comparison arrows become isomorphisms
off the zero cotangent section. We verify their cones
on actual coefficient sheaves.

The cone contributed by \(u\) is
\(\mathbf C_{P\times P^*}*B[2N]\).
For a fixed endpoint \(p'\), ordinary global sections
of \(Rj_*\mathbf C_\Omega\) on the middle compact
projective space are the ordinary cohomology of its
affine nonincidence fibre \(\mathbf C^N\).
The contraction by real dilation, including the
degree-zero constant section, gives just \(\mathbf C\).
These complexes are locally constant in the endpoint:
the determinant-one matrix used in LI.8.3 sends a
fixed endpoint vector to the current one and
trivializes the entire incidence pair. On such a
product the actual de Rham parameter homotopy
identifies the pushforward with the constant fibre
complex. The compact-fibre comparison LI.34–LI.35
justifies every restriction. The unused first endpoint
is already constant. Hence this convolution cone is
locally a finite complex of constant sheaves on the
full endpoint pair.

The cone contributed by \(v\) is
\(L*\mathbf C_{P^*\times P}[2N+1]\).
Here the incidence fibre over the first endpoint is
\(\mathbf P^{N-1}\); the same explicit matrix
trivializes that whole family, and the second endpoint
is unused. Its compact-fibre cohomology is a bounded
finite-dimensional complex, locally constant in the
endpoints. Finiteness may be checked directly with
the finite standard affine cover of \(\mathbf P^{N-1}\).
An intersection is a product of an affine space with
finitely many punctured planes. Dilation contracts
each affine factor; radial contraction and the
normalized angular form give the two-term circle
complex for each punctured factor, as in LI.8.2.
Finite tensor products and the finite Čech filtration
then give bounded finite-dimensional cohomology.
This computes through an acyclic de Rham resolution;
it does not assert that the cover is acyclic for the
constant sheaf. Over \(\mathbf C\), a bounded vector
complex with finite-dimensional cohomology is
quasi-isomorphic to a finite-dimensional complex:
choose complements to its cycles and boundaries.
This last observation is used only to apply the
finite constant-coefficient vanishing, not to choose
any convolution map.

For a finite constant coefficient complex \(V\),
\(\mu\operatorname{hom}(V\otimes\mathbf C_M,F)\)
is the corresponding finite Hom complex of
\(\mu\operatorname{hom}(\mathbf C_M,F)\).
One checks this first on a finite vector space by
a basis, then by finite totalization; finite Hom
commutes with the actual resolutions and filtered
germs. It is zero off zero by OCM.A. Thus both
convolution cones in SN.5 vanish under the indicated
microlocal Hom. This proves the assertion about the
comparison arrows with their exact source maps.

The second order is the same complete construction
with \(P,P^*\) interchanged. Equivalently use the roof
from \(B*L[2N]\), with one arrow to \(B*A[2N]\)
and one to \(L^{\rm op}*L[2N]\). Its two cones have
the same affine and projective compact-fibre
descriptions. It gives
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mu\operatorname{hom}(L*L^{\rm op}[2N],F)\\
        \simeq\mu\operatorname{hom}(\mathbf C_{\Delta_P},F),\\
 \mu\operatorname{hom}(L^{\rm op}*L[2N],F')\\
        \simeq\mu\operatorname{hom}(\mathbf C_{\Delta_{P^*}},F')
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{SN.6}
\]
at nonzero endpoint covectors. The isomorphisms are
the just constructed roofs, including the oriented
topological counits.

##### SN.2. The two different dimension shifts

The coefficient trace in complex middle dimension \(N\)
lowers the Dolbeault degree by \(N\), with
\(\operatorname{Tr}_q=(-1)^{N(q-N)}I_q\), as in V.4.
In a coefficient-composition roof using this trace, its target
coefficient line is consequently shifted by \([-N]\).
The contravariance of the first argument gives
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mu\operatorname{hom}(L*L^{\rm op},F[-N])\\
 =\mu\operatorname{hom}(L*L^{\rm op}[N],F).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{SN.7}
\]
SN.6 uses a different shift: the real compact-fibre
orientation contributes \([2N]\). Combining these
two facts gives, under microlocal Hom off zero, the source
roof with \(\mathbf C_\Delta[-N]\). Thus the corresponding
coefficient-composition target is identified with
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mu\operatorname{hom}(\mathbf C_\Delta[-N],F)\\
 =\mu\operatorname{hom}(\mathbf C_\Delta,F)[N].
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{SN.8}
\]
For the ordered input top-form coefficient, degree zero
of SN.8 is exactly the degree-\(N\) real diagonal
operator group. The spatial number \(d=N-1\) in the
opposite pole of OI.6 is a third count; it cannot
replace either shift above.

This identification is through the source roofs of SN.5–SN.6.
It is not an isomorphism of the two underlying source sheaves
before applying microlocal Hom. Their locally constant
convolution cones are discarded only by OCM.A off zero.
Nor does counting these shifts construct the comparison of
coefficient-composition roofs.

##### SN.3. Actual finite equality witnesses on the roofs

The comparison isomorphisms above have finite representatives,
not only abstract inverses of cohomology maps. We spell this
out for a comparison chain map \(f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet\).
Use the ordinary cone convention
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \operatorname{Cone}(f)^q=D^q\oplus C^{q+1},\\
 d(b,a)=(db+fa,-da).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{SN.9}
\]
Each of the two comparison cones is, locally in the endpoint
pair and through the coefficient comparisons already proved,
a finite constant-coefficient complex in its source argument.
The finite-Hom construction after SN.5, followed by OCM.11,
contracts its microlocal relative complex on a later round
support domain. For finite complexes the contraction is
extended by the ordinary total-degree sign; the two terms
containing the coefficient differential cancel because the
contraction lowers form degree by one. A local chain
quasi-isomorphism used to pass to this model is compared by
R.6–R.7. In the finitely many degrees used by a given finite
list of cochains, their elimination gives actual lifts and
primitives on one common restriction. Thus the statement
needed below is that each displayed cone cycle has a
primitive on that actual restriction. A simultaneous
contraction on an unspecified infinite collection of
germs is not being asserted.

For a closed \(b\in D^q\), the cone element \((b,0)\)
is closed. Choose its just constructed primitive \((x,a)\).
SN.9 says
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 da=0,\qquad b-fa=dx.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{SN.10}
\]
This supplies a preimage cycle and the complete boundary
witness for its image. Conversely suppose \(da=0\) and
\(fa=db\). The element \((-b,a)\) is a closed cone
cochain of degree \(q-1\). If \((x,y)\) is its primitive,
the second entry in SN.9 gives
\[
                         a=d(-y).
 \tag{SN.11}
\]
This is the equality witness for injectivity. Both
arguments retain the two entries of each relative
support cone; their cone cochains themselves are
finite lists of whole-domain and complement cochains.
R.6–R.7 is applied to that full list.

For a finite diagram of the source comparisons, include
all its cycles, chosen lifts, primitives and restrictions
in this construction. The finite common-domain argument
of OCM.3 and HI.A then supplies one actual later support
domain with one strict nonzero covector margin. Applying
SN.10 along one arrow and SN.11 to the difference between
two lifted cycles shows that the corresponding source-roof
identities hold on that domain, with the equality primitive
included. Their shifted versions use the displayed
differentials, so introduce no additional orientation
choice. The scalar of the topological counit is still
the positive compact-fibre integral of LI.D and the
normal-circle map of SN.3.

SN.5–SN.8 identify the source roofs and their degrees.
An equality of the two holomorphic incidence products
with the unit form UC.7 still requires the actual
coefficient composition on these roofs. In particular
the spatial parameter sign UC.19 and the normal-circle
orientation in SN.3 must both be retained in that
calculation.


#### Finite hyperplane descent of the diagonal form

Keep the normal coordinates, scalar \(c_N\), full coefficient
line and total differentials of UC.1–UC.19. Put \(d=N-1\).
The construction below gives every cochain in a spatial
hyperplane descent. Its parameter space is the full
projective hyperplane space.

##### HP.0. The normalized affine parameter bundle

Over the punctured normal domain let \(\mathcal A\)
be the total space of the following affine fibres:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathcal A_w=\{a:\langle a,w\rangle=1\},\\
 w\ne0,\\
 \pi:\mathcal A\longrightarrow\{w\ne0\}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HP.1}
\]
The fibre is an affine space of complex dimension \(d\).
The vector \(s(w)=\overline w/|w|^2\) is a smooth
section. The formula
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 h_\lambda(w,a)\\
 =\bigl(w,(1-\lambda)a+\lambda s(w)\bigr),\\
 0\le\lambda\le1
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HP.2}
\]
is a fibre-preserving strong deformation onto that section:
the scalar pairing remains one, and a point already on the
section is fixed. On a compact subset of \(\mathcal A\)
its image is compact. All of its derivatives in any fixed
finite list of coordinate directions are bounded there,
since the normal projection stays away from zero.

The projective parameter space with
\(\langle\xi,w\rangle\ne0\) is isomorphic to HP.1:
\[
                a=\frac{\xi}{\langle\xi,w\rangle}.
 \tag{HP.3}
\]
This is independent of the representative for \([\xi]\).
Conversely \(a\) determines \([a]\), and these maps are
inverse. Thus HP.2 is also an explicit contraction in the
full nonincident projective fibre. The full form
\(\mathcal W_N\) of UC.16 pulls back along the section to
\(\beta_N\wedge dw\). UC.9–UC.11 gives the associated
form homotopies, with their exact simplex signs.

##### HP.1. The top simplex determinant

On an intersection \(U_{i_0\ldots i_k}\) of the coordinate
puncture cover use the holomorphic generating vertices
\(a^i=e_i/w_i\). For an ordered tuple \(I=(i_0,\ldots,i_k)\)
of distinct indices put \(D=d_u+\bar\partial\) and define
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 a_I(u)=\sum_{\nu=0}^k u_\nu a^{i_\nu},\\
 T_I=c_N\int_{\Delta^k}\omega'_D(a_I(u)).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HP.4}
\]
Parameter differentials precede the antiholomorphic
coefficient differentials, as in UC.11. Its remaining
antiholomorphic degree is \(d-k\). Because all the vertices
are holomorphic, \(T_I=0\) for \(k<d\): after selecting
parameter degree \(k\), a positive antiholomorphic
degree remains and has no nonzero factor.

For \(k=d\), the exact determinant identity is
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \omega'_{d_u}(a_I(u))\\
 =\det(a^{i_0},\ldots,a^{i_d})\,du.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HP.5}
\]
Here \(du=du_1\wedge\cdots\wedge du_d\), as in the
ordered-block convention of UC.1. To prove it, evaluate the alternating form on the ordered
parameter vectors. The resulting determinant has columns
\(a(u),a^{i_1}-a^{i_0},\ldots,a^{i_d}-a^{i_0}\).
Replace its first column by \(a^{i_0}\); every discarded
column is a linear combination of the remaining columns,
so contributes zero. Add the first column to each remaining
one. This gives exactly HP.5, without a factorial.
The oriented standard simplex has volume \(1/d!\).
Indeed repeated integration over
\(0\le u_j\) and \(\sum u_j\le1\) proves inductively
that its volume is \(1/d!\): the last slice at \(u_d=t\)
has volume \((1-t)^{d-1}/(d-1)!\), whose integral is
\(1/d!\). The point simplex for \(d=0\) has volume one.
Consequently
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 T_{0\ldots d}
   =\frac{c_N}{d!\,w_0\cdots w_d}
   =r_N\varphi .
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HP.6}
\]
A permutation of the ordered vertices multiplies this
cochain by its permutation sign, exactly as required for
the alternating Čech convention. The factorial in \(c_N\)
has therefore canceled the simplex volume.

##### HP.2. Every lower cochain and its differential

Insert the smooth section as the first vertex and put
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 G_I=H_{s,a^{i_0},\ldots,a^{i_k}},\\
 \deg_{\bar\partial}G_I=d-k-1.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HP.7}
\]
Here \(H\) is precisely the simplex integral UC.11, with
\(k+1\) parameter directions. All its arguments pair
with \(w\) to one, so the entire simplex stays in
HP.1. The cochain is defined on the whole actual
intersection \(U_I\). Its degree makes it zero for \(k\ge d\).
Set \(G^{(-1)}=\beta_N\); its augmented Čech
differential means the restrictions of that one global
form.

Use the alternating Čech differential \(\Delta\).
UC.11 on the ordered vertices in HP.7 gives
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \bar\partial G^{(k)}\\
     =(-1)^k\bigl(T^{(k)}-\Delta G^{(k-1)}\bigr).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HP.8}
\]
In detail, deleting the first vertex \(s\) has coefficient
\((-1)^k\) and gives \(T_I\). Deleting vertex
\(a^{i_\nu}\) has coefficient
\((-1)^{k+\nu+1}\), exactly
\((-1)^{k+1}\) times its Čech-face coefficient.
For \(k=0\) this says
\(\bar\partial G_i=T_i-\beta_N|_{U_i}\).
For \(k=d\), its left side is zero, and it gives
\(\Delta G^{(d-1)}=T^{(d)}\).

Let \(D_{\mathrm{tot}}=\Delta+(-1)^k\bar\partial\)
in Čech degree \(k\), the convention of V.6.
The finite sum \(G=\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}G^{(k)}\)
has total degree \(d-1\), and HP.8 gives the literal
full-cochain identity
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 D_{\mathrm{tot}}G
       =T^{(d)}-\operatorname{aug}(\beta_N).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HP.9}
\]
Its Čech-degree-zero component is \(-\beta_N\);
the intermediate components cancel term by term by HP.8;
the top component is HP.6. When \(d=0\), the sum is
empty and the two endpoints coincide. Thus this identity
includes all lower intersections and not just the top
rational expression. None of its general cochains is
extended across an omitted coordinate hyperplane.
The relative-cone connecting map and the cone-to-cube
map of UC.15 turn HP.9 into the same unit with literal
top cube entry \(r_N(-1)^N\varphi\).

For any finite list of such cochains, their restrictions
and homotopies, choose actual domains before integration.
On a compact subset of an intersection, all its displayed
nonzero \(w_i\)'s have a positive lower bound, as does
\(|w|\). The simplices are compact. Differentiation in
any fixed finite list of variables therefore commutes
with their integrals and with restriction. This verifies
the full-parameter and finite-witness assertions without
a boundary growth assumption or a passage to a quotient
limit.

##### HP.3. Arbitrary independent hyperplane vertices

The construction is covariant under an invertible linear
normal frame. Let \(\ell_0,\ldots,\ell_d\) be independent
constant vectors, let \(M\) have those columns, and put
\(\alpha_j=\langle\ell_j,w\rangle\).
Use \(a^j=\ell_j/\alpha_j\) on \(\{\alpha_j\ne0\}\).
HP.5 and the ordered change of variables give
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 T_{0\ldots d}\wedge dw\\
   =\frac{r_N\det M}{(2\pi i)^N\prod_j\alpha_j}\,dw\\
   =\frac{r_N}{(2\pi i)^N\prod_j\alpha_j}\,d\alpha .
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HP.10}
\]
Here \(d\alpha=\det(M^{\mathsf T})\,dw=\det M\,dw\).
Thus the simplex determinant and the endpoint input
frame transform together. HP.7–HP.9 applies with the
same section \(s\) and these new generating vertices;
only the open intersections change.

In particular one may take
\(\ell_0=e_0\) and
\(\ell_j=e_0+\varepsilon e_j\) for \(1\le j\le d\),
with \(\varepsilon\ne0\). Their determinant is
\(\varepsilon^d\), and all their projective classes
are near \([e_0]\) as \(\varepsilon\) tends to zero.
This does not put the interpolating simplices into
that same projective chart: a convex combination of
the normalized vectors can have zeroth coordinate zero
even though it remains generating. HP.2 and HP.7
are assertions in the full nonincident projective
fibre. An application confined to one actual middle
coordinate domain must supply its own containment and
proper-collar comparison.

There is an exact two-dimensional example. Let
\(N=2\), \(\varepsilon r\ne0\), and take
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 w=(r,-2r/\varepsilon),\\
 \ell_0=(1,0),\quad \ell_1=(1,\varepsilon),\\
 \alpha_0=r,\qquad \alpha_1=-r,\\
 a^0=(1,0)/r,\\
 a^1=(-1,-\varepsilon)/r.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HP.11}
\]
The midpoint is \((0,-\varepsilon/(2r))\).
It pairs with \(w\) to one, but its projective class
is outside the chart \(\xi_0\ne0\). The two original
projective vertices both lie in that chart and tend
to \([e_0]\) as \(\varepsilon\) tends to zero.
For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), choosing \(r\) small
puts \(w\) in any prescribed normal neighbourhood.
Thus neither a small normal domain nor nearby
projective vertices proves chart containment of
the affine simplex.

For these two vertices there is nevertheless a
chart-contained curved path:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 y(t)=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}(1-e^{i\pi t}),\\
 \xi(t)=(1,y(t)),\\
 \langle\xi(t),w\rangle=r e^{i\pi t},\\
 a(t)=\frac{\xi(t)}{r e^{i\pi t}},\\
 0\le t\le1 .
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{HP.12}
\]
Its endpoints are \(a^0,a^1\), its denominator has
modulus \(|r|\), and \(|y(t)|\le|\varepsilon|\).
Every fixed parameter derivative is bounded for
fixed nonzero \(r,\varepsilon\). UC.9 applies to
this smooth generating path, with \(d_t\) in
place of the straight-path differential: its proof
uses only the generating relation and the two
endpoints. This example gives an actual compact
path in that one parameter chart. It supplies
neither the higher compatible parameter faces nor
a proper-support comparison for a general
incidence convolution.

The reverse spatial frame in UC.19 still contributes
\((-1)^d\) to its holomorphic differential block.
Neither HP.9 nor HP.10 removes that factor. The
topological source counit and the actual coefficient
composition have to be compared with this full descent
before either normalized incidence inverse product
is identified with the unit.

### 5.65. Bounded generating hyperplanes and proper contour support

The exact earlier programme dependencies are §§5.34, 5.35, 5.53, 5.63, 5.64. Specifically, R.6–R.7 and V.1/V.4 give the full supported comparison and trace; RM.3–RM.9 gives actual real-stalk supports and finite common witnesses; OI.18 and OI.20 gives the two ordinary residues; UC.1, UC.3, UC.9–UC.11 and UC.16–UC.19 gives the ordered scalar, generating homotopies and universal form.

Let \(N=d+1\ge1\), and write the endpoint normal variable as
\(w=(w_0,z)\in\mathbf C\times\mathbf C^d\).
Put \(\rho=|w|=(|w_0|^2+|z|^2)^{1/2}\).
Pair covectors and vectors bilinearly, without a conjugate in
that pairing. All norms below are Euclidean norms.
Use the ordered differential blocks, the scalar \(c_N\),
the universal form and the full relative differential of
UC.1, UC.16 and V.1. In particular \(\bar\partial\)
includes the output antiholomorphic directions of the pair.

Fix a spatial middle-coordinate ball of radius \(R_y>0\).
Let \(\mathcal K_{\mu,\nu}\) be the Hermitian matrices
satisfying the following bounds:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 0<\mu\le\nu<R_y/2,\\
 H=H^*,\qquad \mu I\le H\le\nu I.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.1}
\]
The inequalities mean inequalities of Hermitian quadratic
forms on \(\mathbf C^d\). For \(d=0\) the matrix is empty
and this parameter set is a singleton.

The family constructed below stays in this one actual
spatial chart. The supports and margins are part of the
construction, rather than a consequence of nearby
projective vertices.

#### RC.0. The support and every zero of the denominator

Choose \(\epsilon>0\) and
\(K>\sqrt{1+\mu^{-2}}\). Define the closed cone
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 G=G_{K,\epsilon},\\
 w_0=-\ell+ib,\quad \ell\ge0,\\
 |b|\le\epsilon\ell,\qquad |z|\le K\ell .
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.2}
\]
It is convex: the time and imaginary inequalities are
convex linear/norm inequalities, and the spatial
inequality is preserved by the triangle inequality.
It contains the zero normal vector.

For \(H\in\mathcal K_{\mu,\nu}\), on \(w\ne0\), put
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 y_H(w)=H\overline z/\rho,\\
 \xi_H=(1,y_H),\\
 F_H(w)=\langle\xi_H,w\rangle,\\
 a_H(w)=\xi_H/F_H(w),\\
 F_H(w)\ne0.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.3}
\]
Although the pairing is bilinear, the extra term in
the denominator is a real positive Hermitian form:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 Q_H=z^{\mathsf T}H\overline z,\\
 F_H=w_0+Q_H/\rho,\\
 \mu|z|^2\le Q_H\le\nu|z|^2 .
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.4}
\]
Indeed take the vector \(v=\overline z\); then
\(v^*Hv=z^{\mathsf T}H\overline z\).

We also have \(\|Hv\|\le\nu\|v\|\). Here is a proof
that does not require diagonalizing \(H\). Positivity
of the form on \(u+\lambda v\), for every complex
\(\lambda\), gives
\(|u^*Hv|^2\le(u^*Hu)(v^*Hv)\): minimize the resulting
quadratic expression in \(\lambda\), with the zero
quadratic-coefficient case following by a linear
variation. Thus \(|u^*Hv|\le\nu\|u\|\|v\|\).
Taking \(u=Hv/\|Hv\|\) when \(Hv\ne0\) gives the
asserted norm bound; the zero case is immediate.
Consequently \(|y_H|\le\nu\), strictly inside the
chosen middle ball.

Every zero of \(F_H\) with \(w\ne0\) lies in the
strict interior of \(G\). To prove this, a zero
forces \(w_0\) to be real and negative. It cannot
have \(z=0\), since then \(F_H=w_0\ne0\).
Write \(w_0=-\ell\), \(\ell>0\), and set
\(q=|z|/\ell\). RC.4 gives
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \ell=Q_H/\rho
       \ge\mu |z|^2/\rho,\\
 \mu q^2\le\sqrt{1+q^2}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.5}
\]
Both sides are nonnegative. Squaring and solving the
quadratic inequality in \(q^2\) gives
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 q^2\le
 \frac{1+\sqrt{1+4\mu^2}}{2\mu^2}\\
 \le1+\mu^{-2}<K^2 .
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.6}
\]
For the second inequality, square the positive
inequality \(\sqrt{1+4\mu^2}\le1+2\mu^2\).
The imaginary coordinate is zero and hence has
strict inequality in RC.2 as well. This proves the
strict-interior assertion. In dimension \(d=0\)
there are no such zeros.

In particular \(a_H\) is a smooth generating vector
on the entire actual complement of \(G\):
\(\langle a_H,w\rangle=1\). Its projective class is
always \([1:y_H]\); its zeroth homogeneous
coordinate never vanishes there.

The cone is admissible at the nonzero normal
covector \(e_0\), with a uniform nearby-covector
margin. Every nonzero vector in \(G\) satisfies
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 -\Re w_0=\ell\\
   \ge\frac{|w|}{\sqrt{1+\epsilon^2+K^2}}>0.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.7}
\]
Perturbing the covector by norm less than half the
reciprocal square root preserves half this positive
margin, by the ordinary complex Cauchy inequality
\(|\langle p,w\rangle|\le|p||w|\).
Thus RC.2 has exactly the negative displacement
polar sign of RM.3–RM.6.

It can contain any finite list of the earlier
admissible supports after an actual restriction.
First use RM.4–RM.6 to obtain finitely many finite
time/aperture and componentwise spatial constants.
Take a common larger \(\epsilon\) and take \(K\)
larger than the Euclidean norm of those spatial
constants, as well as the bound in RC.2.
This gives actual containment in \(G\).
RC.7 then supplies one smaller actual covector
neighbourhood. No aperture is asserted uniform
over an infinite list of real germs.

#### RC.1. Uniform denominator and derivative bounds

There is a constant \(c>0\), depending only on the
displayed dimensions and constants, such that
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 c\rho\le|F_H(w)|\le(1+\nu)\rho,\\
 w\notin\operatorname{int}G,\quad w\ne0,\\
 H\in\mathcal K_{\mu,\nu}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.8}
\]
The upper bound follows from RC.4 and
\(|z|^2/\rho\le\rho\).
For the lower bound restrict to \(|w|=1\) outside
\(\operatorname{int}G\). This is compact.
The matrix set in RC.1 is compact as a subset of
the finite-dimensional real space of Hermitian
matrices: its quadratic inequalities define a
closed set, and the norm bound proved above
bounds every entry by \(\nu\).
The continuous function \(|F_H(w)|\) has no zero
on the product of these compact sets, by RC.5–RC.6.
Its minimum is therefore positive. Positive real
homogeneity \(F_H(rw)=rF_H(w)\) proves RC.8
for every \(\rho>0\).

For every fixed real normal-coordinate multiindex
\(\alpha\), the following bounds hold uniformly
in the same directions and matrices:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 |\partial^\alpha y_H|\le C_\alpha\rho^{-|\alpha|},\\
 |\partial^\alpha F_H|
          \le C_\alpha\rho^{1-|\alpha|},\\
 |\partial^\alpha a_H|
          \le C_\alpha\rho^{-1-|\alpha|}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.9}
\]
Here and below the constants need not be the same
in different lines. For completeness the functions
are smooth on a neighbourhood of the compact
unit-direction/matrix product used above. RC.8
keeps the reciprocal denominator smooth there;
a smaller neighbourhood retains half its lower
bound. Each fixed derivative is continuous and
bounded on that compact product. Differentiating
the positive-real homogeneities of degrees
\(0,1,-1\), respectively, scales those derivatives
by the displayed powers of \(\rho\). This proves
all of RC.9, without a bound for a varying
derivative order.

#### RC.2. All finite parameter faces stay in the chart

For any finite list \(H_0,\ldots,H_k\) in RC.1,
use the oriented standard simplex and put
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 H(\sigma)=\sum_{j=0}^k\sigma_jH_j,\\
 \sigma_j\ge0,\qquad\sum_j\sigma_j=1 .
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.10}
\]
The quadratic-form inequalities are convex, so
every point remains in RC.1. RC.3 and RC.8
therefore hold on the entire simplex, on every
face and on the same endpoint complement.
In particular \(|y_{H(\sigma)}|\le\nu\)
and the entire family is in one fixed inner
middle chart. This is interpolation of the
Hermitian matrices followed by normalization;
it is not affine interpolation of arbitrary
normalized projective vectors.

Set \(D=d_\sigma+\bar\partial\), with parameter
differentials first, and define
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 J_{0\ldots k}
   =c_N\int_{\Delta^k}
      \omega'_D(a_{H(\sigma)}),\\
 \deg_{\bar\partial}J_{0\ldots k}=N-1-k .
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.11}
\]
The argument of UC.3 applies because the scalar
pairing is one throughout this simplex. It makes
\(D\omega'_D(a_{H(\sigma)})=0\).
For \(k=0\) this gives
\(\bar\partial J_H=0\).
For \(k\ge1\), parameter Stokes in the
explicit ordering of UC.11 gives
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \bar\partial J_{0\ldots k}\\
 =\sum_{j=0}^k(-1)^{k+j+1}
       J_{0\ldots\widehat j\ldots k}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.12}
\]
For \(k>N-1\) the integral is zero and this
identity is its alternating face relation.
All faces are restrictions of the same
matrix-simplex construction, with the same
denominator and chart margins. Thus these are
actual compatible finite faces, including the
higher face homotopies.

Write \(\beta_H=J_H\). In the full relative
complex for \(Z=\{w\in G\}\) on any small
endpoint pair domain, the cochain
\[
                         k_H=(0,-\beta_H)
 \tag{RC.13}
\]
has degree \(N\) and is closed. It represents
the diagonal unit. Indeed let
\(s_0(w)=\overline w/\rho^2\), and interpolate
the normalized vectors
\((1-t)s_0+t a_H\) on the endpoint complement.
Their scalar pairing is one. UC.9 gives an
explicit coefficient homotopy \(H(s_0,a_H)\),
and UC.10 gives the literal boundary
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 k_H-k_{\mathrm{unit}}\\
        =d(0,H(s_0,a_H)).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.14}
\]
This last homotopy is in the endpoint coefficient
complex. It is not used as a middle-coordinate
path, and its projective coordinates are not
asserted to stay in the middle chart.
The actual middle parameter faces are RC.10.
This distinguishes RC.14 from the chart crossing
of HP.11 while retaining its full relative
equality witness.

The fixed-derivative bounds also hold after
any finite number of simplex derivatives:
the parameter domains are compact, their
matrix derivatives are bounded, and RC.8
holds uniformly on them. In particular the
coefficients of RC.11 satisfy
\[
 |J_{0\ldots k}(w)|
       \le C_k\rho^{-2N+1+k}.
 \tag{RC.15}
\]
There are one undifferentiated \(a_H\), \(k\)
parameter derivatives of degree \(-1\), and
\(N-1-k\) antiholomorphic derivatives of degree
\(-2\). This gives exactly the exponent in
RC.15. These coefficients are integrable
near the normal origin: their radial absolute
bound is a constant times
\(\int_0^\eta r^k\,dr\).
Extension by zero from the cone complement
thus gives locally integrable coefficients
if an extension is wanted. Its differential
can have cone-boundary terms; it is not
silently identified with just the diagonal
current. RC.14 is the full relative unit
comparison and keeps those boundary effects.

#### RC.3. The first normal-circle family and a common proper collar

Let the endpoints in the first incidence order be
\((t,x)\), \((t',x')\), so
\(w=(t'-t,x'-x)\). Write the middle coordinates
as \((s,y)\). The two actual incidence functions
are
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 f=s-t-x^{\mathsf T}y,\\
 g=t'-s+(x')^{\mathsf T}y,\\
 f+g=w_0+z^{\mathsf T}y .
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.16}
\]
On the endpoint complement use the middle family
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 y=y_{H(\sigma)}(w),\\
 f=\tfrac12 F_{H(\sigma)}(w)e^{i\theta},\\
 s=t+x^{\mathsf T}y+f,\\
 0\le\theta\le2\pi .
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.17}
\]
It is periodic in \(\theta\). Its positive
normal circle surrounds \(f=0\) and excludes
\(g=0\), since
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 |f|=\tfrac12|F_H|,\\
 |g|=|F_H-f|\ge\tfrac12|F_H|,\\
 |F_H|\ge c\rho>0.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.18}
\]
The finite simplices, their faces and this
circle have the same bounds.

The ordinary normal residue is an equality
of parameter forms:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \frac1{2\pi i}
 \int_{S^1}^{+}
 \frac{df\wedge dy\wedge dw}{f(F_H-f)^N}\\
 =\frac{dy\wedge dw}{F_H^N}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.19}
\]
To verify it directly, on \(|f|=|F_H|/2\)
expand \((F_H-f)^{-N}\) by its convergent
power series in \(f/F_H\). The sum is uniformly
convergent there, with all fixed derivatives
on compact parameter subsets of the endpoint
complement. Only its constant term survives
the circle integral of \(df/f\), giving
\(F_H^{-N}\), as in OI.18.
There is no derivative-of-radius correction:
after pullback, \(df\) has \(\theta\)-component
\(if\,d\theta\); every other component contains
no \(d\theta\). The factors \(dy\) and \(dw\)
also contain no \(d\theta\). Fibre integration
therefore selects exactly that displayed
normal component. At fixed endpoints
\(ds\wedge dy=df\wedge dy\), since
the extra \(x^{\mathsf T}dy\) has a repeated
spatial differential. The same
\(\theta\)-selection proves the full-family
identity when the endpoints vary.

Multiplying RC.19 by \(c_N\), then selecting
parameter degree \(k\) and integrating its
matrix simplex, gives
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 c_N\int_{\Delta^k}
       \frac{dy_H\wedge dw}{F_H^N}\\
                 =J_{0\ldots k}\wedge dw .
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.20}
\]
This is the pullback of the projectively
invariant universal form UC.16.
Its holomorphic \(w\)-differentials vanish
against \(dw\); its remaining differential
is \(d_\sigma+\bar\partial\), exactly
RC.11. Thus RC.12 accounts for every
parameter boundary in these ordinary
periods.

There is a common actual proper middle-variable
collar for this entire family, including its
closure at \(w=0\). Fix outer middle radii
\(R_s,R_y\), and small endpoint bounds
\(|t|\le r_t\), \(|x|\le r_x\),
\(\rho\le r_w\), chosen so that
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 |y_H|\le\nu<R_y/2,\\
 |s|\\
 \le r_t+\nu r_x+\tfrac12(1+\nu)r_w\\
                         <R_s/2 .
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.21}
\]
These follow from RC.8 and RC.17 and hold
for every matrix and parameter face.
The endpoint bounds can be made this small
after the constants and the actual outer
domain are fixed.

Take the closure of the family's image
in the endpoint-domain times middle-domain
product. It is closed by definition.
Over a compact endpoint set it is contained
in that compact set times the closed middle
balls in RC.21. Those balls are compact
and strictly inside the actual middle domain.
The closed intersection is compact.
This proves properness of that closure
over the actual endpoint domain, including
the collapsed normal circle at \(w=0\).
A unique limit of \(y_H\) at \(w=0\) is
neither needed nor asserted.

A single smooth collar can be chosen
independently of the endpoint, the matrix,
the parameter face and the circle.
For explicitness put \(b(t)=e^{-1/t}\)
for \(t>0\) and zero otherwise. For \(r<R\)
in an ordinary Euclidean ball write
\(q_v=|v|^2\), and set
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 b_+=b(R^2-q_v),\\
 b_-=b(q_v-r^2),\\
 \chi_{r,R}(v)=\frac{b_+}{b_++b_-}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.22}
\]
The denominator never vanishes; the two
arguments cannot both be nonpositive.
The function is smooth, equals one on
\(|v|\le r\), and equals zero on
\(|v|\ge R\). At the joining value \(t=0\),
every derivative of \(b\) tends to zero:
for \(t>0\) it is a polynomial in \(1/t\)
times \(e^{-1/t}\), whose limit is zero.
Choose inner radii strictly larger than
the bounds in RC.21 and outer radii
strictly smaller than \(R_s,R_y\).
The product of the corresponding two
functions is one near the closed family
and compactly supported in the middle
domain. The same function works for
every finite diagram constructed here.
In dimension \(d=0\) the spatial factor
is one.

For smooth cochains or currents defined
on the chosen actual endpoint-times-middle
domain and supported in that closed family,
this collar permits controlled zero
extension in the middle variable, by
R.7 and V.4. A different source
neighbourhood must satisfy R.7's own
neighbourhood and support hypotheses.
It does not extend arbitrary complement
cochains through \(G\), nor show that an
arbitrary microlocal-Hom composition
already has that support.

#### RC.4. The opposite order and its separate spatial sign

Let the endpoints now be \((s,y)\),
\((s',y')\), and put
\(w'=(s'-s,y'-y)\).
Use middle coordinates \((t,x)\) and
the conventional functions
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 g=t-s+y^{\mathsf T}x,\\
 f'=s'-t-(y')^{\mathsf T}x,\\
 g+f'=w'_0-(z')^{\mathsf T}x .
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.23}
\]
Choose \(x=-y_{H(\sigma)}(w')\), and set
\(g=F_H(w')e^{i\theta}/2\),
\(t=s-y^{\mathsf T}x+g\).
All denominator, derivative, chart and
proper-collar bounds above apply after
interchanging the endpoint spaces.
In particular the ordered ordinary
normal integral is
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \frac1{2\pi i}\int_{S^1}^{+}
       \frac{dg}{g^N(F_H-g)}\\
                          =F_H^{-N}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.24}
\]
Expand \((F_H-g)^{-1}\) in \(g/F_H\);
its coefficient of \(g^{N-1}\) is
\(F_H^{-N}\). RC.18 gives uniform
convergence on the same compact circle,
so termwise integration proves RC.24
including \(N=1\).

The conventional ordered input block
in this middle space is \(dt\wedge dx\).
The normal-circle selection replaces it
by \(dg\wedge dx\) with positive normal
orientation. Since \(x=-y_H\),
the spatial block satisfies
\(dy_H=(-1)^d dx\). Consequently the
reverse normalized ordinary family is
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 (-1)^d c_N\int_{\Delta^k}
           \frac{dx\wedge dw'}{F_H(w')^N}\\
                       =J_{0\ldots k}\wedge dw' .
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RC.25}
\]
This retains exactly the spatial factor
UC.19. Its normal circle residue is
positive; the spatial factor is a
different calculation.

The two ordinary period families
RC.20 and RC.25 give the full relative
unit representatives RC.13–RC.14.
They have compatible finite parameter
faces in one actual middle chart and
a common proper collar for their
explicit contour supports.
Identifying either family with the
actual microlocal-Hom coefficient
composition on the source roofs of
SN.5–SN.8 is a separate equality of
derived morphisms. In particular the
scalar \(c_N\) in these unit-normalized
ordinary periods does not determine
the scalar of that composition map.
No general incidence inverse product
or whole-real contact isomorphism
is asserted by the contour calculation.

Free primary context for the classical hyperplane form: [Harold P. Boas, *Math 685 Notes: Topics in Several Complex Variables*, 2005, revised 2010](https://haroldpboas.gitlab.io/courses/685-2005c/notes.pdf), Sections1.3 and1.5. The matrix family, support margins, bounds, finite faces and collar used here are proved above and in the exact earlier programme proofs linked above.


### 5.66. Affine Spencer reduction and free source directions

The exact earlier programme support prerequisites are §§5.34, 5.47, 5.59, 5.60, 5.64, 5.65. The algebraic functor, coherence, solution and trace prerequisites are in Adjunctions, base change and the projection formula, The de Rham functor, and The Riemann–Hilbert correspondence, with the theorem and chain-formula locators given below.

All differential operators in this argument are algebraic. Put \(N=d+1\ge1\). Use the programme's left-module direct image, density side change and relative Spencer complex, with the last relative form in degree zero. The exact prerequisites are the adjunctions lesson, Theorems 2.1, 3.4 and 4.7; regular-singularities, Theorem 5.17; the Riemann–Hilbert lesson, Theorems 1.18–1.23 and its signed closed-normal calculation; and the de Rham lesson's closed normal Spencer calculation. The support and coefficient conventions are OCM.2–OCM.4 and HI.1. The vanishing assertion used below is proved in *A free source direction and derivative-torsion cones*.

#### AS.0. The actual proper algebraic convolution

Let the endpoint variables be \((t,x),(t',x')\), and the middle variables \((s,y)\), with \(x,x',y\in\mathbb A^d\). Set
\[
\begin{gathered}
u=(t,x),\quad w=t'-t,\\
z=x'-x,\\
f=s-t-x^{\mathsf T}y,\\
g=t'-s+(x')^{\mathsf T}y,\\
F=f+g=w+z^{\mathsf T}y .
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.1}
\]
Write \(\delta_h=\mathcal O[h^{-1}]/\mathcal O\), with distinguished class \([h^{-1}]\), for a smooth hypersurface \(h=0\). This is a left differential-operator module: derivatives act on its displayed rational representatives. In particular
\[
 D_h^r[h^{-1}]=(-1)^r r![h^{-r-1}].
 \tag{AS.2}
\]
Its closed normal presentation and regular holonomicity are the earlier closed-embedding calculation.

On the affine triple product the pair \((f,g)\) consists of two independent coordinates. Indeed
\[
\begin{gathered}
(u,z,y,f,g)\longmapsto\\
\begin{cases}
x'=x+z,\\
s=t+x^{\mathsf T}y+f,\\
t'=t+f+g-z^{\mathsf T}y .
\end{cases}
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.3}
\]
is a polynomial coordinate inverse. Thus the derived structure-sheaf tensor of the two pulled-back incidence modules is concentrated in degree zero:
\[
 \delta_f\otimes_{\mathcal O}^{L}\delta_g
 =\mathcal H^2_{\{f=g=0\}}(\mathcal O).
 \tag{AS.4}
\]
Here is also a flat-complex verification. Resolve each \(\delta_h\) by \([\mathcal O\to\mathcal O[h^{-1}]]\) in degrees \(-1,0\). In the coordinates AS.3 their tensor is the two-variable coordinate localization cube. Successive one-variable Laurent principal parts show that its only cohomology is in degree zero and is the quotient
\(\mathcal O[(fg)^{-1}]/(\mathcal O[f^{-1}]+\mathcal O[g^{-1}])\).
Each principal part is a finite sum in its negative coordinate powers, with coefficients regular in the remaining coordinates. This also identifies the ordered normal generator. The same calculation is the coordinate closed-transfer presentation of the right side of AS.4.

There is an actual proper realization of its direct image. Compactify the common middle affine space to \(\mathbb P^N\). On each incidence pair extend the closed hypersurface module by the ordinary algebraic open direct image across the middle hyperplane at infinity. Call the two extensions \(\widetilde M_+\) and \(\widetilde M_-\). Pull them to the triple product with projective middle factor and put
\[
\begin{gathered}
p:\mathbb A^N\times\mathbb P^N\times\mathbb A^N\\
\longrightarrow\mathbb A^N\times\mathbb A^N,\\
Q=p_+(\widetilde M_+
          \otimes_{\mathcal O}^{L}\widetilde M_-).
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.5}
\]
The smooth inverse images here are the unshifted transfer pullbacks. Equivalently they are the programme's extraordinary inverse images shifted by the negative relative dimension.

Both extensions, their smooth pullbacks and their derived structure tensor are bounded regular holonomic. This is precisely algebraic open direct stability, inverse stability and structure tensor stability in the stated prerequisites. Theorem 3.4 applies to the displayed proper projection, so \(Q\) is bounded coherent. Regular stability makes it regular holonomic.

This is also the affine incidence direct image, with its actual maps. The common middle open is the complement of one Cartier hyperplane. On an affine chart, its ordinary operator direct image is ordinary coefficient localization. This localization is flat, and the two localized factors have their common localization parameter invertible. Their tensor is consequently the localization of their affine tensor; applying localization once or twice gives the same complex. These chart identities glue. The actual direct-image composition therefore identifies AS.5 with the affine middle direct image of AS.4. This argument uses proper coherence for AS.5, rather than assuming coherence for a general nonproper analytic direct image.

#### AS.1. Elimination of the first normal coordinate

The change from the ordered normal coordinates \((f,g)\) to \((f,F=f+g)\) has determinant \(+1\). The closed normal transfer and its ordered determinant contraction identify their normal generators with coefficient \(+1\). One can check that coefficient by the two-coordinate residue: integrating first in the positive \(f\)-circle and then in the positive \(F\)-circle gives the same iterated normal residue as the ordered \((f,g)\) generator. This is a comparison of localization cubes on their common complement cover; it does not declare \(1/(fF)\) to be a function on the single open \(fg\ne0\).

The closed \(f\)-normal relative Spencer complex is
\[
 \mathbb C[D_f]\,e_f
 \xrightarrow{D_f}
 \mathbb C[D_f]\,e_f\,df ,
 \tag{AS.6}
\]
in degrees \(-1,0\), with the remaining coefficients carried along. The map is injective and its cokernel is generated by \(e_f\,df\). Its operator residue sends that generator to \(1\), by the earlier closed trace normalization. Thus the closed normal elimination is an actual quasi-isomorphism, without a residual shift.

The sign can be verified in the total relative complex, without an implicit interchange of two shifted complexes. Write a form with \(df\) first as \(D_f^k e_f\,df\wedge dy_I\), carrying the other coefficient along. Send it to zero for \(k>0\), and to \(dy_I\) for \(k=0\); send every form without \(df\) to zero. The source differential has the total shift sign \((-1)^{d+1}\). On a form containing \(df\), the relative \(y\)-differential crosses that first factor and therefore has sign \((-1)^d\), exactly the target shift sign. The \(f\)-derivative has zero residue. This proves the chain identity with coefficient \(+1\) on the ordered top form. The inclusion \(dy_I\mapsto e_f\,df\wedge dy_I\) is a chain section. A homotopy sends \(D_f^k e_f\,df\wedge dy_I\), for \(k>0\), to \((-1)^{d+1}D_f^{k-1}e_f\,dy_I\), and is zero on the other terms. Expansion gives \(dH+Hd=1-i\,\operatorname{res}_f\); the two \(y\)-terms cancel. Thus every relative degree and both shift signs are included.

The remaining module is \(\delta_F\) on the endpoint-times-\(y\) space. Put
\[
\begin{gathered}
\tau=D_w,\qquad e=[F^{-1}],\\
\gamma=[e\,dy_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dy_d],\\
\gamma\in H^0Q .
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.7}
\]
For \(d=0\), the empty exterior product is one. The entire complex \(Q\) is the relative \(y\)-Spencer complex of \(\delta_F\), in degrees \([-d,0]\). Its coefficient normal form is
\[
 R=\mathbb C[u,z,y,\tau]\,e .
 \tag{AS.8}
\]
To justify this normal form, use \(F\) and the other coordinates as polynomial coordinates before projecting. Every finite normal principal part is a finite polynomial in \(D_F\) applied to \(1/F\), with the factorials and signs of AS.2. Replacing \(F\) by \(w+z^{\mathsf T}y\) gives AS.8.

Derivatives of the original endpoint variables differ from their expressions at fixed \(f\) by a coefficient times the eliminated \(f\)-derivative. That term has zero \(f\)-residue by the preceding explicit chain map. Thus the endpoint action after elimination is the action in the displayed \(F\)-coordinates, with its full horizontal derivatives retained.

The endpoint and relative actions in this form are
\[
\begin{gathered}
D_w=\tau,\quad w=-z^{\mathsf T}y-\partial_\tau,\\
D_{z_j}=\partial_{z_j}+y_j\tau,\\
D_{u_i}=\partial_{u_i},\\
T_j=D_{y_j}^{\rm rel}=\partial_{y_j}+z_j\tau .
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.9}
\]
For example \(D_{y_j}(1/F)=z_jD_w(1/F)\). The term
\(-\partial_\tau\) follows from \([D_w,w]=1\). Direct commutator expansion shows that the endpoint actions commute with all \(T_j\), and that the \(T_j\)'s commute with one another. Thus the complex and its endpoint action have been specified, including their differential signs: on relative forms it is
\[
\begin{gathered}
d_{\rm rel}=\sum_{j=1}^d dy_j\wedge T_j,\\
\text{shifted by }[d].
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.10}
\]
The shift multiplies the unshifted differential by \((-1)^d\). Multiplying relative exterior degree \(k\) by \((-1)^{d(k-d)}\) identifies it with the displayed unshifted Koszul differential, with coefficient one in the top column \(k=d\). Hence neither its top quotient nor the ordered top class AS.7 changes.

#### AS.2. Polynomial Ore localization and the whole Spencer complex

Let \(A\) be the global polynomial Weyl algebra of the endpoint affine space. In this paragraph localization means localization of global \(A\)-modules at the powers of \(\tau\). It is not the assertion that these powers form an Ore set in every ring of rational or holomorphic coefficient germs.

For \(P\in A\), \(\operatorname{ad}(\tau)\) is differentiation of its polynomial \(w\)-coefficients and is locally nilpotent. The finite identity
\[
\begin{gathered}
\tau^nP\\
=\sum_k\binom nk
       \operatorname{ad}(\tau)^k(P)\tau^{n-k}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.11}
\]
and its right-handed version prove both Ore conditions. The Weyl algebra is a domain: the leading symbol of a product in its polynomial order filtration is the product of its nonzero polynomial leading symbols. Hence this denominator set has no zero divisors. As a right \(A\)-module the localization is the filtered union of the copies \(\tau^{-n}A\); each is free of rank one. Equivalently its transition maps, on copies of \(A\), are left multiplication by \(\tau\). Filtered colimits of exact vector-space/module sequences are exact. The localization is therefore right flat, and
\[
\begin{gathered}
A[\tau^{-1}]\otimes_A M=0\\
\Longleftrightarrow\\
\forall m\in M\ \exists k\ge0:\\
\tau^k m=0 .
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.12}
\]
The equivalence follows directly from equality of fractions in this torsion-free denominator system.

After localization replace AS.8 by
\[
 R_\tau=\mathbb C[u,z,y,\tau,\tau^{-1}]\,e .
 \tag{AS.13}
\]
The operator
\[
\begin{gathered}
L=\tau^{-1}\sum_j\partial_{z_j}\partial_{y_j},\\
C=\exp L .
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.14}
\]
is an actual finite sum on every polynomial in \(y\). Its inverse is \(\exp(-L)\); multiplication of these finite sums gives the identity by the binomial formula in each \(y\)-degree. No infinite analytic series or asymptotic argument is used. Since
\[
\begin{gathered}
{}[L,z_j\tau]=\partial_{y_j},\\
{}[L,\partial_{y_j}]=0 .
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.15}
\]
we have
\[
 C^{-1}T_j C=z_j\tau .
 \tag{AS.16}
\]
Apply \(C\) to each coefficient of every relative exterior degree. This is an isomorphism of the entire localized Spencer complex with the Koszul complex for \(z_1\tau,\ldots,z_d\tau\).

These form a regular sequence. Successively quotienting by its first terms leaves the polynomial ring in the unremoved \(z\)'s, \(u,y\), and the invertible variable \(\tau\); the next \(z_j\tau\) is not a zero divisor. The elementary induction on the two-term multiplication complexes therefore gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
H^k(Q[\tau^{-1}])=0\quad(k\ne0),\\
H^0(Q[\tau^{-1}])\\
=\mathbb C[u,y,\tau,\tau^{-1}]\,\gamma .
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.17}
\]
The induction proves exactness in all lower degrees, not just the top quotient. For \(d=0\), this statement is the identity of the empty Koszul complex.

#### AS.3. Every endpoint action and the exact diagonal map

Conjugation by \(C^{-1}\), followed by the top quotient in AS.17, gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
z_j=-\tau^{-1}\partial_{y_j},\\
D_{z_j}=y_j\tau,\quad D_w=\tau,\\
w=-\partial_\tau\\
+\tau^{-1}\left(\sum_j y_j\partial_{y_j}+d\right),\\
u_i=u_i,\quad D_{u_i}=\partial_{u_i}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.18}
\]
Here are checks of the two less immediate formulas. First
\(C^{-1}z_jC=z_j-\tau^{-1}\partial_{y_j}\) and
\(C^{-1}(\partial_{z_j}+y_j\tau)C=y_j\tau\).
For the time coordinate put \(E_z=\sum z_j\partial_{z_j}\) and
\(E_y=\sum y_j\partial_{y_j}\). Then
\[
\begin{gathered}
{}[L,w]\\
=-\tau^{-1}(E_z+E_y+d)\\
-\tau^{-1}L,\\
{}[L,[L,w]]\\
=-2\tau^{-1}L,\\
{}[L,[L,[L,w]]]=0,\\
C^{-1}wC=-z^{\mathsf T}y-\partial_\tau\\
+\tau^{-1}(E_z+E_y+d).
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.19}
\]
The terms with a left factor \(z_j\) vanish in the top quotient. This gives AS.18, including the constant \(+d\).

Let
\[
\begin{gathered}
\Delta_{\rm alg}=A/J_\Delta,\\
J_\Delta=Aw+\sum_jAz_j\\
+\sum_iAD_{u_i}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.20}
\]
be the diagonal closed-transfer module, with generator \(e_\Delta\). Its normal form after localization is
\(\mathbb C[u,\tau,\tau^{-1},\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_d]e_\Delta\),
where \(\nu_j=D_{z_j}\), \(w=-\partial_\tau\), and
\(z_j=-\partial_{\nu_j}\). The map
\[
 I\bigl(y^\alpha\tau^m\gamma\bigr)
 =\tau^{m-|\alpha|-d}\nu^\alpha e_\Delta
 \tag{AS.21}
\]
is a bijection of vector spaces and commutes with **every** endpoint generator. For instance the two \(w\)-actions both multiply the displayed monomial by
\(|\alpha|+d-m\) and lower its \(\tau\)-power by one. The \(z_j\)-actions both give
\(-\alpha_j\tau^{m-|\alpha|-d}\nu^{\alpha-e_j}e_\Delta\).
The \(D_{z_j}\)-actions raise both \(m\) and \(|\alpha|\) by one. The remaining actions are immediate from AS.18. Thus AS.21 is an actual localized Weyl-module isomorphism.

There is also a diagonal map before localization. In \(H^0Q\), relative derivatives give
\[
\begin{gathered}
z_j\tau\gamma=0,\\
(1+z_jy_j\tau)\gamma=0 .
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.22}
\]
The second relation means the relative derivative of \(y_je\), and the first that of \(e\). For \(d\ge1\), the class
\[
 a=\tau^d\gamma
 \tag{AS.23}
\]
is killed by every \(z_j\). Also
\[
\begin{gathered}
w\tau^d\gamma=-z^{\mathsf T}y\,\tau^d\gamma\\
-d\tau^{d-1}\gamma=0,\\
D_{u_i}a=0 .
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.24}
\]
The first equality uses AS.9 and the Weyl commutator; summing the second relation in AS.22, multiplied by \(\tau^{d-1}\), proves its last zero. When \(d=0\), \(F=w\), \(Q=\Delta_{\rm alg}\) in degree zero, and \(a=\gamma\) satisfies the same relations without a negative power. Therefore
\[
\begin{gathered}
j:\Delta_{\rm alg}\longrightarrow H^0Q,\\
j(e_\Delta)=a .
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.25}
\]
is a well-defined global differential-operator map in every dimension. Under AS.21 its localization is the identity on the distinguished diagonal generator. In particular \(a\ne0\).

The full endpoint relation \(D_u a=0\) is part of AS.25. It is the sum of the original endpoint derivatives at fixed normal difference, and not a relation omitting the simultaneous endpoint action.

An expression containing a middle variable \(y_j\) in this top quotient denotes the class of that displayed representative. Multiplication by \(y_j\) alone is not asserted to be an induced action on the quotient: it does not commute with \(T_j\). All endpoint operators used in AS.18 and AS.25 do commute with the relative differential.

#### AS.4. The opposite pole and the algebraic factorial

Retain the ordered relative density \(ds\wedge dy_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dy_d\); the surviving input density is held as an additional ordered coefficient block. The raw forward/opposite pair has poles \(f^{-1}\) and \(g^{-N}\). At fixed \(f,u,z,y\), \(D_{t'}=D_g=D_w\). Equation AS.2 and the determinant-one normal change in AS.1 give the exact convolution class
\[
\begin{gathered}
h=\\
\left[\frac{ds\wedge dy_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dy_d}
                    {f\,g^{d+1}}\right],\\
h\in H^0Q,\\
h=\frac{(-1)^d}{d!}\tau^d\gamma\\
=\frac{(-1)^d}{d!}\,j(e_\Delta).
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.26}
\]
The first bracket denotes the ordered normal-localization/Spencer class, rather than an integral of a function through its poles. The \(f\)-normal operator residue is \(+1\) by AS.6. No factor \(2\pi i\) is inserted into this operator residue. Thus the algebraically normalized class is
\[
 (-1)^d d!\,h=a .
 \tag{AS.27}
\]
This is an algebraic normalization in the explicit source roof AS.28–AS.29 below. The conversion of its solution frame and source counit to a prescribed microlocal convolution counit still has its own orientation and period factors.



#### A free source direction and derivative-torsion cones

The relative support complex and its signs are OCM.2–OCM.4. The product homotopy comparison for pulled-back bounded coefficients is HI.1. All assertions below are local in the base and in a nonzero cotangent chart.

##### FD.0. Product internal Hom

Let \(p:T\times I\to T\) be projection from an open real interval. For bounded complexes \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B\) on \(T\), the actual pullback/evaluation map is an isomorphism
\[
\begin{gathered}
p^{-1}R\mathcal Hom(\mathcal A,\mathcal B)\\
\longrightarrow\\
R\mathcal Hom(p^{-1}\mathcal A,p^{-1}\mathcal B).
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.1}
\]
To prove this, work on every product \(W\times J\), with \(J\) an open subinterval. Derived adjunction and HI.1 identify the right side's derived sections with
\[
\begin{gathered}
R\operatorname{Hom}_{W\times J}
       (p^{-1}\mathcal A,p^{-1}\mathcal B)\\
=R\operatorname{Hom}_{W}
       (\mathcal A,Rp_*p^{-1}\mathcal B)\\
=R\operatorname{Hom}_{W}(\mathcal A,\mathcal B).
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.2}
\]
The left side has exactly these sections by the same product projection comparison. The map FD.1 is this identity: the adjoint of pulled-back evaluation is evaluation after the unit \(\mathcal B\to Rp_*p^{-1}\mathcal B\).

The internal Hom can be unbounded above. It is bounded below, since its first input is bounded above and its second is bounded below. HI.1 extends to bounded-below inputs by good truncation: the cone of \(\tau_{\le n}K\to K\) is in \(D^{\ge n+1}\), and a right derived direct image is left t-exact. Thus every fixed degree is already determined by a bounded truncation. The same argument applies to derived sections on \(W\). It justifies the preceding use of product comparison without a bounded-Ext or finite-rank assumption on the target. Product rectangles are a basis. Passing to stalks in all degrees proves FD.1.

Successively applying FD.1 handles several real free coordinates. In particular a complex independent of one complex coordinate is independent of each of its two real coordinates in the derived internal Hom calculation.

##### FD.1. One free source direction

Suppose \(M=\mathbb R_r\times B\) locally and
\(\mathcal A=\operatorname{pr}_B^{-1}\mathcal A_0\), with \(\mathcal A_0\) bounded. If the real covector \(p\) does not annihilate the free vector \(\partial_r\), then, for every bounded complex \(\mathcal F\),
\[
 \mu\operatorname{hom}(\mathcal A,\mathcal F)_p=0.
 \tag{FD.3}
\]
This includes a complex manifold with a free real direction in a complex coordinate. The microlocal projection shift is the real dimension of \(M\); it has no effect on a vanishing assertion.

Here is the full relative-support argument. In the pair \((u,v)\), the first coefficient is pulled back from \(u\), and the source is pulled back from the \(B\)-coordinates of \(v\). By FD.1,
\[
\begin{gathered}
R\mathcal Hom(q_2^{-1}\mathcal A,q_1^{-1}\mathcal F)\\
\text{is pulled back independently}\\
\text{of }v_r .
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.4}
\]
Fix the central covector. Choose its sign and rescale the free vector so that the real polar functional is negative on that vector. Split the normal space as its line plus the central polar hyperplane. In coordinates \((a,b)\) for this split, the central positive polar functional is \(a\), while the \(a\)-line is the free source direction. The \(b\)-coordinates depend only on the quotient by that line. The coefficient FD.4 consequently remains independent of \(a\), even after this linear shear.

For a finite set of support representatives, strict polar separation and the compact unit normal-cone argument of IG.1 give a common later support
\[
\begin{gathered}
G_\eta=\{(a,b):a\le-\eta|b|\},\\
\eta>0,\\
D=U\times(-R,R)\times B_\rho,\\
H=D\cap(U\times G_\eta).
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.5}
\]
Indeed every vector in the finitely many original normal cones has a uniformly negative central polar coordinate. Its ratio \((-a)/|b|\), where the denominator is nonzero, is bounded below by a positive number. Choose smaller \(\eta\), then shrink the actual pair domain. Failure of actual containment would give a normalized limiting normal-cone vector violating that bound. The coordinate change preserves the diagonal and the free direction.

The cone in FD.5 has a strict polar margin:
\[
\begin{gathered}
-a\ge\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{1+\eta^2}}|(a,b)|,\\
(a,b)\in G_\eta\setminus0 .
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.6}
\]
A covector perturbation of norm less than half this positive constant retains half the margin, in these fixed coordinates. Thus one support is admissible on an actual open covector neighbourhood.

Fix \(c=R/2\). Keeping \(u,b\) fixed, the homotopy
\[
\begin{gathered}
h_s(u,a,b)\\
=(u,(1-s)a+sc,b),\\
0\le s\le1 .
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.7}
\]
stays in \(D\). It also stays in \(D\setminus H\) when it starts there: both endpoints satisfy \(a>-\eta|b|\), and that fibre is an interval. The common section \(a=c\) belongs to both opens.

Resolve the pulled-back coefficient of FD.4 by the real de Rham resolution tensored with that coefficient, exactly as in OCM.8. Homotopy FD.7 gives \(K_A,K_B\) on the whole domain and its complement, with
\[
\begin{gathered}
dK+Kd=j\varepsilon-1,\\
\varepsilon j=1,\\
\operatorname{res}K_A=K_B\operatorname{res},\\
\operatorname{res}j_A=j_B,\\
\varepsilon_B\operatorname{res}=\varepsilon_A .
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.8}
\]
For bounded-below coefficients apply this in each finite degree range. Only a bounded truncation of the coefficient enters a fixed range of the nonnegative de Rham resolution, so the same finite argument suffices. Scalar integration along compact paths is legitimate with arbitrary sheaf coefficients by OCM.2's finite local tensor expressions; there is no integration of an unspecified infinite-dimensional coefficient space.

For the relative differential \(d(a,b)=(da,\operatorname{res}a-db)\), define
\[
\begin{gathered}
T(a,b)=\\
\left(\begin{gathered}
j_A\varepsilon_Bb-K_Aa,\\
K_Bb
\end{gathered}\right).
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.9}
\]
Expanding FD.8 gives \(dT+Td=1\), with exactly the signs of OCM.11. It contracts the entire relative complex, including its complement entry. It does not extend a complement section across its support.

R.6–R.7 transfers every finite cycle, relation and primitive to the injective support model on a common later domain. Exact filtered colimits then prove FD.3. The margin FD.6 proves sheaf vanishing on a covector neighbourhood, rather than only at one covector.

For a complex free coordinate \(w\), a nonzero complex \(dw\)-component gives a real free vector on which the real polar functional is nonzero. Therefore
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathcal A=\mathbb C_{\mathbb C_w}\boxtimes\mathcal A_0\\
\Longrightarrow\\
\mu\operatorname{hom}(\mathcal A,\mathcal F)_p=0\\
\text{if }p(D_w)\ne0 .
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.10}
\]

##### FD.2. Polynomial derivative torsion is an actual free factor

Let \(A=A_B\otimes_\mathbb C A_1\) be a polynomial Weyl algebra, with \(A_1=\mathbb C\langle w,\tau\rangle/([\tau,w]-1)\). Let \(M\) be a finitely generated left \(A\)-module, and suppose its polynomial Ore localization at \(\tau\) is zero. By AS.12, \(\tau\) acts locally nilpotently on every vector of \(M\). Put \(K=\ker(\tau:M\to M)\). Define, on each vector, the finite sum
\[
 \Pi(m)=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-w)^k}{k!}\tau^k m .
 \tag{FD.11}
\]
The Weyl identity
\(\tau w^k=w^k\tau+kw^{k-1}\)
makes consecutive terms cancel, so \(\tau\Pi(m)=0\). Also \(\Pi(k)=k\) on \(K\). The exact finite Taylor identity is
\[
 m=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{w^j}{j!}\Pi(\tau^jm).
 \tag{FD.12}
\]
For the coefficient of \(w^n\tau^n m\) in the right side, the finite binomial sum is
\(\sum_{j=0}^n(-1)^{n-j}/(j!(n-j)!)\), equal to one for \(n=0\) and zero otherwise. This proves FD.12 without a completion.

Multiplication induces an isomorphism
\[
 \mathbb C[w]\otimes_\mathbb C K\xrightarrow{\sim}M .
 \tag{FD.13}
\]
Surjectivity is FD.12. For injectivity, apply \(\Pi\tau^r\) to a finite relation \(\sum_{j=0}^r w^j k_j=0\). Its top coefficient gives \(r!k_r=0\). Descending on \(r\) gives every \(k_j=0\). The \(A_B\)-action commutes with \(w,\tau,\Pi\), so FD.13 is an \(A\)-module map; \(\tau\) becomes ordinary differentiation on the polynomial factor.

Moreover \(K\) is finitely generated over \(A_B\). Choose finitely many \(A\)-generators \(m_i\) of \(M\). Their Taylor coefficients \(\Pi\tau^j m_i\), with \(j\) below the respective nilpotence bounds, form a finite set. If \(K'\) is their \(A_B\)-span, then \(\mathbb C[w]\otimes K'\) is an \(A\)-submodule containing all \(m_i\); it is \(M\). The injectivity in FD.13 shows \(K'=K\). The polynomial Weyl algebra \(A_B\) is Noetherian by its good symbol filtration and polynomial Noetherianity, as proved in the differential-operator lesson, so this finite module is coherent.

Sheafifying on the affine space gives the genuine external product
\[
 M^\sim=\mathcal O_{\mathbb A^1_w}\boxtimes K^\sim .
 \tag{FD.14}
\]
No local nilpotence assertion is made after multiplication by arbitrary rational or analytic coefficient germs. The global polynomial Taylor calculation is what produces this external product.

If \(M^\sim\) is regular holonomic, \(K^\sim\) is regular holonomic. For the embedding \(i:B\to\mathbb A^1_w\times B\) at \(w=0\), the unshifted transfer inverse of FD.14 is exactly \(K^\sim\), by the transfer tensor with its locally free polynomial factor. In the programme's extraordinary convention this is \(i^!M^\sim[1]\). Algebraic regular inverse stability and shift stability therefore apply. The unshifted solution complex is
\[
\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{Sol}(M^\sim)\\
=\mathbb C_{\mathbb C_w}\boxtimes
                    \operatorname{Sol}(K^\sim).
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.15}
\]
This map can be checked directly by the one-variable connection Spencer resolution, whose holomorphic derivative complex has kernel the constants and zero higher local cohomology, tensored with a finite operator resolution in the other coordinates. Equivalently it is the actual solution exterior comparison in the Riemann–Hilbert lesson. There is no relative dimension shift in unshifted solutions of this free connection factor.

Combining FD.10 and FD.15 proves
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mu\operatorname{hom}(\operatorname{Sol}M,\mathcal F)_p=0\\
\text{for }p(D_w)\ne0 .
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.16}
\]
for every bounded target \(\mathcal F\). A bounded complex whose coherent cohomology modules have zero polynomial \(\tau\)-localization has the same property: its finitely many truncation triangles, the contravariant solution functor and exactness of microlocal Hom in its source give the assertion. This proves the precise vanishing for both actual comparison cones AS.28, with no appeal to whole-real scalar-change flatness or to general analytic proper-image regularity.



#### AS.5. The two comparison cones

The finite global-module assertion used here follows from the coherent-generator lemma in the adjunctions lesson. A coherent operator module on an affine space has a coherent structure-sheaf subsheaf generating it. That subsheaf is generated by finitely many global sections, by the affine module–sheaf correspondence. These same sections generate the operator module over its global polynomial Weyl algebra. Exact affine sections on quasi-coherent structure-sheaf modules compute both kernels and cohomology. This applies to every coherent cohomology sheaf of \(Q\).

Let \(\pi:Q\to H^0Q\) be the actual truncation map. The complex \(Q\) is in degrees \([-d,0]\), so this is the usual canonical map to its degree-zero cohomology object. The algebraic proper-coherence argument above makes all its cohomology modules finitely generated over \(A\). AS.17 and exactness of Ore localization show that every cohomology module of \(\operatorname{Cone}(\pi)\) is killed by localization. The same is true for the kernel and cokernel of AS.25, by AS.21. Hence both comparison cones have bounded coherent cohomology with locally nilpotent global \(\tau\)-action:
\[
\begin{gathered}
Q\xrightarrow{\pi}H^0Q\xleftarrow{j}\Delta_{\rm alg},\\
H^k\operatorname{Cone}(\pi)[\tau^{-1}]=0,\\
H^k\operatorname{Cone}(j)[\tau^{-1}]=0 .
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.28}
\]
The derivative-torsion lemma FD.2 proves, without a microlocal proper-image theorem, that each such module is a polynomial free time factor tensored with a coherent module on the other coordinates. Its unshifted analytic solution complex is therefore pulled back independently of \(w\). The free-source-direction theorem then annihilates the microlocal Hom from that solution complex at every covector with nonzero \(dw\)-component, for every bounded target complex.

Write \(\operatorname{Sol}M=R\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal D^{an}}(M^{an},\mathcal O)\), unshifted. Finite truncation triangles for the two cones in AS.28 give isomorphisms
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mu\operatorname{hom}(\operatorname{Sol}Q,\mathcal F)_p\\
\Big\downarrow\\
\mu\operatorname{hom}(\operatorname{Sol}H^0Q,\mathcal F)_p\\
\Big\uparrow\\
\mu\operatorname{hom}(\operatorname{Sol}\Delta_{\rm alg},\mathcal F)_p,\\
p(D_w)\ne0 .
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.29}
\]
These maps are induced by the two actual maps AS.28, with their contravariance accounted for twice. They are not chosen identifications of ranks. The closed normal Spencer calculation identifies
\(\operatorname{Sol}\Delta_{\rm alg}=\mathbb C_\Delta[-N]\)
in its specified ordered normal solution frame.

#### AS.6. Evaluation in this exact roof

A global degree-zero relative Spencer cocycle representing \(h\) gives a map \(b:\mathcal D_{\rm end}\to Q\) in the operator derived category. It exists directly in the affine relative Spencer model; the source global Weyl module is free of rank one. Its composite with \(\pi\) is the section \(h\) of \(H^0Q\). Write \(b_\Delta:\mathcal D_{\rm end}\to\Delta_{\rm alg}\) for \(1\mapsto e_\Delta\). The equality of actual module sections in AS.26 is
\[
 \pi b=\frac{(-1)^d}{d!}\,j b_\Delta .
 \tag{AS.30}
\]
Applying the contravariant solution functor gives equality of the corresponding ordinary evaluation maps. Applying the natural map from ordinary derived Hom to its microlocal Hom and using AS.29 preserves that equality. Consequently, under the precise roof AS.29, the ordinary convolution class \(h\) evaluates to
\[
\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{ev}(h)\\
=\frac{(-1)^d}{d!}\operatorname{ev}(e_\Delta).
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.31}
\]
This includes the entire target coefficient complex: it is functoriality of the actual morphism AS.30, and not a comparison on a selected normal component.

In AS.31, \(\operatorname{ev}\) denotes ordinary solution evaluation followed by its natural microlocal Hom map and transport through AS.29. The right-hand class is the raw ordered diagonal evaluation, with no normalized period factor inserted.

AS.31 concerns the ordinary algebraic direct-image section and the source roof AS.28. The canonical microlocal composition comparison and intrinsic diagonal-unit normalization are proved in §5.67, using the specialization, exterior-product and proper-trace maps and the ordered normal period. Neither identity follows from AS.17 or AS.25 alone. The localization and source-roof statements above do not require faithful flatness of the whole real kernel ring.

#### AS.7. The opposite order and its separate spatial sign

Use endpoints \((s,y),(s',y')\), middle variables \((t,x)\), and put
\[
\begin{gathered}
u'=(s,y),\quad w'=s'-s,\\
z'=y'-y,\quad Y=-x,\\
a=t-s-y^{\mathsf T}Y,\\
b=s'-t+(y')^{\mathsf T}Y,\\
a+b=w'+(z')^{\mathsf T}Y .
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.32}
\]
The polynomial reflection \(x=-Y\) extends to the projective middle compactification. Consequently every properness, coherence, normal-form and torsion-cone assertion above applies to this order as well. Let \(\tau'=D_{w'}\), and let \(\gamma'\) be AS.7 with the normal sum in AS.32 and the ordered \(Y\)-density. There is an actual map
\[
\begin{gathered}
j':\Delta'_{\rm alg}\longrightarrow H^0Q',\\
j'(e_{\Delta'})=(\tau')^d\gamma' .
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.33}
\]
Both maps of its analogue of AS.28 have the vanishing comparison cones FD.16 on \(p(D_{w'})\ne0\).

The raw poles in this order are \(a^{-d-1}b^{-1}\): the high pole is now on the first normal coordinate. At fixed \(b\), changing the first coordinate to \((a,F'=a+b)\) replaces its derivative by \(D_a^{\rm new}+D_{F'}\). These commute. In their \(d\)-th power, every term with a positive \(D_a^{\rm new}\)-power has zero first-normal residue by AS.6. Only \(D_{F'}^d\) remains. Equation AS.2 therefore gives the same factor \((-1)^d/d!\) before the spatial reflection.

Write \(\eta_x=dt\wedge dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_d\) and \(\eta_Y=dt\wedge dY_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dY_d\) for the two ordered middle densities. Their relation is
\[
\eta_x=(-1)^d\eta_Y .
\tag{AS.34}
\]
Thus, with that actual density, the opposite raw class is
\[
\begin{gathered}
h'=\\
\left[\frac{dt\wedge dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_d}
                       {a^{d+1}b}\right],\\
h'\in H^0Q',\\
h'=\frac{1}{d!}(\tau')^d\gamma'
\\
=\frac1{d!}j'(e_{\Delta'}).
\end{gathered}
\tag{AS.35}
\]
In this formula the surviving input density remains in its original ordered block. The only coordinate reflection used is the displayed middle spatial block. The sign in AS.34 is independent of the positive first-normal operator residue. The opposite source roof therefore identifies its ordinary evaluation with \(1/d!\) times its own raw ordered diagonal evaluation. These two explicit algebraic factors do not silently fix the separate microlocal source-counit and normalized-period conversions described after AS.31.
