### 5.82. Common-domain continuation of actual holonomic function solutions

Let \(X=\mathbf C_t\times\mathbf C_x^n\), let
\(q_0=(0,0)\), and let \(p_0=(q_0;1,0)\).
Let \(M\) be a coherent actual finite-order
microlocal module whose reduced support \(A\)
is a homogeneous analytic Lagrangian in generic
position:
\[
\begin{gathered}
A\cap\pi^{-1}(q_0)=\mathbf C^\times p_0.
\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.1}
\]
All statements concern the whole module,
including its principal nilpotents and
intersecting characteristic branches.
Write \(S=\pi(A)\) on a sufficiently small
base neighbourhood.

We use the directional function module
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathcal C=\underset{V,Z}{\operatorname{colim}}
 H_Z^1(V;\mathcal O),\\
C_0(Z)\subset\{\operatorname{Re}t\ge0\}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.2}
\]
Here \(V\) is an ordinary neighbourhood of
zero, \(Z\) is relatively closed, and
\(C_0(Z)\) consists of limits of positive
rescalings of points of \(Z\) tending to zero.
The support condition includes the zero
vector. There is no growth condition on a
holomorphic representative at its open
boundary.

**Theorem CF.1.** Let
\(\Phi:M_{p_0}\to\mathcal C\) be an actual
\(\mathscr E_{p_0}\)-linear map.
For any finite list \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\) and
holomorphic representatives of
\(\Phi(s_1),\ldots,\Phi(s_m)\), there is one
ordinary neighbourhood \(V\) of zero on
which all these representatives continue
as multivalued holomorphic functions on
\(V\setminus S\).
A branch of each continuation agrees with
its prescribed representative on a smaller
admissible negative domain.
For finitely many maps \(\Phi\), the same
neighbourhood can be used.

Multivalued means analytic continuation
along every path from a fixed initial germ,
with equality along homotopic paths with
fixed endpoints. Finite determination and
faithful evaluation are separate assertions.
They are not hypotheses or conclusions of
this theorem.

The actual lattice, full factorial norms
and finite-head division used below are
§5.32, J.1–J.3
and
§5.55, DP.1–DP.4.
The complete canonical support action and
convex Dolbeault proof are
§5.43
and
§5.80, CP.A.
The primitive normalization is
§5.33, K.2
and its actual supported comparison in
§5.53, AM.B.

#### CF.A. Convex representatives and the full directional action

Put \(r=\operatorname{Re}t\) and
\(z=(\operatorname{Im}t,x)\), with
\(|z|=|\operatorname{Im}t|+|x|\).
For each \(a>0\), put
\[
G_a=\{(r,z):r\le-a|z|\}.
\tag{CF.3}
\]
Every support in CF.2 is locally contained
in a larger admissible support whose
complement is convex and invariant under
\(G_a\).

Indeed, on its negative-\(r\) part,
\((-r)/|z|\) tends uniformly to zero.
Failure would give, by normalizing a
sequence and taking a unit-sphere
subsequence, a tangent vector with
negative \(r\).
The same argument excludes points with
\(z=0,r<0\) sufficiently near zero.
Choose a continuous nondecreasing modulus
\(\omega(s)\to0\) such that
\[
\begin{gathered}-r\le |z|\omega(|z|),\\
\text{on }Z\cap\{r<0\}.\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.4}
\]
For completeness, first bound the ratio
on shrinking punctured balls by its
supremum. Choose radii where this bound
is below \(2^{-k}\), and interpolate
monotonically above the bound using
the preceding radius. This gives the
stated continuous majorant.
Define
\[
\begin{gathered}
\phi(s)=\int_0^{2s}\omega(v)\,dv,\\
Z'=\{r\ge-\phi(|z|)\}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.5}
\]
The function \(\phi\) is convex,
nondecreasing, dominates \(s\omega(s)\),
and is \(o(s)\). On a small interval it
has Lipschitz constant \(L<a\).
Extend it linearly beyond that interval
with the final slope when necessary.
The set \(Z'\) contains \(Z\) locally,
has the required tangent cone, and has
convex complement. For \(s\ge a|w|\),
\[
\begin{gathered}r-s+\phi(|z+w|)\\
\le r+\phi(|z|)-s+L|w|<0\\
\text{if }r+\phi(|z|)<0.\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.6}
\]
Thus its complement is \(G_a\)-open.

This construction also supplies the
compact cap needed for the actual
operator action. Let
\(\Omega=B_\epsilon+G_a\), using the
sum norm for the ball.
For \(b+(-s,w)\in Z'\cap\Omega\),
the inequalities
\(r\le\epsilon-s\),
\(|z|\le\epsilon+s/a\), and
\(r\ge-L|z|\) give
\[
(1-L/a)s\le(1+L)\epsilon.
\tag{CF.7}
\]
Consequently the closed carrier is
contained in a fixed constant times
this small ball. Choose \(\epsilon\)
so its closure is compact in the
coefficient domain and the original
ordinary neighbourhood.
Both \(\Omega\) and \(\Omega\setminus Z'\)
are convex and cone-open.

The full convex Dolbeault vanishing
of CP.A and DLH gives, by the
ordinary support triangle,
\[
\begin{gathered}
H_{Z'}^k(\Omega;\mathcal O)=0\quad(k\ne1),\\
H_{Z'}^1(\Omega;\mathcal O)\\
=\mathcal O(\Omega\setminus Z')/
                    \mathcal O(\Omega).
\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.8}
\]
The degree-zero group vanishes by
the identity theorem. Ordinary
excision transfers a class from
the original neighbourhood to
this completion, since the closed
carrier is compact in their overlap.
It follows that CF.2 consists
precisely of these actual function
classes. A class is zero exactly
when, after one refinement, its
representative extends holomorphically
to an ordinary neighbourhood of zero.
Any finite family of classes and
equalities admits one common refinement.

The full real kernel representatives
of AM.H have strict negative pairing
with \(dt\) on their nonzero normal
cones. Compactness of the unit normal
cone puts any finite family in one
carrier \(G_a\), after shrinking.
If no such actual containment held,
normalizing the failing points would
contradict that strict pairing.
DL.6–DLG.7 acts on the cone-closed
supports just constructed, with the
common cap CF.7. Its cup, excision
and normalized trace comparisons
identify refinements and both products.
Taking the filtered colimit gives
the whole real kernel action on
\(\mathcal C\). Restriction along
the proved inclusions
\(\mathscr E\to\mathscr E^\infty
\to\mathscr E^{\mathbb R}\)
gives the action used in the theorem.
No map from an arbitrary canonical
kernel to a finite symbol is asserted.

In particular, for a coefficient
depending only on \(x\), the actual
action of \(h^k=D_t^{-k}\) on a
representative is, modulo a
holomorphic germ,
\[
\begin{gathered}h^k f(t,x)=\\
\int_A^t\frac{(t-s)^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}f(s,x)\,ds,\\
k\ge1.\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.9}
\]
The path lies initially in the convex
negative domain. This is exactly the
positive primitive normalization of
K.2 and its supported AM.B comparison.
In the quotient \(hD_t=1\), because
the omitted initial value is
holomorphic on the full neighbourhood.

#### CF.B. Finite coefficient modules from an isolated principal fibre

Choose the actual \(h\)-injective
lattice \(M_0\subset M\) of J.1,
and set \(L=M_0/hM_0\).
The following variant of the finite
division argument is useful:
\[
\begin{gathered}
\dim_{\mathbf C}L/(x)L<\infty\\
\Longrightarrow
M_0=\sum_{j=1}^q R_0u_j,\\
R_0=\left\{\begin{gathered}
\sum_{k\ge0}a_k(x)h^k:\\
 |a_k|_K\le BC^k k!
\end{gathered}\right\}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.10}
\]
Every coefficient list has one common
holomorphic parameter domain.

Here is why the weaker premise suffices.
In DP.5 take the normal variables
\(v=(t,\xi/\tau)\). The specialized
principal relation module has quotient
\(L/(x)L\). Each normal coordinate
acts nilpotently on this finite local
quotient: a nonzero eigenvalue would
contradict invertibility of that
coordinate minus the eigenvalue.
Their commuting actions therefore
make a power of \((v)\) annihilate
the quotient. The specialized head
diagram has finite complement.

Lift its finitely many minimal heads
to actual relations. The principal
kernel equality is obtained by
subtracting \(h\) times a lift of
the image divided by \(h\).
Use precisely the hierarchical
normal radii, component weights,
parameter shrink and positive-index
shrink in DP.7–DP.11.
They give its two one-eighth error
bounds on one domain. For a time
head the complete correction is
\[
\begin{gathered}
Q\circ(t^az^\beta)-Qt^az^\beta\\
=\sum_{j=1}^a\binom aj
 (\partial_\tau^jQ)t^{a-j}z^\beta.
\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.11}
\]
The weighted coefficient inverse
of the head map has norm at most
one, and the total error has norm
at most one quarter.
Its Neumann solution therefore
converges with norm at most
four thirds of the input norm,
as in DP.12–DP.14.
The finite inverse-ordering formula
DP.16 converts its ordinary remainder
to actual coefficient products.
This proves CF.10 for every germ,
with the full factorial bound.
No formal specialization of \(h\)
has been used.

The same argument with \(h\) absent
proves the ordinary finite-fibre
lemma for coherent analytic modules:
an isolated finite principal fibre
over the base makes the module finite
over the base germ ring.
The head projections, radius choices,
geometric inverse and finite remainder
are the preceding argument with its
positive-index terms removed.
Apply it first to the variables
\(z=\xi/\tau\), using J.3.
Thus \(L\) is finite over
\(\mathcal O_{t,x}\).

This also proves the required local
finite projection of its support.
The algebra
\(\mathcal O_{t,x,z}/\operatorname{Ann}L\)
injects into
\(\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O_{t,x}}L\).
The latter is finite: a finite
presentation embeds this Hom into
a finite power of the finite module
\(L\), and the coefficient ring is
Noetherian. Hence the support algebra
is finite over the base.
Its normal coordinates satisfy monic
equations and are nilpotent on the
central finite fibre. Their roots
therefore stay in a compact smaller
normal polydisc after shrinking the
base. This gives properness of this
local finite projection.
The image is exactly the analytic
support of \(L\) as a base module.
For example, on a nonzero fibre
the commuting normal-coordinate
matrices have a simultaneous
eigencharacter: take an eigenspace
of one, restrict the others, and
repeat. It supplies a point of
the fibre support. The converse
is immediate by restriction.
The minor test for a finite
base presentation shows that
this image \(S\) is analytic.

Finite integrality preserves
component dimensions, as in
the finite-projection proof of
analytic dimension, Theorem 5.4.
Thus \(S\) is a pure
\(n\)-dimensional germ in
\(\mathbf C^{n+1}\).
It has a reduced hypersurface
equation. One direct verification
uses factoriality of the analytic
germ ring, proved in
The local ring of holomorphic germs, §3.
Factor any nonzero equation
vanishing on \(S\).
Each irreducible component of
\(S\) lies in one irreducible
factor hypersurface. Their
dimensions agree; strict inclusion
would lower dimension by
Proposition 5.5 of the dimension
lesson. The reduced product
of the selected factors defines
exactly \(S\).

#### CF.C. Spanning ordinary linear fibrations

Let \(f\) be that reduced equation,
with first nonzero homogeneous part
\(f_m\). Choose a vector \(v_0\)
with \(f_m(v_0)\ne0\) and
\(p_0(v_0)\ne0\), and normalize
\(p_0(v_0)=1\).
The excluded vectors are zeros
of two nonzero polynomials,
so they do not fill the vector
space. Take \(v_0\) as the time
axis and a basis \(e_1,\ldots,e_n\)
of \(\ker p_0\) as spatial axes.
For sufficiently small nonzero
\(\lambda\), put
\[
\begin{gathered}v_j=v_0-\lambda e_j,\\
1\le j\le n,\\
 F_0(t,x)=x,\\
F_j(t,x)=x+\lambda t e_j.\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.12}
\]
All \(f_m(v_j)\) remain nonzero.
Each vertical line meets \(S\)
only at zero locally.
The \(n+1\) vertical directions
span the ambient tangent space:
\[
\begin{gathered}\left|\det(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_n)\right|\\
=|\lambda|^n.\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.13}
\]
Moreover \(p_0(v_j)=1\).

For each \(F_j\), the normalized
support over its central fibre
is isolated: its base point must
be zero, and CF.1 then fixes its
normalized covector.
The analytic Nullstellensatz and
the finite-monomial argument of
J.3 give the finite-dimensional
principal fibre in CF.10.
Thus the whole actual module is
finite over its coefficient ring
\(R_{0,j}\) in every fibration.

These are ordinary linear
coordinate changes. Their finite,
infinite and real actions and
inverse maps are proved in
§5.56, BCT.5.3.
They keep \(t\) unchanged.
Consequently they keep the
directional tangent condition
in CF.2 unchanged. The full
normal derivative changes by
an elliptic order-zero factor
times the old derivative;
its inverse has the compatible
actual action.
All finite lists and their
relations can be represented
on one common refinement.

In these directions preparation
of \(f\) gives a monic
Weierstrass equation
\(p_j(t,x)=0\).
Its coefficient orders and
the elementary root bound give
\(|t|\le C_j|x|\) on \(S\)
in this fibration.
The exact preparation proof
is
AG-QC, §2;
the coefficient orders and root
bound are
analytic parametrization, Lemma 2.1 and Proposition 2.2.
The discriminant \(H_j\) is proper:
the reduced polynomial is
square-free over the coefficient
fraction field in characteristic
zero. Its resultant with its
derivative is therefore nonzero.
Off \(H_j\), its roots are
distinct holomorphic graphs by
the implicit-function proof
in AG-QC, Lemma 2.2.

#### CF.D. A rectangular Volterra equation with the exact support

Fix one fibration.
Choose \(u_1,\ldots,u_q\) lifting
a basis of \(L/(x)L\).
They generate \(L\) over
\(\mathcal O_x\). They also
generate \(M_0\) over \(R_0\):
express a finite generating list
modulo \(h\) in their lifts,
and invert the finite matrix
\(I-hC\) by DP.20.
Use coefficient rows and the
generator column \(u\).
There is an actual matrix
\[
tu=T(x,h)u.
\tag{CF.14}
\]
A row relation \(a\) means
\(au=0\).
Take a finite presentation
of \(L\) over \(\mathcal O_x\).
Every principal relation row
lifts to an actual \(R_0\)-row
relation: divide its image
in \(hM_0\) by \(h\), express
the quotient in the same
generators, and subtract \(h\)
times those coefficients.
Denote the finite lifted
matrix by \(a(x,h)\).

Put \(T_0=T\bmod h\) and
\(a_0=a\bmod h\).
The matrix \(T_0(0)\) is
nilpotent: it is the action
of \(t\) on the finite local
fibre with basis \(u\bmod(x,h)\).
The rectangular matrix
\[
B_0(t,x)=
\begin{pmatrix}tI-T_0(x)\\ a_0(x)\end{pmatrix}
\tag{CF.15}
\]
has full column rank at every
point outside \(S\).

To prove this exact assertion,
evaluate a coefficient row
\(\sum_{m\ge0}c_m(x)t^m\)
as \(\sum_m c_m(x)T_0(x)^m\).
Choose a weighted basis making
the norm of the nilpotent
\(T_0(0)\) arbitrarily small,
then shrink \(x\). The series
converges normally on smaller
products. The identity
\[
\begin{gathered}
t^mI-T_0^m\\
=(tI-T_0)\sum_{b=0}^{m-1}
                       t^{m-1-b}T_0^b
\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.16}
\]
has a normally summable
coefficient-series version.
The principal relation rows
are stable under \(T_0\),
because \(t\) acts on \(L\).
Evaluation therefore identifies
the base-module cokernel of
CF.15 with \(L\) as a base
module. These are finite
coherent base presentations.
Their germ isomorphism and
its inverse extend to one
smaller base neighbourhood:
extend the finitely many
images of generators, their
relation identities and the
two composition identities,
as in J.1. Its support is exactly
\(S\), by CF.B. At a base
point, a finite presentation
has zero cokernel precisely
when its value is onto, by
finite commutative Nakayama.
Equivalently CF.15 has full
column rank there. This proves
the claim without inverting
a transverse parameter minor.

All entries of the positive
\(h\)-parts have one factorial
estimate. Their kernels are
\[
\begin{gathered}K_A(t,s,x)=\\
\sum_{k\ge1}A_k(x)\frac{(t-s)^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}.\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.17}
\]
If \(|A_k|\le BC^kk!\), their
absolute sum is at most
\[
\frac{BC}{(1-C|t-s|)^2}.
\tag{CF.18}
\]
Thus they and every fixed
derivative converge normally
on one smaller two-time
product with \(C|t-s|<1\).
The finite list permits a
single such product.
Stack the kernels of \(-T\)
and \(+a\), with their zero
coefficients omitted, to
obtain the rectangular kernel
\(K\).

Let \(f\) be the column of
representatives of \(\Phi(u)\).
The finite relation residuals
are zero in \(\mathcal C\).
By CF.A they extend as
holomorphic functions near
zero. The actual primitive
comparison gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
B_0(t,x)f(t,x)\\
{}+\int_A^t K(t,s,x)f(s,x)\,ds\\
=g(t,x).
\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.19}
\]
Here \(g\) is holomorphic on
one full product, including
the initial slice \(t=A\).

That last domain assertion
requires choosing the anchor
twice. Begin with an anchor
\(A_0<0\) in the common convex
representative domain.
The finitely many residuals
extend near zero, possibly
to a time disc not containing
\(A_0\). Choose a new negative
\(A\) inside that disc.
The difference of the two
primitive formulas is the
integral over the fixed
compact path from \(A_0\)
to \(A\). Its output and
parameter dependence is
holomorphic on the whole
new product, by CF.17 and
the original representative
along that path.
Subtract this memory correction
from the extended residual.
This gives CF.19 with \(A\)
inside its full domain.
Shrink the transverse ball
so \((A,x)\) lies in the
initial domain and every
root of \(p_j\) lies in
\(|t|<|A|/4\).

#### CF.E. Every path outside one vertical discriminant

Suppose a branch is known
along a compact vertical path
from \(A\) to \(a\), avoiding
\(S\). Its old memory
\[
\begin{gathered}I_{\mathrm{old}}(t,x)=\\
\int_{A\rightsquigarrow a}K(t,s,x)f(s,x)\,ds.\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.20}
\]
is holomorphic in the new
output \(t\) and in nearby
parameters. At \(a\), choose
a nonzero square minor of
CF.15 and obtain a holomorphic
left inverse \(J\) of \(B_0\).
In the following formula, the arguments
\(t,x\) of \(J,g,I_{\mathrm{old}},b\)
are suppressed in the first two rows, and
\(H(t,s,x)=J(t,x)K(t,s,x)\).
On a small disc the new
branch solves
\[
\begin{gathered}H=JK,\\
b=J(g-I_{\mathrm{old}}),\\
 f(t,x)=b(t,x)\\
{}-\int_a^t H(t,s,x)f(s,x)\,ds.\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.21}
\]
If the last kernel is bounded
by \(L\), its \(k\)-fold
successive integral has bound
\[
\frac{L^k|t-a|^k}{k!}.
\tag{CF.22}
\]
Parametrize each integration
by the ordered real simplex
in a complex segment; its
volume is \(1/k!\), by
successive elementary integration.
The series therefore converges
normally and solves CF.21.
The same bound for a difference
proves uniqueness.
All bounds are uniform on a
smaller parameter compact,
so the solution is jointly
holomorphic.

Every rectangular row of
CF.19 still holds. Its
residual is holomorphic and
zero on the open overlap
with the preceding branch.
The identity theorem makes
it zero on the whole
connected product. A finite
disc cover thus continues
the branch along every
vertical path in the punctured
time disc.

Off the discriminant \(H_j\),
the punctured time discs are
locally topologically trivial,
with \(A\) fixed.
Here is an explicit construction.
At a parameter value choose
disjoint small discs about
the distinct roots, away
from \(A\) and the boundary.
Choose smooth cutoffs equal
to one near their centres.
Translate each root by its
cutoff times its small
displacement. The resulting
map is the identity plus
a perturbation with Lipschitz
constant less than one.
The iteration \(y=w-\delta(y)\)
converges geometrically to
its unique inverse. It
therefore gives the required
homeomorphism, fixing the
boundary and \(A\).

A path in
\[
X\setminus\bigl(S\cup F_j^{-1}(H_j)\bigr)
\tag{CF.23}
\]
has a finite cover by these
trivializations. Transport
the vertical memory path
through that cover.
Its actual holomorphic
formulas use fixed compact
contour pieces on each
smaller parameter neighbourhood,
where those pieces still
avoid \(S\), together with
small holomorphic endpoint
segments. CF.20–CF.22 prove
joint holomorphy there.
The cutoff motion is used
only to identify contour
classes, not as a
holomorphic formula.
This proves continuation
along every path of CF.23.

We recall explicitly the
path-homotopy argument.
An analytic continuation
is a chain of holomorphic
germs agreeing on nonempty
overlaps. Uniqueness is
the identity theorem on
small balls. For a fixed
path its finitely many
overlap balls also support
all sufficiently close
paths, with the same
endpoint germ. Subdivide
a homotopy square into
finitely many rectangles
inside such overlap
neighbourhoods. The two
edge continuations around
each rectangle agree.
Successively cancelling
interior edges proves
equality at the endpoint
for the two boundary paths.
This proves fixed-endpoint
homotopy invariance and
applies to every continuation
constructed here.

#### CF.F. All branches and all fibrations

Put \(D_j=F_j^{-1}(H_j)\).
The common bad set
\[
Z=\bigcap_{j=0}^n D_j
\tag{CF.24}
\]
has complex codimension at
least two. Otherwise an
irreducible hypersurface
component \(T\) of \(Z\)
is a component of every
\(D_j\). Each \(D_j\) is
invariant along its constant
vertical direction \(v_j\).
At a regular point of \(T\)
away from the other finitely
many components of all
\(D_j\), each \(v_j\) is
therefore tangent to \(T\).
Such a point exists because
a proper analytic subset
of an irreducible component
has smaller dimension.
CF.13 contradicts the
dimension of its tangent
space. For \(n=0\) the
bad transverse set is
empty.

Fix one of the prescribed
elements \(s\). In each
fibration choose \(N\)
with \(h_j^Ns\in M_0\),
and adjoin this element
to its finite coefficient
generators.
Express the \(t\)-action
on the added generator
using the original ones.
The enlarged \(T_0(0)\)
is block triangular with
the old nilpotent block
and a zero redundant
diagonal block.
The principal presentation
still presents \(L\).
Thus the same argument
continues a representative
of \(\Phi(h_j^Ns)\).
Apply \(D_{t,j}^N\) to
recover a representative
of \(\Phi(s)\).
Its difference from the
prescribed representative
is holomorphic near zero,
by CF.8. Add this ordinary
holomorphic germ back
on a common smaller
neighbourhood.
The continuations from
all fibrations now agree
with exactly the same
initial scalar germ.

Choose one ordinary ball
\(V\) inside all their
finitely many product
domains. A sufficiently
narrow negative cone
misses \(S\), by the
linear root bound in CF.C.
It contains an initial
point outside every
\(D_j\), since finitely
many proper analytic
sets cannot fill an open.
Write \(M'=V\setminus S\).

Agreement of one initial
branch alone does not
justify gluing all branches.
The required path argument
is as follows.
A path in \(M'\setminus Z\)
has a finite cover by balls,
each missing one \(D_j\).
Choose its intermediate
overlap points outside
all the \(D_j\).
Inside one such ball,
two of these points can
be joined while avoiding
all the other \(D_k\):
the complex line through
them is not contained in
their union, so its
intersection with that
union is discrete.
A compact line segment
meets only finitely many
of these points after
choosing a slightly
larger segment domain;
small planar detours
avoid them.
This new path is homotopic
to the old segment in
the original ball,
which misses the selected
\(D_j\).

Inductively the continuation
arriving at an overlap can
be reached along a path
avoiding every \(D_k\).
The next fibration therefore
continues precisely that
branch; CF.E and its
homotopy argument identify
the two paths through
the ball. This proves
continuation of every
branch along every path
in \(M'\setminus Z\).

#### CF.G. Removal of the codimension-two intersection

We give the two local
facts required to cross
\(Z\setminus S\), without
a boundedness assumption.

An analytic subset of
complex dimension at
most \(N-2\) has a
countable cover by
Lipschitz images of real
boxes of dimension at
most \(2N-4\), where
\(N=n+1\).
To see this, use
local parametrization, Theorem 4.1
on its finitely many
irreducible local components.
The generic-sheet part
is a smooth manifold.
Its remaining analytic
part has smaller dimension
by Proposition 5.5.
Repeat on that part;
dimension decreases at
each repetition.
Countable coordinate
charts and compact
subcharts yield the
claimed Lipschitz cover.
The finite component
decomposition follows
directly from Noetherianity:
a nonprime radical ideal
splits its zero set
using \(ab\) in the
ideal but neither factor
in it; Noetherian
induction terminates
these proper splittings.

Let \(B\) be a small
convex ball disjoint
from \(S\).
Every loop in \(B\setminus Z\)
contracts there.
First approximate it by
a polygonal loop within
its positive compact
distance from \(Z\).
Fill that loop by its
Lipschitz cone in \(B\).
Perturb the filling \(F\)
by \(\beta v\), where
\(\beta\) is Lipschitz,
zero on the boundary
and positive in the
interior.
A boundary collar
remains disjoint from
\(Z\) for sufficiently
small \(v\).
On the sets \(\beta\ge1/k\),
the forbidden vectors
are images of pairs
\((z,y)\) under
\[
v=\frac{z-F(y)}{\beta(y)}.
\tag{CF.25}
\]
Their parameter boxes
have dimension at most
\((2N-4)+2=2N-2\).
Each such Lipschitz
image has zero
\(2N\)-dimensional
volume. Indeed a
bounded \(m\)-box
has \(O(\delta^{-m})\)
cubes of side \(\delta\);
their images fit cubes
of diameter \(O(\delta)\),
whose total ambient
volume tends to zero
when \(m<2N\).
Countably many such
images still have zero
volume. An arbitrarily
small permitted \(v\)
therefore gives a
contraction missing
\(Z\). Paths between
two points are obtained
by the complex-line
detours used in CF.F.
Thus \(B\setminus Z\)
is connected and simply
connected. CF.E makes
every continued branch
single valued there.

Such a single-valued
holomorphic function
extends across \(Z\).
Choose a nonzero local
equation vanishing on
\(Z\), and a line on
which its first nonzero
homogeneous part does
not vanish.
This line meets \(Z\)
only at the centre
locally. Take a small
circle on it and a
transverse polydisc
so the full cylinder
over the circle misses
\(Z\).
The projection of the
part of \(Z\) inside
the cylinder is locally
closed, by compactness
and the side-boundary
exclusion. Its image
has empty interior:
the preceding box cover
now projects sets of
dimension at most
\(2N-4\) into dimension
\(2N-2\).
Define the extension
by the fixed-circle
Cauchy integral in
the line coordinate.
It is jointly holomorphic.
Over the dense set
of transverse points
outside that projection,
the whole fibre disc
misses \(Z\); Cauchy's
formula gives the
original function.
Continuity identifies
the two functions at
every remaining point
outside \(Z\).
Uniqueness makes these
extensions agree on
overlaps.

We may consequently
continue along paths
through \(Z\setminus S\)
as well. For \(N=1\)
there is no such
codimension-two set.
This proves Theorem
CF.1 for one element.
There are finitely
many fibrations,
relations, prescribed
elements and maps.
Intersect their finitely
many ordinary neighbourhoods
and take a smaller ball.
This proves its common-domain
assertion.

#### CF.H. Exact examples and the scope of continuation

For the complex cusp
\(S=\{t^2=x^3\}\), take
\[
F_0=x,\qquad F_1=x+t/2.
\tag{CF.26}
\]
Their vertical vectors,
ordered as \((t,x)\),
are \((1,0)\) and
\((1,-1/2)\).
The respective local
discriminants are
\(x=0\) and \(x+t/2=0\);
their cylinders meet
only at the origin.
For the second projection,
the critical equation
on the cusp is
\(2t+3x^2/2=0\).
Together with \(t^2=x^3\)
it gives
\(x^3(9x/16-1)=0\).
The second solution is
outside a sufficiently
small neighbourhood,
so the stated local
discriminant is exact.

A scalar kernel
calibration is
\[
\begin{gathered}A=-1/2,\quad\alpha=1/8,\\
 f(t)=\frac{81}{625}\frac{(t-\alpha)^3}{(t+\alpha)^5},\\
 (t^2-\alpha^2)f(t)\\
{}-\int_A^t f(s)\,ds=1.\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.27}
\]
Differentiate the last
left side. The identity
\((t^2-\alpha^2)f'
+2tf=f\) makes its
derivative zero.
Its value at \(A\)
is one, proving the
equation on every
continued contour.
This checks the sign
and the fixed memory
mechanism, not a
classification theorem.

One fibration alone
is insufficient.
The equation
\[
\begin{gathered}(t^2-x^3)\partial_t f=f,\\
 f(A,x)=1.\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.28}
\]
has a holomorphic
initial negative-cone
representative
\[
\begin{gathered}R(t,\rho)=\log\frac{t-\rho}{t+\rho},\\
 U(t,\rho)=\\
\frac{R(t,\rho)-R(A,\rho)}{2\rho},\\
 f(t,x)=e^{U(t,\rho)},\\
\rho^2=x^3.\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.29}
\]
The initial logarithms
expand in odd powers
of \(\rho\); division
by \(2\rho\) leaves
a convergent series
in \(x^3\), when \(t\)
and \(A\) are on the
initial negative side.
A positive loop about
\(t=\rho\) multiplies
this branch by
\(\exp(\pi i/\rho)\),
which has an essential
transverse singularity
at \(x=0\), even for
fixed nonzero \(t\).
Integration by parts
gives its uniform
analytic Volterra
equation
\[
\begin{gathered}(t^2-x^3)f(t,x)\\
{}-\int_A^t(2s+1)f(s,x)\,ds\\
=A^2-x^3.\end{gathered}
\tag{CF.30}
\]
Thus a full two-time
kernel and the exact
principal singular set
do not by themselves
prove continuation
across a vertical
discriminant.
The single differential
relation in two
variables has
characteristic equation
\((t^2-x^3)\tau=0\),
of dimension three;
it is not holonomic
of dimension two.
The full holonomic
hypothesis in CF.1
supplies the finite
systems in all the
spanning fibrations,
which is the additional
step in CF.F.

Theorem CF.1 proves
continuation on one
common ordinary
neighbourhood for
every prescribed
finite list.
It does not assert
finite rank of the
whole directional
solution space,
a common monodromy
annihilator under
all infinite-order
operators, singular
evaluation separation,
or the faithful
D-type embedding.
Those require their
own arguments.


### 5.83. Finite directional solution spaces and transverse fibres

Let \(M\) be the whole actual holonomic
microlocal module in generic position
at \(p_0=(0,0;1,0)\), as in
§5.82, CF.1.
Write \(X=\mathbf C_t\times\mathbf C_x^n\),
\(F(t,x)=x\), and \(S=\pi(\operatorname{Supp}M)\).
Use the directional function module
\(\mathcal C_{p_0}\) of CF.2, with its
complete actual finite, infinite and real
kernel actions proved in CF.A.

There is a bounded finite actual resolution
of the whole module on the nonzero-time
covector chart, together with its
compatible canonical kernel complex
\(P^\bullet\), by
§5.31, L.4–L.6
and
§5.49, ISF.3–ISF.4.
It is exact outside degree zero throughout
that chart. Its degree-zero support
can be arranged to satisfy
\[
|\xi|\le|\tau|.
\tag{FD.1}
\]
All complexes below use those identical
finite matrices and the genuine
module-derived supported objects.
No map from arbitrary canonical kernels
to finite microlocal symbols is used.

**Theorem FD.1.** The entire space
\[
V(M)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr E_{p_0}}
                 (M_{p_0},\mathcal C_{p_0})
\tag{FD.2}
\]
is finite dimensional, and
\[
\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathscr E_{p_0}}^k
                 (M_{p_0},\mathcal C_{p_0})=0,\\
k>0.
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.3}
\]
More precisely it is canonically
identified, through the finite support
comparisons below, with the direct sum
of the directional solution spaces at
all the points of a suitable generic
transverse fibre.
If the whole infinite extension at
the \(j\)-th such conormal point has
the constant Euler rank \(r_j\), then
\[
\dim_{\mathbf C}V(M)=\sum_j r_j.
\tag{FD.4}
\]
The ranks include all blocks and
principal nilpotents.

Consequently a basis of all directional
solutions and any prescribed finite
list of module elements have
representatives continuing on one
common ordinary neighbourhood
minus \(S\), by Theorem CF.1.
Stability under every continued
monodromy branch, singular evaluation
separation and full infinite-order
linearity require further arguments.

#### FD.A. Vanishing on an inner open

Put \(u=-\operatorname{Re}t\), and use
the common round coefficient domain
and future cap of
§5.81, CS.3.
Thus the relevant closed carriers are
compact in \(U\), the auxiliary
truncated ray hull is compact in
the one coefficient domain \(D\),
and the common future is
\(E=\{u>e\}\).
Let \(G_0\) be the negative real
time ray.

Suppose \(I\subset O\) are \(G_0\)-opens,
\(Y=O\setminus I\), and
\[
\overline Y\Subset U,\qquad O\cap S=\varnothing.
\tag{FD.5}
\]
Then
\[
\begin{gathered}
R\mathcal Hom_R\bigl(P^\bullet,\\
 R\Gamma_Y(q_*\mathcal O|_O)\bigr)=0,\\
R=E(G_0;D).
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.6}
\]
The ambient closure of \(Y\) is
allowed to meet \(S\) outside \(O\).
This assertion uses \(Y\) closed
in the cone topology of \(O\);
it is not a change to the
closed-carrier hypothesis in CP.F.

Here is its local proof.
Fix \(y\in Y\). The truncated
\(G_0\)-ray from \(y\) through
the level \(u=e+\eta\), for
small \(\eta>0\), is compactly
inside \(O\). A small closed ball
about \(y\), followed by that
truncated ray, is still inside
\(O\). For
\[
G_a=\{u\ge a(|\operatorname{Im}t|+|x|)\},
\tag{FD.7}
\]
the corresponding truncated
thick cones decrease to this
compact set as \(a\) increases.
Consequently choose \(\delta>0\)
and \(a\) so that the closed
truncation through \(u=e\) of
\[
V=(B_\delta(y)+G_a)\cup E
\tag{FD.8}
\]
is compactly in \(O\) and \(D\).
These \(V\) are a cofinal basis
for the supported stalk calculation:
adjoining \(E\) changes nothing,
since the supported object is
zero there, and CS.5 proves the
cofinality on every original
cone-open neighbourhood.

On \(V\) the inner open is
\(J\cap V\), where \(J=I\cup E\).
The closed carrier
\(\overline{V\setminus J}\)
is compactly inside \(O\), hence
disjoint from \(S\).
For \(b\ge a\), use the erosion
\[
J(b)=\{z:z+G_b\subset J\}.
\tag{FD.9}
\]
The uniform two-piece cone
decomposition CS.8 proves
\[
\bigcap_{b\ge a}
 \overline{V\setminus J(b)}
 =\overline{V\setminus J}.
\tag{FD.10}
\]
All these closed carriers are
compact after the common future
truncation. Thus for sufficiently
large \(b\) they are compactly
inside \(D\) and disjoint from
\(S\).

The round-domain hypothesis is
also preserved. The order-diamond
hull of a compact subset of
the round \(D\) is compact in
\(D\): the positive-functional
length bound CP.6 bounds its
cone parameters, and roundness
puts all the limiting intervals
inside \(D\). A sufficiently
small round neighbourhood of
that compact hull remains in
\(D\). Include its forward
segments through \(u=e\)
in the hull: they lie in
the original closed truncated
cone, whose extension through
\(e+\eta\) was chosen
compactly in \(O\cap D\).
Small enough neighbourhoods
therefore retain the common
future-cap condition.
Use one such neighbourhood
for one sufficiently late closed
carrier and all its successors.
It may meet \(S\) elsewhere;
CP.F requires actual acyclicity
only over the changing closed
carrier.

Apply
§5.80, CP.F
to \(V\) and \(V\cap J(b)\),
with the original operator
carrier \(G_0\), cone field
\(\operatorname{int}G_b\)
and time function \(u\).
Every required negative covector
has nonzero time coefficient,
and every base point is outside
\(S\). The whole actual complex
is exact there. The resulting
supported Hom is zero in
every degree.

The increasing complements
\(V\cap J(b)\) give exactly
the derived inverse limit of
CS.9. The explicit
\(1-\mathrm{shift}\) sequence
CP.24 kills both its limit
and first derived limit,
since all the cohomology
groups are zero.
Thus every cohomology stalk
at \(y\) vanishes.
Off \(Y\) the supported
object is zero as well.
This proves FD.6.
All terms use the same
auxiliary module resolution
and coefficient domain before
the erosion limit.

#### FD.B. Support pairs with no inner closure buffer

Let \(I\subset\Omega\) be
\(G_0\)-opens and let \(W\)
be an ordinary transverse
open set. Assume
\[
\begin{gathered}
\overline{\Omega\setminus I}\Subset U,\\
S\cap F^{-1}(W)\subset\Omega\setminus I.
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.11}
\]
There is no closure on
the inner open in the
second condition.
Set
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathscr A_{\Omega,I}
 =R\mathcal Hom_R\bigl(P^\bullet,\\
 R\Gamma_{\Omega\setminus I}
                  (q_*\mathcal O|_\Omega)\bigr),\\
\mathscr L_{\Omega,I}
 =R(F|_\Omega)_*\mathscr A_{\Omega,I}|_W.
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.12}
\]
This complex is canonically
independent of the pair
satisfying FD.11.
Every one of its cohomology
sheaves is locally constant
on \(W\).

For independence compare two
pairs over \(W'\Subset W\).
Use the common outer
intersection and the union
of the two inner opens
intersected with that outer
intersection, as in CS.12.
In the outer restriction
triangle the removed closed
carrier is contained in the
original compact carrier
and outside one of the
outer opens. It avoids
\(S\), since \(S\) is
inside both outer opens
over \(\overline{W'}\).
CS.A makes that term zero.

For inner enlargement
\(I\subset I'\subset\Omega\),
write \(j:I'\hookrightarrow\Omega\).
The third support-triangle
term, after finite Hom, is
\[
\begin{gathered}
Rj_*R\mathcal Hom_R\bigl(P^\bullet|_{I'},\\
 R\Gamma_{I'\setminus I}
                 (q_*\mathcal O|_{I'})\bigr).
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.13}
\]
It is zero by FD.A, since
the outer domain \(I'\)
avoids \(S\).
The closure of the inner
difference may meet \(S\)
on the boundary of \(I'\);
FD.A is precisely the
local assertion needed here.

We verify FD.13 as a map
of actual complexes.
For \(I\subset I'\), the
three restriction maps
from \(\Omega\) to \(I'\)
to \(I\) give the three
relative cones in a finite
commuting square.
Its total cone is the
support triangle displayed
above. In the strict
module-derived models of
DL.6–DLG.7 these are the
same support cubes.
The exact inverse-image
functor \(j^{-1}\) has
right adjoint \(j_*\);
therefore \(j_*\) preserves
injectives. Each finite
free term of \(P^\bullet\)
gives only a finite power
of that injective complex.
Its matrix entries commute
with restriction.
Thus finite internal Hom
commutes with this derived
open image, term by term,
including its differential.
This proves FD.13 with its
actual comparison map.
No exactness over the
polynomial coefficient
ring is needed.

A third pair is compared
through the intersection
of all three outer opens
and the union of their
inner opens there.
The same finite cubes
commute, proving the
cocycle identity.

For local constancy,
shrink \(W\) relatively
compactly. The set
\(S\cap F^{-1}(\overline W)\)
is compact in \(U\), by
FD.11. Choose an ordinary
neighbourhood of it with
closure compact in \(U\),
independently of the old
inner boundary.
The order-diamond
construction CS.14–CS.15
gives a new thick-cone
pair whose closed
difference is compact
in \(U\), and for which
\(S\) is outside the
closure of its inner
open. The strong
CS.C–CS.F theorem applies
to that pair.
The pair independence
just proved compares it
canonically with the
original pair.
This proves the asserted
local constancy.

On a ball contained in
\(W\) there are natural
isomorphisms
\[
\begin{gathered}
H^k(B;\mathscr L_{\Omega,I})\\
 \simeq\mathcal H^k(\mathscr L_{\Omega,I})_x,\\
x\in B.
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.14}
\]
Indeed the constant-vector
sheaf resolution and radial
homotopy CS.33 give zero
higher cohomology on balls,
even for arbitrary vector
fibres. In each fixed
degree the bounded-below
truncation argument CS.34
uses only a finite tower
of these sheaves.
Derived sections of the
remaining truncation start
in the next degree.
This proves FD.14 and its
restriction compatibility.

#### FD.C. Flat tangent geometry and cofinal supports

The whole projected support
has tangent cone in
\(\{t=0\}\).
Here is a proof including
its singular fibres.
The finite normalized
projection in CF.B and
CF.1 imply that, for
every \(\eta>0\), one
may shrink so that
\[
|\xi|\le\eta
\quad\text{on }A\cap\{\tau=1\}.
\tag{FD.15}
\]
Otherwise a compact
subsequence of finite
fibre lifts would limit
to a different normalized
covector above zero.

On every smooth graph
\(t=h_j(x)\) away from
the finite discriminant,
the Liouville form
vanishes on the conic
Lagrangian.
To see this, contract
the symplectic form
with the homogeneous
radial vector field,
which is tangent to
that Lagrangian.
Both tangent arguments
give zero. Its contraction
is the Liouville form.
Thus
\[
\begin{gathered}
dh_j=-\sum_i\xi_i\,dx_i,\\
|dh_j|\le\eta.
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.16}
\]

Take a transverse \(x\)
whose complex radial line
is not contained in the
discriminant.
Its discriminant equation
has no zero near the
scalar origin other than
that origin, and only
finitely many zeros on
compact segments away
from it. Join \(rx\)
to \(x\) by a radial
segment with arbitrarily
small planar detours
around those zeros.
Its length tends to
\((1-r)|x|\).
Lift it backwards from
any prescribed root over
\(x\).
The root over \(rx\)
tends to zero, by the
monic root bound.
Integrating FD.16 and
letting the detours and
\(r\) tend to zero gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
|t|\le\eta|x|\\
\text{on every such fibre}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.17}
\]
These line directions
are dense, since a
nonzero first homogeneous
part of the discriminant
does not vanish on a
dense open set.
Root multiset continuity,
proved in
analytic parametrization, §4,
extends FD.17 to every
fibre. This proves the
tangent assertion for
all branches and all
collisions.

Let \(G_+=-G_0\).
The closed positive
ray hull \(S+G_+\)
is an admissible
directional support
near zero.
If \(y=s+g\to0\),
its transverse coordinates
are those of \(s\).
The finite root bound
forces \(s\to0\),
and then \(g\to0\).
For every \(\eta>0\),
FD.17 gives
\[
\operatorname{Re}t_y\ge-\eta|x_y|.
\tag{FD.18}
\]
Every tangent limit
therefore has nonnegative
real time.
Local closedness follows
by truncating the ray
over a smaller closed
transverse ball; the
discarded far tail
cannot approach zero.

Start with any support
in CF.2. Enlarge it by
this positive hull.
Finite unions retain
the tangent condition,
by a subsequence in
one of the two sets.
Apply the convex-majorant
construction CF.A to
that union.
Consequently there is
a cofinal family of
convex-future supports
\(Z\) which contain
\(S\), have \(G_0\)-open
complement, and still
satisfy
\[
C_0(Z)\subset\{\operatorname{Re}t\ge0\}.
\tag{FD.19}
\]
They avoid each fixed
strict negative cone
after a sufficiently
small shrink.

#### FD.D. The actual directional Hom and a fixed transverse complex

Take a small product
\[
\begin{gathered}
B_{\epsilon,\delta}
 =\{|t|<\delta,\ |x|<\epsilon\},\\
\Omega=B_{\epsilon,\delta}+G_0.
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.20}
\]
For a support \(Z\)
from FD.C put
\(I=\Omega\setminus Z\).
The product can be
chosen so that the
closed changing carrier
is compact in \(U\).
This is the thin-ray
case of the explicit
cap estimate CF.7:
the transverse coordinates
are bounded by the
initial product and
the future boundary
is bounded by its
convex modulus.
Ordinary excision compares
the group on \(\Omega\)
with its ordinary germ
neighbourhood.
Both \(\Omega\) and
\(I\) are convex, so
the support complex is
concentrated in degree
one, with quotient
\(\mathcal O(I)/\mathcal O(\Omega)\).
The exact filtered limit
of those quotients is
\(\mathcal C_{p_0}\),
by CF.A.

Fix one cone
\[
\begin{gathered}
W_a=\bigl\{(t,x):\\
\operatorname{Re}t<-a(|\operatorname{Im}t|+|x|)\bigr\}
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.21}
\]
and the pair
\((\Omega,\Omega\cap W_a)\).
Its closed difference
is bounded: imaginary
time and \(x\) are
bounded by the product,
real time is bounded
on the right by
\(\delta\), and outside
\(W_a\) it is bounded
on the left by
\(-a(\delta+\epsilon)\).
Choose the radii small
enough to put this
whole closure inside
\(U\).
FD.17 puts every
point of \(S\) over
a smaller transverse
ball inside \(\Omega\)
and outside \(W_a\).
Both this fixed pair
and every sufficiently
refined support pair
satisfy FD.11.

The pair comparisons
in FD.B and their
cocycle identity identify
all their direct-image
complexes over a common
smaller base ball.
For varying radii use
their common outer
intersection and inner
union. For varying
transverse balls use
FD.14. Thus the
identifications commute
with every refinement.
There is one fixed
coefficient domain and
auxiliary module resolution
throughout these comparisons.

The finite actual
resolution of \(M\)
computes its Ext into
the directional quotient.
Finite powers commute
with the exact filtered
class limit, and a
finite system of kernel
or boundary equalities
holds on one common
refinement. The action
of each actual matrix
on a representative is
the calibrated canonical
action in CF.A.
Consequently, if
\(\mathscr L\) denotes
the fixed-pair complex
FD.12, then
\[
\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathscr E_{p_0}}^k
 (M_{p_0},\mathcal C_{p_0})\\
\simeq\mathcal H^{k+1}(\mathscr L)_0.
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.22}
\]
The shift is explicit:
\(R\Gamma_Z\mathcal O\)
has its quotient in
degree one, so its
finite Hom has that
same shift.
The comparison uses
identical finite matrices;
it does not require
the canonical complex
to be exact over its
polynomial coefficient
ring.

In particular this
identifies the entire
directional Hom space
with one fixed transverse
cohomology stalk.
A representative domain
depending on an individual
solution is not being
used to choose a different
generic fibre for that
solution.

#### FD.E. Euler solutions in the full directional module

For a finite constant
matrix \(A\), let
\(N_A\) be the actual
Euler module of
§5.54, EE.2.
It has the finite free
resolution EE.11.
Its solution complex
in \(\mathcal C_n\)
is the cochain Koszul
complex on
\[
\begin{gathered}
tD_tI-A,\\
D_{x_1}I,\ldots,D_{x_n}I.
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.23}
\]

Use the cofinal quotient
representatives of CF.A
on
\[
\begin{gathered}
U_{\phi,r,\epsilon}
 =(\Delta_r\times B_\epsilon)\\
\cap\bigl\{(t,x):\\
\operatorname{Re}t<-\phi(|\operatorname{Im}t|+|x|)\bigr\}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.24}
\]
Both this domain and
the full product are
preserved by
\((t,x)\mapsto(t,sx)\),
\(0\le s\le1\).
The exact radial
homotopy EE.14–EE.15
therefore descends to
their quotient.
It commutes with
\(tD_tI-A\).
On a total cochain
\(\alpha+e_0\wedge\beta\)
its homotopy is
\(H_x\alpha-e_0\wedge H_x\beta\),
so the mixed terms
cancel.
Evaluation at \(x=0\)
and extension independent
of \(x\) contract the
tangential complex onto
the one-variable quotient
\[
\begin{gathered}
Q_{\phi,r}
 =\mathcal O(U_{\phi,r})/\mathcal O(\Delta_r),\\
U_{\phi,r}=\Delta_r\cap\\
 \{\operatorname{Re}t<-\phi(|\operatorname{Im}t|)\}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.25}
\]
The extension is
defined because FD.24
projects into \(U_{\phi,r}\).
All maps commute with
the support refinements.

On \(W=\mathcal O(U_{\phi,r})^q\)
the remaining operator
\(T=tD_tI-A\) is
surjective. The domain
is convex in the strict
left half-plane.
With its common logarithm
branch and an anchor
\(a\in U_{\phi,r}\), set
\[
v(t)=t^A\int_a^t s^{-A}g(s)\,\frac{ds}{s}.
\tag{FD.26}
\]
Differentiation gives
\(Tv=g\); its kernel
is \(t^A\mathbf C^q\).
No boundary growth
estimate is used.
On \(V=\mathcal O(\Delta_r)^q\),
Taylor expansion gives
the coefficient maps
\(mI-A\), \(m\ge0\).
For \(m>2\|A\|\)
their inverse norm is
at most \(2/m\);
the remaining invertible
maps have a finite
uniform bound.
Hence the coefficient
solutions converge on
each compact subdisc,
and
\[
\begin{gathered}
\ker_VT\\
=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}t^m\ker(mI-A),\\
\operatorname{coker}_VT\\
 =\bigoplus_{m\ge0}\operatorname{coker}(mI-A).
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.27}
\]
Only the finitely
many noninvertible
summands are retained.
Their dimensions agree.
The elementary quotient
sequence
\[
\begin{gathered}
0\to\ker_VT\to\ker_WT\\
\to\ker_{W/V}T\\
\to\operatorname{coker}_VT\to0
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.28}
\]
follows by subtracting
a \(V\)-preimage when
the obstruction vanishes;
surjectivity at its
last term is FD.26.
It proves quotient
kernel dimension \(q\)
and zero quotient
cokernel.

The \(q\) explicit
power/logarithm columns
\(F_A\) of EE.21 are
defined on the entire
left half-disc.
Their classes remain
independent on every
\(U_{\phi,r}\):
if a combination
extends as a holomorphic
germ there, the identity
theorem gives the same
extension on the smaller
left half-disc.
The pole, jump and
Jordan triangular argument
EE.21 makes all its
coefficients zero.
They consequently form
a basis of every
refined quotient kernel.
Every transition carries
these same columns
to themselves.
Taking the filtered
limit and the finite
resolution gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
\dim\operatorname{Hom}_E(N_A,\mathcal C_n)=q,\\
\operatorname{Ext}_E^k(N_A,\mathcal C_n)=0,\\
k>0.
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.29}
\]

The right \(E\)-flatness
of the whole infinite
ring \(B\), proved in
§5.47,
and ordinary Hom
adjunction give the
identical complex for
\(B\otimes_E N_A\)
over \(B\).
CF.A provides the
full \(B\)-action
on \(\mathcal C_n\).
Thus FD.29 holds
there as well.

For clarity, the
halfspace module
of EE.3 injects in
\(\mathcal C_n\):
the closed support
\(\{\operatorname{Re}t\ge0\}\)
is one admissible
support in CF.2.
If its class becomes
a holomorphic germ
after a refinement,
the identity theorem
on the connected
left half-product
shows that its
original class was
already zero.
The inclusion respects
the full real kernel
action, since both
actions use the same
supported cup, excision
and trace maps.
In particular the
full-coefficient detector
EE.4 remains injective
with target \(\mathcal C_n^q\).

#### FD.F. A generic fibre of the entire complex

Choose a small transverse
patch outside the finite
discriminant. Its sheets
are holomorphic graphs
\(t=h_j(x)\).
The actual smooth-branch
construction
§5.69, GM.A–GM.B
gives a proper analytic
coefficient-minor exceptional
set on each sheet.
Avoid the finitely
many such sets.
At every remaining
point the entire
full-infinite module
is actually isomorphic
to a constant Euler
module of finite
rank \(r_j\).
This is the proved
inverse Gevrey gauge,
not a formal normal
form.

One may also arrange
that the sheet values
have distinct imaginary
parts.
No difference \(h_j-h_k\)
can be a nonzero
constant \(c\) on
an open set.
Otherwise the resultant
\[
\operatorname{Res}_t(p(t,x),p(t+c,x))
\tag{FD.30}
\]
vanishes there and
hence identically on
the connected original
base. At \(x=0\),
where \(p(t,0)=t^m\),
it is a nonzero
power of \(c\),
a contradiction.
A nonconstant holomorphic
function cannot have
zero imaginary part
on an open set:
the Cauchy–Riemann
equations would make
all its derivatives
zero there.
Thus these finitely
many imaginary-equality
sets have empty interior.
Choose \(x_*\) outside
them and the analytic
exceptional sets.

Over a smaller ball
about \(x_*\), choose
\(\rho>0\) with
\[
\begin{gathered}
|\operatorname{Im}(h_j-h_k)|>4\rho,\\
j\ne k.
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.31}
\]
Put \(T_j=t-h_j(x)\).
The \(G_0\)-opens
\[
\begin{gathered}
\Omega_j=\bigl\{(t,x):x\in B_r(x_*),\\
 |T_j|<\rho\bigr\}+G_0,\\
I_j=\Omega_j\cap\\
\{\operatorname{Re}T_j<-\rho/2\}
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.32}
\]
are pairwise disjoint
in \(j\).
Their closed changing
carriers are compact
in the fixed ordinary
coefficient neighbourhood,
after choosing the
base ball with closure
inside the graph patch.
They include every
sheet over a smaller
base ball, with a
strict inner buffer.
Their union satisfies
FD.11.

Pair independence
compares this union
with the fixed pair
of FD.D.
Disjointness gives
the direct sum of
its component supported
complexes.
Shrink the transverse
ball and each normal
cap. In the ordinary
graph coordinate
\(T_j\), apply the
local construction
of FD.C–FD.D at
the conormal point
\[
\begin{gathered}
p_j=(h_j(x_*),x_*;\\
1,-dh_j(x_*)).
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.33}
\]
It compares the
component cap with
the local directional
module \(\mathcal C_{p_j}\).
All comparisons use
the same finite
actual matrices and
the same strict
supported models.
FD.14 makes every
transverse shrinking
map an isomorphism.
The weak pair comparison
makes every sufficiently
small normal-cap map
an isomorphism.
Consequently the cap
and its filtered
directional limit have
the same finite Hom
cohomology.

The graph time shift
has the actual finite,
infinite and real
coordinate maps proved
in
§5.56, BCT.5.
It also preserves
the thin carrier
exactly: on its
spatial diagonal the
two values of \(h_j(x)\)
are equal, so the
time difference is
unchanged. Its support
cube and trace maps
therefore identify
the preceding canonical
comparisons with the
actual local directional
actions.
We compare the Hom
complexes after these
maps; an unrestricted
cap function is not
being identified with
a directional germ.

At \(p_j\) the
actual \(B\)-module
gauge and finite
resolution identify
\[
\begin{gathered}
R\operatorname{Hom}_{E_{p_j}}
       (M_{p_j},\mathcal C_{p_j})\\
\simeq R\operatorname{Hom}_{B_{p_j}}\bigl(\\
 B_{p_j}\otimes_{E_{p_j}}M_{p_j},\\
 \mathcal C_{p_j}\bigr).
\end{gathered}
\tag{FD.34}
\]
Indeed tensor the
finite actual free
resolution with the
right-flat \(B_{p_j}\);
ordinary adjunction
identifies each Hom
term and differential.
Use the actual inverse
Euler gauge and FD.29.
Each summand is
concentrated in degree
zero and has dimension
\(r_j\).

FD.14 transports that
calculation back to
the stalk at zero.
Together with the
shift FD.22 it proves
FD.3 and FD.4 for
the entire original
module.
For \(n=0\) the
transverse base is
a point and this
is the same local
Euler calculation;
the finite discriminant
step is empty.
The zero module is
immediate.

Choose a basis of
the resulting finite
space \(V(M)\).
For any finite list
of module elements,
Theorem CF.1 gives
one common continuation
domain for the basis
representatives.
Their linear combinations
give representatives
for every element
of \(V(M)\) on
that same domain.
This last statement
does not yet identify
every continued branch
with another actual
module homomorphism.
Monodromy compatibility,
singular separation
and faithful full
infinite-order linearity
remain separate.

The upper panel is only

\(x_*=-1/4\), with
roots \(t=\pm i/8\)
and conormals
\((\tau,\xi)=(1,\pm3i/4)\).
For \(\rho=1/32\)
the two disc-plus-ray
opens of FD.32 are
disjoint: their imaginary

### 5.84. Directional functionals separate the whole infinite extension

Keep the whole actual generic-position
holonomic module \(M\) at
\(p_0=(0,0;1,0)\), its projected
hypersurface \(S\), and its
directional function module
\(\mathcal C_{p_0}\) from
§5.82, CF.A.
Put
\[
\begin{gathered}
E=\mathscr E_{p_0},\quad
B=\mathscr E^\infty_{p_0},\\
N=B\otimes_E M,\\
V=\operatorname{Hom}_E(M,\mathcal C_{p_0}).
\end{gathered}
\tag{SE.1}
\]
All tensors are algebraic.
The complete actual kernel action
makes \(\mathcal C_{p_0}\) a
left \(B\)-module.
Every \(\Phi\in V\) consequently
has the unique \(B\)-linear extension
\[
\Phi^\infty(b\otimes m)=b\Phi(m).
\tag{SE.2}
\]
The formula respects the finite-ring
balancing relation because
\(\Phi(Pm)=P\Phi(m)\).

**Theorem SE.1.** If \(s\in N\) satisfies
\[
\Phi^\infty(s)=0
\quad\text{for every }\Phi\in V,
\tag{SE.3}
\]
then \(s=0\).
In particular, for any basis
\(\Phi_1,\ldots,\Phi_q\) of the
entire finite-dimensional space \(V\),
the actual \(B\)-linear map
\[
\begin{gathered}
N\longrightarrow\mathcal C_{p_0}^{\,q},\\
s\longmapsto
 \bigl(\Phi_1^\infty(s),\ldots,\Phi_q^\infty(s)\bigr)
\end{gathered}
\tag{SE.4}
\]
is injective.
Finite dimensionality is
§5.83, FD.1.
The assertion includes every
infinite coefficient tail, singular
characteristic point and principal
nilpotent of the whole module.

The target in SE.4 is the
directional function module.
A finite coherent D-type target
and the compatibility of continued
branches with all operators
require additional proofs.

#### SE.A. Identity for actual infinite sections on a smooth branch

First consider the whole constant
Euler extension \(T_A=B\otimes_E N_A\)
over a graph chart
\(\Lambda=\{t=z=0\}\),
where \(z=\xi/\tau\).
The full coefficient normal form
§5.52, AM.A
gives a unique row
\[
R=\sum_{j\in\mathbf Z}r_j(x)\tau^j
\tag{SE.5}
\]
for each locally represented section.
Every \(r_j\) is holomorphic
on one common parameter domain.
The positive every-epsilon and
negative factorial estimates
of AM.2 hold there.

We check the required restriction
property of this normal form.
Its spatial division AM.5 consists
of finite holomorphic differences
and divisions by spatial variables.
Its normal division AM.8–AM.10
consists of evaluation at \(t=0\),
the holomorphic quotient
\((f-f|_{t=0})/t\), constant
matrix products, and normally
convergent coefficient sums.
All these operations commute
with restriction in \(x\).
The estimates AM.11–AM.15
use a common normal radius
and compact parameter norms.
They apply uniformly on every
smaller parameter ball,
with the same radius for
all homogeneous indices.
Thus the normal form on
an overlap is the restriction
of SE.5, by its proved uniqueness.
This is an identity of actual
coefficient sequences, including
both tails.

Suppose a section of \(T_A\)
vanishes on a nonempty open
part of a connected parameter
ball on which that section
has one representative.
At each point of that open
part, uniqueness makes the
germ of every \(r_j\) zero.
The identity theorem makes
every \(r_j\) zero on the
whole parameter ball.
One elementary proof of that
identity theorem is to consider
the set where all Taylor
coefficients of a holomorphic
function vanish. It is closed
by continuity of its derivatives
and open by its convergent
Taylor expansion. If nonempty
on a connected domain it is
the entire domain.
This argument applies to
each of the countably many
coefficients separately; their
common domain was fixed first.
The actual zero normal form
makes the section zero.

Local representatives suffice.
The set of parameter points
where a sheaf section has zero
germ is open. At a boundary
point choose one representative
on a smaller connected parameter
ball. That ball meets the
open zero set, so the preceding
argument makes its entire
normal form zero.
The zero set is therefore
also relatively closed.
Consequently a section of the
whole Euler extension that is
zero on a nonempty open part
of a connected graph patch
is zero on that patch.

Now let the reduced support
of an arbitrary holonomic
\(M\) be a single smooth
graph on a small chart.
The graph time shift and its
actual finite and infinite
maps are
§5.56, BCT.5.
They put the graph into
\(\Lambda=\{t=z=0\}\).
The actual lattice construction
and finite minor argument in
§5.69, GM.A–GM.C
give a nonzero holomorphic
\(g(x)\) on the parameter
ball \(B_0\).
On \(\{g\ne0\}\), the
entire infinite extension is
locally isomorphic to a
constant Euler extension by
the two actual inverse
gauge matrices GM.9–GM.11.

The complement of \(\{g=0\}\)
in a complex ball is path
connected. For two points
outside it, restrict \(g\)
to their affine complex line.
It is not identically zero
because its value at the
first point is nonzero.
Its zeros on a compact
neighbourhood of the real
joining segment are finite.
Replace the segment by a
path with small planar detours
around those zeros.
The segment has a positive
margin inside the ball,
so the detours stay inside.
Isolated zeros and their
finiteness follow directly
by factoring out the first
nonzero Taylor power locally
and using a finite compact
cover.

If an infinite section is zero
on a nonempty open part of
the graph, that part meets
\(\{g\ne0\}\).
The Euler identity just proved
makes its zero set both open
and closed on the connected
set \(\{g\ne0\}\).
It is zero there.
Off \(\Lambda\) the source
module is zero, by the full
extension support equality
§5.49, ISR.13.
The section is thus supported
on the fixed closed analytic set
\[
Z_g=\Lambda\cap\{g(x)=0\}.
\tag{SE.6}
\]
If \(d=\dim_{\mathbf C}B_0\),
then its dimension is at most
\(d-1\), while the normalized
ambient chart has dimension
\(2d+1\).
Its codimension is at least
\(d+2\), strictly larger than
the base dimension \(d+1\).
The actual full-coefficient
support-purity theorem
§5.51, PG.1
kills this section.
No analyticity of its own
support has been assumed.
For \(g=1\) the exceptional
set is empty.
For \(d=0\), the parameter
base is a point and the
Euler identity is immediate.

We have proved the following
local assertion at every isolated
smooth characteristic branch
which is a graph over
the transverse base,
including its coefficient-minor
exceptional points:
an actual infinite section
which is zero on a nonempty
open part of a connected
smooth graph patch is zero
on that patch.
The proof used actual normal
coefficients and one local
analytic purity step.

#### SE.B. One canonical expression for an arbitrary infinite germ

Keep the actual whole-module
generators \(u_1,\ldots,u_b\)
and finite polynomial complex
of
§5.49, ISD.1 and ISR.1–ISR.2.
The full Späth division gives
for the arbitrary element
\(s\in N\) a finite expression
\[
s=\sum_{i=1}^b a_i u_i,
\qquad a_i\in A^\infty,
\tag{SE.7}
\]
where each \(a_i\) is
independent of the spatial
covariable \(z\).
All other relations of \(M\)
remain in force.
This generation is ISR.2;
it is neither a free-module
identification nor a formal
coefficient completion.
Finite sums and the actual
division estimates give
one common coefficient
domain for this expression.
The coefficients extend
over the finite normalized
covariable product, as
ISF.9 proves.
After shrinking, SE.7 is
an actual section expression
on the whole finite support
representative used below.
Indeed its germ equality
has an ordinary neighbourhood
witness, by the finite
balancing argument FEP.9.
The normalized support
projection is finite and
has only \(p_0\) over
the base origin.
The image of its closed
part outside that witness
is therefore closed and
misses zero, after choosing
a compact finite representative.
A smaller base ball
puts its entire support
inside the witness.

These particular coefficients
also have actual canonical
thin-ray kernel representatives.
Here is the analytic reason.
Write
\[
a=\sum_{j\in\mathbf Z}a_j(t,x)D_t^j.
\tag{SE.8}
\]
For \(j\ge0\), the positive
time kernel has coefficients
\(j!a_j(t,x)/(s-t)^{j+1}\),
with the common Cauchy
normalization of AM.B.
On any compact set with
\(|s-t|\ge\delta>0\),
choose the input epsilon
less than \(\delta/2\).
The every-epsilon bound
makes its series geometric.
For the negative part use
the Volterra kernel
\[
\begin{gathered}
K_a(t,x,s)=\\
\sum_{n\ge1}a_{-n}(t,x)
             \frac{(t-s)^{n-1}}{(n-1)!},\\
|K_a|\le
\frac{MC}{(1-C|t-s|)^2}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{SE.9}
\]
The bound follows from
\(|a_{-n}|\le MC^n n!\)
and the differentiated
geometric series.
It holds for \(C|t-s|<1\).
Spatial variables are diagonal
kernel variables, since no
spatial derivative occurs.
Every fixed parameter derivative
has the same assertion after
one reserved Cauchy margin.

The complete cochain,
primitive and composition
calibration in
§5.53, AM.B
and
§5.49, ISF.3–ISF.4
identifies these kernels
with the full \(B\)-actions.
It also identifies their
supported restrictions and
the action on the actual
directional module CF.A.
Use one coefficient domain
for the finite list \(a_i\)
and all presentation matrices.
The kernel support carrier
remains the original negative
time ray \(G_0\).

Let \(R=E(G_0;D)\) on this
coefficient domain, and let
\(P^\bullet_R\) be the
matched finite canonical
complex of FD.1, in
nonpositive degrees.
Its actual finite counterpart
resolves the whole \(M\)
on the nonzero-time chart.
Put
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathfrak M=H^0(P_R^\bullet),\\
\widetilde s=\sum_i a_i\bar u_i\in\mathfrak M.
\end{gathered}
\tag{SE.10}
\]
This is a canonical coefficient
module used for evaluation.
We only compare the displayed
common coefficient expressions
and their genuine function
actions.
An arbitrary canonical kernel
is not sent to a finite symbol.
Exactness of \(P_R^\bullet\)
over the polynomial coefficient
ring is not needed.

#### SE.C. Finite solution dimension gives one vanishing cap

For a sufficiently small
product and a fixed \(a>0\),
write
\[
\begin{gathered}
\Omega=B_{\epsilon,\delta}+G_0,\\
W_a=\bigl\{(t,x):\\
\operatorname{Re}t<-a(|\operatorname{Im}t|+|x|)\bigr\},\\
I=\Omega\cap W_a,\\
Q_{\Omega,I}=\mathcal O(I)/\mathcal O(\Omega).
\end{gathered}
\tag{SE.11}
\]
The closed changing carrier
has compact closure in
the fixed coefficient
neighbourhood, as FD.D proves.
Both opens are convex.
Their supported holomorphic
complex has its quotient
in degree one.
Because \(P_R^\bullet\)
is nonpositive and finite free,
its degree-one supported
Hom is literally
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_R
       (\mathfrak M,Q_{\Omega,I}).
\tag{SE.12}
\]
The weak pair comparisons
FD.B and fixed-stalk
comparison FD.D identify
SE.12 canonically with \(V\),
compatibly with sufficiently
small cap and base refinements.

Choose a basis of the entire
finite space \(V\).
Represent its finitely many
generator images and their
finite relation equalities
on one common convex
directional support.
The hypothesis SE.3 says
that the finitely many
sums SE.7 evaluated on
this basis vanish as
directional classes.
The actual kernel action
and the definition of
the filtered class limit
put all these zero equalities
on one further common
support refinement.
Take a convex future
majorant again, by CF.A.
This preserves all equalities
and all finite relation maps.

That majorant avoids the fixed
strict cone \(W_a\) after
a small enough shrink.
Supported restriction therefore
gives representatives of the
basis in SE.12 satisfying
\[
\psi(\widetilde s)=0
\quad\text{in }Q_{\Omega,I}
\tag{SE.13}
\]
for every member of that
basis.
These restrictions still form
a basis of SE.12, by the
canonical isomorphisms in
FD.B–FD.D.
Linearity proves SE.13
for every cap homomorphism.
The common cap here is
chosen using a finite basis,
not a domain chosen
separately for each of
infinitely many solutions.

#### SE.D. Evaluation survives the comparison with disjoint normal caps

Choose the generic point
\(x_*\ne0\) and all sheets
\(t=h_j(x)\) as in FD.F,
avoiding the finite
discriminant and all
generic Euler-minor exceptions.
Shrink its base ball so
that its closure misses zero.
By the flat tangent estimate
FD.17 choose \(\eta<a\)
and arrange
\[
|h_j(x)|\le\eta|x|
\tag{SE.14}
\]
on these sheets.
Let \(b=\min_{\overline{B_r(x_*)}}|x|>0\).
Choose the common normal
radius \(\rho>0\) so small
that the opens
\[
\begin{gathered}
T_j=t-h_j(x),\\
\Omega_j=\bigl\{(t,x):x\in B_r(x_*),\\
|T_j|<\rho\bigr\}+G_0,\\
I_j=\Omega_j\cap\\
\{\operatorname{Re}T_j<-\rho/2\}
\end{gathered}
\tag{SE.15}
\]
are disjoint, lie inside
\(\Omega\) over that base
ball, and contain all sheets.
Use FD.31 for disjointness,
and also impose
\[
\rho/2<(a-\eta)b.
\tag{SE.16}
\]
For every point in \(W_a\)
over this ball,
\[
\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{Re}T_j
< -a|x|-\operatorname{Re}h_j(x)\\
\le -(a-\eta)|x|<-\rho/2.
\end{gathered}
\tag{SE.17}
\]
Consequently
\[
J_j:=W_a\cap\Omega_j\subset I_j.
\tag{SE.18}
\]
Each \(J_j\) is nonempty
within the common coefficient
completion, before its future
cutoff \(u=e\).
Indeed \(x_*\) can be
chosen arbitrarily near zero.
Let \(c=\max_{\overline{B_r(x_*)}}|x|\).
In addition choose it and
\(\rho\) so small that
\[
\begin{gathered}
a(\eta+1)c+2\eta c\\
{}+2\rho<e.
\end{gathered}
\tag{SE.18a}
\]
For fixed \(x\), the point
\[
\begin{gathered}
t=h_j(x)-L,\\
L=a(\eta+1)c+\eta c+\rho.
\end{gathered}
\tag{SE.18b}
\]
is on the negative real
ray from the graph point,
lies in \(W_a\), and
has \(u<e\).
Its ray segment is
in the common coefficient
domain by CS.3.
The strict inequalities
give a nonempty open
intersection there.

First restrict the base
of SE.11 to \(B_r(x_*)\).
FD.14 makes the Hom
restriction an isomorphism.
Next restrict the outer open
to the disjoint union of
the \(\Omega_j\), retaining
the old inner open there.
The removed closed carrier
is compact and misses \(S\),
since all its sheets are
inside the new outer opens
over the base-ball closure.
The outer comparison of
FD.B is therefore an
isomorphism after finite Hom.
Its support maps commute
with evaluation at the
fixed canonical element
\(\widetilde s\).
Thus all old-inner cap
homomorphisms on the
disjoint tubes annihilate
\(\widetilde s\).

For precision, no convexity
of \(J_j\) is needed in
this step. In graph
coordinates \((T_j,x)\),
\(\Omega_j\) is biholomorphic
to a product of a convex
disc-plus-ray domain and
a ball. Its holomorphic
higher cohomology vanishes
by the explicit convex
acyclicity proof DLH.1–DLH.4
and coordinate pullback.
It is connected, and
\(J_j\) is nonempty.
Hence its degree-zero
supported cohomology is
zero and its degree-one
supported cohomology is
the quotient
\[
Q_{\Omega_j,J_j}
=\mathcal O(J_j)/\mathcal O(\Omega_j).
\tag{SE.19}
\]
The support triangle proves
these two statements even
if \(J_j\) has higher
holomorphic cohomology.
For a nonpositive finite
free \(P_R^\bullet\), terms
of supported degree at
least two contribute total
degree at least two to
its Hom.
The degree-one truncation
therefore identifies the
degree-one Hom with
\(\operatorname{Hom}_R
(\mathfrak M,Q_{\Omega_j,J_j})\).
This proves the literal
degree-zero map assertion
used above without a
Stein claim for that
intersection.

The inner comparison
FD.A–FD.B for SE.18 gives
an isomorphism on these
Hom spaces from the
new-inner pair to the
old-inner pair.
The underlying quotient
restriction
\[
Q_{\Omega_j,I_j}\longrightarrow
Q_{\Omega_j,J_j}
\tag{SE.20}
\]
is itself injective.
Indeed \(I_j\) is connected
in graph coordinates.
If \(f\in\mathcal O(I_j)\)
agrees on \(J_j\) with a
function \(g\in\mathcal O(\Omega_j)\),
the identity theorem on
the connected \(I_j\)
makes \(f=g|_{I_j}\).
Its class was already zero.

Take any homomorphism for
the disjoint new-inner caps.
Its old-inner restriction
corresponds to a homomorphism
in SE.12, so its value on
\(\widetilde s\) is zero
there by SE.13.
Injectivity of SE.20 now
proves
\[
\psi_j(\widetilde s)=0
\quad\text{in }Q_{\Omega_j,I_j}
\tag{SE.21}
\]
for every new-inner cap
homomorphism, on every
component.
This uses an actual
injection of the evaluation
targets, in addition to
the isomorphism after Hom.

The same reasoning applies
to every sufficiently small
normal cap and smaller
base ball about \(x_*\).
Condition SE.16 persists.
Outer restriction preserves
a zero evaluation.
Inner enlargement again
has injective quotient
restriction by the same
connectedness argument.
Thus SE.21 holds throughout
the shrinking-cap comparisons.

#### SE.E. The local directional evaluation is zero

At
\[
\begin{gathered}
p_j=(h_j(x_*),x_*;\\
1,-dh_j(x_*)).
\end{gathered}
\tag{SE.22}
\]
use \(T_j\) as normal
time coordinate and \(x-x_*\)
as parameter.
The actual graph coordinate
maps preserve \(G_0\) on
the spatial diagonal,
as FD.F proves.
They send SE.8 to a
time-only operator with
coefficients
\(a_m(T_j+h_j(x),x)\).
Its complete estimates
hold on one smaller
parameter product.
Thus the finite canonical
matrix comparisons and
the evaluations SE.7 use
the same actual \(B_{p_j}\)
actions as the local
directional module.

We record exactly how
zero cap evaluation detects
a local directional class.
Represent such a class
on a cofinal convex
future support \(Z\),
with completed outer
product \(\Omega_Z\).
Its numerator domain
\(I_Z=\Omega_Z\setminus Z\)
is convex.
By ordinary excision
CF.A and FD.D, the
class is represented by
\[
f\in\mathcal O(I_Z)
\quad\bmod\mathcal O(\Omega_Z).
\tag{SE.23}
\]
Choose a sufficiently small
normal cap \(\Omega'\)
and its inner \(I'\)
of the form SE.15
in these local coordinates.
Choose its parameter
radius at most its
normal radius.
The inequality
\(\operatorname{Re}T<-\rho'/2\),
with \(|\operatorname{Im}T|<\rho'\)
and \(|x-x_*|<\rho'\),
places \(I'\) inside the
fixed strict negative cone
of aperture \(1/4\).
After a sufficiently small
shrink that cone misses \(Z\).
The completed tubes also
satisfy \(\Omega'\subset\Omega_Z\).
Thus \(I'\subset I_Z\).

If the image of SE.23
in \(Q_{\Omega',I'}\)
is zero, there is
\(g\in\mathcal O(\Omega')\)
agreeing with \(f\)
on \(I'\).
The intersection
\(I_Z\cap\Omega'\)
is convex, nonempty
and connected in these
local coordinates.
The identity theorem
extends the agreement
to that intersection.
The function \(g\)
therefore extends the
directional representative
through the origin,
so its original directional
class is zero.
Only this detection
statement is used.
An arbitrary unrestricted
cap function is not
identified with a
directional germ.

Now take any
\(\Psi\in\operatorname{Hom}_{E_{p_j}}
(M_{p_j},\mathcal C_{p_j})\).
Its finite generator images,
their relation equalities
and their SE.7 evaluation
have one common convex
future support representative.
For small enough caps,
FD.C–FD.F gives its
matched cap homomorphism,
with exactly the same
matrix and coefficient
actions.
SE.21 makes its
SE.7 evaluation zero
on that cap.
The detection argument
SE.23 consequently proves
\[
\Psi^\infty(s_{p_j})=0
\quad\text{for every }\Psi.
\tag{SE.24}
\]

At this generic point the
whole \(B_{p_j}\)-module
is actually Euler by GM.B.
The full-coefficient
detector EE.4 separates
that whole module into
powers of the halfspace
quotient.
The halfspace quotient
injects into \(\mathcal C_{p_j}\)
with its actual actions,
by FD.E.
The finite right-flat
adjunction FD.34 identifies
these \(B\)-linear functionals
with the displayed
\(E\)-linear \(\Psi\)'s.
SE.24 therefore gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
s_{p_j}=0\\
\text{for every point of the}\\
\text{chosen generic fibre}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{SE.25}
\]
A zero stalk of a sheaf
section has an open
neighbourhood on which
that section is zero.
Hence this gives vanishing
on an open part of every
sheet over that fibre.

#### SE.F. Every smooth sheet and the singular exceptional set

Choose one nonzero
discriminant equation \(h(x)\)
for the finite normalized
support projection of CF.B,
enlarged by the finitely
many component intersections
and projection singularities.
Over
\[
B_0\setminus H,\qquad H=\{h=0\},
\tag{SE.26}
\]
all reduced sheets are
smooth and disjoint
finite graphs locally.
The generic fibre above
was chosen outside \(H\).
The base complement is
path connected by the
complex-line detour proof
in SE.A.

From any point of a
sheet over that complement,
lift a base path back
to \(x_*\).
Finite proper projection
and its graph charts
give the lift along
the whole compact path:
in a local graph chart
the next part is unique,
and compactness gives
a finite subdivision
and prevents escape.
The endpoint is one
of the points in SE.25.
Its zero germ propagates
backwards along the lifted
path by the smooth-branch
identity SE.A.
More explicitly, the set
of path parameters with
zero germ is open.
At a boundary parameter,
one connected smooth graph
patch meets that open
zero set; SE.A makes
the whole patch zero.
The set is also closed,
and is therefore the
entire path interval.
No transitivity assumption
on the sheet monodromy
is required, since every
point of the ending
generic fibre is zero.

It follows that the
actual section SE.7 is
zero at every point
of the reduced normalized
support above \(B_0\setminus H\).
It is zero off that
support as well, by
ISR.13.
Its support is contained
in the fixed analytic set
\[
Z=A\cap F^{-1}(H).
\tag{SE.27}
\]
Here \(A\) is the
whole reduced normalized
characteristic support,
not only its smooth part.
The support projection
is finite.
The analytic dimension
calculation in CF.B
therefore gives in the
normalized ambient chart, with
\(n=\dim_{\mathbf C}B_0\),
\[
\begin{gathered}
\dim Z\le n-1,\\
\dim(\text{ambient})=2n+1,\\
\operatorname{codim}Z\ge n+2>n+1.
\end{gathered}
\tag{SE.28}
\]
The last quantity \(n+1\)
is the ordinary complex
base dimension of \(M\).
PG.1 applies to the
entire actual \(B\)-extension
and this fixed analytic
\(Z\).
It gives \(\mathcal H_Z^0(N)=0\),
and thus \(s=0\).
The section's own support
has not been declared
analytic or coherent.

When \(n=0\), the normalized
support near \(p_0\) is
an isolated smooth point.
There is no transverse
discriminant.
The generic lattice and
Euler gauge have no
parameter-minor exception,
so the local Euler
detector proves SE.1
directly.
The zero module is
immediate in every
dimension.
This finishes Theorem SE.1.

Finally the extensions SE.2
are \(B\)-linear by their
literal balancing formula.
Their finite product is
therefore \(B\)-linear,
and SE.3 proves its
injectivity, giving SE.4.
No tensor-flatness for the
real kernel ring over \(B\)
has been used.

Theorem SE.1 separates every
singular infinite-extension
germ by finitely many
actual directional functionals.
A monodromy representation
on their common continued
representatives and a
coherent D-type realization
still require the full
continuation/action and
infinite-order linearity
arguments.
