### 5.85. Monodromy of actual directional solution homomorphisms

Let \(M\) be the whole actual
generic-position holonomic module
at \(p_0=(0,0;1,0)\).
Keep the directional function
module \(\mathcal C_{p_0}\) and
all its actual actions from
§5.82, CF.A.
Write
\[
\begin{gathered}
V=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr E_{p_0}}
             (M,\mathcal C_{p_0}),\\
q=\dim_{\mathbf C}V<\infty .
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.1}
\]
Finite dimensionality is
§5.83, FD.1.
Choose one basis of \(V\)
and the finite actual generators
\(u_1,\ldots,u_b\) of the
matched presentation in FD.1.

**Theorem MC.1.** There is one
ordinary product neighbourhood \(X\)
of zero on which representatives
\(f_{ai}\) of all the finitely
many generator images
\(\Phi_a(u_i)\) continue on the
universal cover of \(X\setminus S\).
For every continuation loop, their
continued classes satisfy all
actual finite presentation relations.
They define another element of
the entire space \(V\).
This gives a genuine linear
representation
\[
\begin{gathered}
\rho:\Gamma\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(V),\\
\Gamma=\pi_1(X\setminus S).
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.2}
\]
Changes of representatives which
continue on the same complement
give the same action.
Restriction to a common smaller
admissible product pulls back
this representation along the
induced map of groups.

Let \(m\) be the number of
distinct points in a generic
time fibre of the reduced
support hypersurface.
The group \(\Gamma\) has a
generating set of size \(d\le m\).
There is a two-sided ideal
\(\mathfrak a\subset\mathbf C[\Gamma]\)
which annihilates all functions
\(f_{ai}\), as functions, and
\[
\dim_{\mathbf C}\mathbf C[\Gamma]/\mathfrak a
\le 1+dq^2 .
\tag{MC.3}
\]
Thus the same finite determination
applies to every chosen generator
representative and all its branches.
This assertion concerns actual
functions and actual homomorphisms.
It does not yet identify their
finite D-type realization or
prove infinite-order linearity
of that realization.

#### MC.A. Finite fibres, covers and arbitrarily small meridians

The complete finite projection
and root bound are CF.B–CF.C.
After shrinking, take
\[
\begin{gathered}
X=\Delta_R\times B_\epsilon,\\
F(t,x)=x,\\
S=\{p(t,x)=0\},\\
p(t,0)=t^m .
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.4}
\]
The polynomial is monic and
reduced. All its roots are
inside \(\Delta_{R/8}\) after
a smaller base ball.
Let \(H\) be a proper analytic
discriminant hypersurface containing
all root collisions, put
\[
\begin{gathered}
Y=B_\epsilon\setminus H,\\
D=F^{-1}(H),\\
Z=X\setminus(S\cup D).
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.5}
\]
Empty exceptional sets are allowed.
The complex-line detour proof
SE.A
shows that \(Y\) is
path connected.

Choose a negative real
anchor \(A=-R/2\).
Make the base small enough
that its anchor product lies
inside a fixed strict negative
cone \(W\), disjoint from \(S\).
The flat root estimate FD.17
permits this choice.
The set \(W\cap X\) is
convex and hence contractible.
Choose the base point in
the anchor product over \(Y\).

The path-class construction in
§5.70, PM.A
gives universal covers and
unique path and homotopy lifting:
append straight paths inside
endpoint balls, and subdivide
a compact homotopy square
into such balls.
All complements here are
ordinary complex manifolds,
so these balls exist.

The map \(Z\to Y\) is
locally a punctured-disc
fibration with its fixed
anchor section.
For clarity its trivializations
are precisely the root-disc
homeomorphisms of CF.E.
At a base point put disjoint
closed discs around its simple
roots. On a smaller base
open, the roots move by
holomorphic functions. Translate
each root using a continuous
cutoff supported in its disc.
Take displacements so small
that the Lipschitz constant
of the displacement map is
less than one.
Then the map is injective;
the equation for its inverse
is a convergent contraction.
It fixes the outer annulus
and the anchor.
These are homeomorphisms of
the time disc, carrying
all punctures to their new
positions. They provide the
claimed trivializations.
Analytic formulas below use
fixed contour pieces instead
of differentiating these
topological maps.

We will use an explicit
lifting construction.
On any compact base path
or homotopy, the root
sets have a positive
minimum separation and
positive margins from the
anchor and the outer
boundary. Uniform continuity
permits a finite subdivision
of its time parameter
such that each new root
is uniquely matched to
the nearby old root.
On every step use the
cutoff translations above,
with discs smaller than
the common separation and
displacements small enough
to keep their Lipschitz
constant below one.
The sum of their displacements
is independent of a
labelling of the roots.
It therefore depends continuously
on all the path or
homotopy parameters.
Finite composition gives
homeomorphisms \(L_s\) along
a path, fixing the
anchor, and a continuous
family \(L_{s,u}\) along
a homotopy.
For a based homotopy
the initial maps are
the identity, and all
maps fix the anchor.
The final map of a
loop need not be
the identity on the
rest of the fibre.
This proves the required
homotopy lifting by an
actual finite construction.

For a loop \(\alpha(s)\)
in \(Z\), transport its
base path by these maps
and set \(v(s)=L_s^{-1}\alpha(s)\)
in the initial punctured
fibre. It is a loop
based at the anchor,
since all \(L_s\) fix
that anchor.
The square
\((s,w)\mapsto L_s(v(w))\)
lies in \(Z\).
Its diagonal is the
original loop; its bottom
edge is the anchor
base loop, and its
right edge is a loop
in the initial fibre.
The elementary diagonal-to-two-edges
homotopy in the unit
square proves that the
fibre loops and anchor
base loops generate
\(\pi_1(Z)\).

We also verify the
fibre assertion for the
covers. Over \(Y\), form
the space of endpoint-fixed
homotopy classes of paths
inside each punctured fibre,
starting at the anchor.
A fixed polygonal path
and a short final
endpoint segment give its
local charts over \(Z\).
Two equivalent paths remain
equivalent on a smaller
base open: their compact
fibre homotopy keeps a
positive distance from the
old roots, so it still
avoids all nearby roots.
The same statement for
inequivalent paths follows
by reversing the nearby
cutoff homeomorphisms.
Thus the charts form
a covering of \(Z\),
with its complex structure
inherited from the projection.
Pull it back to the
universal cover of \(Y\).
Each fibre is now,
by construction, the usual
path-class universal cover
of the punctured disc.
The total space is
simply connected as well.
A projected loop bounds
a based homotopy on
that universal base cover.
The continuous cutoff maps
\(L_{s,u}\) constructed above
lift to the fibre
path classes by applying
each map to every
point of a representative
path. They fix the
constant anchor path.
Write the original loop
as \(L_{s,0}(v(s))\).
The paths
\(L_{s,u}(v(s))\) are
based loops throughout
the contraction: both ends
are the constant anchor
path, even when the
final homeomorphism is
nontrivial.
At the contracted base
loop all root displacements
are zero, so \(L_{s,1}\)
is the identity.
The remaining loop \(v\)
is in one simply
connected fibre and
contracts there.
Consequently this is the
universal cover of \(Z\),
and its fibres over the
base cover are indeed
simply connected.
No assertion about the
second homotopy group of
the base is being
imported.

Inclusion \(Z\hookrightarrow X\setminus S\)
is surjective on fundamental
groups. To see this, cover
a loop in \(X\setminus S\)
by small convex balls there.
Perturb its subdivision points
off \(D\) inside the overlapping
balls. Join consecutive new
points by their complex
affine line, replacing the
finitely many zeros of
a defining equation of \(D\)
by small planar detours.
These paths avoid \(D\).
The replacements and endpoint
adjustments are homotopic to
the old segments inside
the same convex balls.
This gives the required
surjection.

Every anchor lift of a
base loop contracts inside
the anchor product in
\(X\setminus S\), since
that whole product includes
the base discriminant and
misses \(S\).
Consequently the image of
any one fibre group
generates \(\Gamma\).

The group of a disc
with \(m\) punctures is
generated by \(m\) meridians.
For the needed elementary
picture, choose a generic
fibre with distinct imaginary
parts, as FD.F permits.
Cut horizontally from each
root to the right boundary.
The cuts are disjoint.
Their complement is contractible:
its horizontal intervals deform
to the curve
\[
\operatorname{Re}t
=-\frac34\sqrt{R^2-(\operatorname{Im}t)^2}.
\tag{MC.6}
\]
At every cut height this
curve lies to the left
of all roots, since they
are in \(\Delta_{R/8}\).
Then contract along the
curve. A polygonal loop
transverse to the finitely
many cuts has finitely
many crossings; each crossing
is removed by the corresponding
meridian. The remaining loop
lies in the contractible cut
domain. This proves generation,
including after a small
perturbation of a general loop.
Thus \(d\le m\).

These generating meridians can
be taken arbitrarily close
to the origin.
Given a smaller product
\(\Delta_r\times B_\eta\),
choose a generic \(x'\)
in its base so small
that all the roots over
\(x'\) lie in \(\Delta_{r/8}\).
The full fibre disc
and this smaller root-containing
disc have the same fibre
group: a strictly increasing
radial map fixes the inner
root disc and retracts the
outer annulus, with its
radial interpolation giving
the two homotopies.
Transport the base point
to that fibre along the
anchor product, then along
the negative time segment
to \(-r/2\).
Both paths can be kept
inside \(W\).
The small meridians, conjugated
by this path, generate
the original \(\Gamma\).
No assertion that arbitrary
neighbourhood groups are
isomorphic is needed.

#### MC.B. A continued holomorphic error has trivial monodromy

Let \(h\) be holomorphic
on the universal cover of
\(X\setminus S\).
Suppose its reference branch
on \(W\) agrees near
zero with an ordinary
holomorphic germ \(h_0\).
Choose the small meridians
of MC.A inside a product
where \(h_0\) is holomorphic.
Along their conjugating paths
inside \(W\), continuation
is the fixed reference
branch. Inside the smaller
product it is \(h_0\),
by the identity theorem.
Each small meridian therefore
returns that branch unchanged,
and the inverse conjugating
path returns the same
germ at the original
base point.
These loops generate
\(\Gamma\), so every loop
returns \(h\) unchanged.
The equality of the two
functions then holds on
the whole connected universal
cover by the identity
theorem in path charts.

In particular a difference
of two globally continued
representatives which is
holomorphic at zero stays
that same holomorphic germ
under every loop.
This is stronger than
merely saying that the
initial difference has zero
directional class.

Use the left continuation
convention of PM.A:
traverse \(\delta\) before
\(\gamma\) in \(\gamma\delta\).
Equivalently use inverse
pullback of geometric deck
transformations for a left
action on functions.
Then
\[
T_{\gamma\delta}=T_\gamma T_\delta.
\tag{MC.7}
\]

#### MC.C. The special action without a finite-monodromy hypothesis

Let \(\Pi=\pi_1(Z)\), and let
\(\widetilde Z\) and \(\widetilde Y\)
be the covers just constructed.
The fibre map gives a
map from \(\widetilde Z\)
to \(\Delta_R\times\widetilde Y\)
away from the roots.
Its fibres are connected
universal covers of the
punctured time disc.
Let
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathscr F=\underset{U}{\operatorname{colim}}\,
 \mathcal O\bigl(c^{-1}(U\cap Z)\bigr),\\
\mathscr G=\underset{U}{\operatorname{colim}}\,
 \mathcal O\bigl(\beta^{-1}(U\setminus D)\bigr).
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.8}
\]
Here \(\beta:\Delta_R\times\widetilde Y
\to X\setminus D\), and
pullback identifies \(\mathscr G\)
with a subspace of
\(\mathscr F\).
Use smaller products containing
all the roots over their
smaller bases.
These products are cofinal,
by the finite root bound.
The covers are restrictions
of the fixed covers;
they are not replaced
by newly identified groups.
Each component of a
restricted base cover is
treated separately.
Its fibres remain the
same universal time covers:
the smaller time disc
contains all punctures,
and the radial annulus
homotopy in MC.A
identifies its fibre
path classes with the
old ones.
A new negative anchor
inside that disc has
a lift on every component,
obtained from the old
anchor along the fixed
root-free negative segment.
Thus no value of an
input outside its smaller
domain is required.

Use exactly the special
fibration ring
\(\widetilde{\mathscr E}^{\,\infty}\)
of
§5.49, ISF.1–ISF.4.
Write its pair as
\(\mu=P_0+V_J\), with
\(J=-K\) in ISF.4.
Its action has the positive
Volterra sign:
\[
\begin{gathered}
P_0=\sum_{\ell,\alpha}
 p_{\ell,\alpha}(t,x)D_t^\ell D_x^\alpha,\\
J=\sum_\alpha j_\alpha(t,s,x)D_x^\alpha,\\
\mathcal A_\lambda(\mu)f=P_0f+V_{\lambda,J}f,\\
V_{\lambda,J}f\\
=\int_{\lambda}^{\,p}(Jf)(t,s,x)\,ds .
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.9}
\]
Here \(Jf\) means the
kernel \(J\) acting in
\(x\) on \(f(s,x)\).
The lower endpoint is a
lift of the anchor over
the base cover.
Paths are in its simply
connected lifted time fibre.
The coefficient hypotheses are
\[
\begin{gathered}
|p_{\ell,\alpha}|
\le M_\varepsilon
 \frac{\varepsilon^{\ell+|\alpha|}}{\ell!\alpha!},\\
\text{every }\varepsilon>0,\\
|j_\alpha|
\le M_\delta\frac{\delta^{|\alpha|}}{\alpha!},\\
\text{every }\delta>0 .
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.10}
\]
The joint time and parameter
domain is fixed before
either epsilon is chosen.

The construction and estimates
PM.C–PM.D apply without
assuming finite determination
of \(f\). We give the
required extension explicitly.
Fix any compact finite
family of lifted paths
and slightly larger root-free
coordinate products around it.
For an arbitrary holomorphic
input \(f\), their finitely
many compact norms have
a finite maximum \(M_f\).
If the spatial Cauchy
margin is \(\eta>0\),
\[
\begin{gathered}
|\partial_x^\alpha f|
\le M_f\alpha!\eta^{-|\alpha|},\\
\sum_\alpha
 |j_\alpha\partial_x^\alpha f|\\
\le M_\delta M_f(1-\delta/\eta)^{-n},\\
0<\delta<\eta .
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.11}
\]
The tail of total degree
at least \(N\), with
\(\theta=\delta/\eta<1\),
is bounded by
\[
M_\delta M_f
\theta^{N/2}(1-\sqrt\theta)^{-n}.
\tag{MC.12}
\]
These are the exact products
of geometric series, as
in PM.14–PM.15.
Integration multiplies the
bound by the finite total
path length.
The ordinary part has the
same estimate in \(n+1\)
variables, after choosing
\(\varepsilon\) below both
normal and spatial Cauchy
margins.
Every fixed further derivative
uses one additional reserved
margin.

There is no bound on
the number of branches
in this argument.
Each compact family uses
only its finite lifted
chart cover and its
finite path family.
All paths stay in the
same physical time disc.
The arbitrary spatial epsilon
does not shrink that disc.
Consequently a long contour
costs its length, while
the full joint kernel
still converges there.

On a small output chart,
choose fixed intermediate
contour pieces and one
short final segment to
the varying endpoint.
The same pieces avoid
the roots for nearby
base parameters.
Normal convergence proves
joint holomorphy by differentiation
under these finite integrals.
The polygonal Cauchy argument
on a lifted homotopy square
proves path independence.
It is the path argument
of PM.C with a single
arbitrary input in place
of finitely many coefficient
labels.

A change of lifted anchor
subtracts a fixed connecting
path integral.
Its output time appears
only in the kernel
coefficient. This integral
is therefore holomorphic
on the whole smaller
output time disc over
the base cover, including
the root points. It
belongs to \(\mathscr G\).
Both parts preserve
\(\mathscr G\): use local
Cauchy estimates for \(P_0\)
and a straight time segment
for \(V_J\), since an
input in \(\mathscr G\)
is nonsingular at the
fibre roots.

The four exact product
formulas ISF.11–ISF.17
remain valid on these
lifted paths.
For two negative parts,
Fubini on the ordered
path triangle gives the
convolution integral ISF.16.
Its inner integrand contains
only joint holomorphic
kernel coefficients, so
its inner path may be
replaced by a straight
segment, even across
the root positions.
The input function remains
on the outer root-avoiding
path.
All spatial products are
the absolutely convergent
ISF.11 sums with bound
ISF.12.
For the two mixed cases,
differentiation and integration
by parts give ISF.14
and ISF.15 on each
fixed contour family.
The complete infinite sums
have the fixed normal
and spatial margins in
that proof.
The lower endpoint series
ISF.17 is retained; as
a function of output
time it is holomorphic
on the full disc and
therefore belongs to
\(\mathscr G\).
The ordinary-ordinary product
is its full Cauchy product.
Thus
\[
\begin{gathered}
(\mu\nu)[f]=\mu(\nu[f]),\\
1[f]=[f]
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.13}
\]
in \(\mathscr F/\mathscr G\),
with exactly the actual
special-ring product.

The action commutes with
the \(\Pi\)-action.
Every deck transformation
induces a base deck
transformation and fixes
the physical time coordinate.
It consequently preserves
\(\mathscr G\).
Indeed for a geometric
deck transformation \(d\),
the two expressions
\(d^*\mathcal A_\lambda(\mu)f\)
and \(\mathcal A_\lambda(\mu)d^*f\)
have the same upper endpoint.
Their difference is the
integral between the two
lifted anchor sections.
This is holomorphic on
the full output time
disc over the base cover,
by MC.11–MC.12.
It lies in \(\mathscr G\).
The ordinary infinite part
commutes exactly.
Hence
\[
\begin{gathered}
T_\gamma\bigl(\mu[f]\bigr)
=\mu\,T_\gamma[f]\\
\text{in }\mathscr F/\mathscr G .
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.14}
\]
Only the chosen-fibration
special ring has been
used on this quotient.

#### MC.D. A cylinder error which is regular at an anchor

We need the following
holomorphic extension statement.
Suppose \(g(t,\widetilde x)\)
is holomorphic on a full
time disc times a connected
covering of \(B\setminus H\).
Suppose that near one
nonzero time \(A'\), it
is the pullback of a
holomorphic function on
a time neighbourhood of
\(A'\) times the whole
base ball \(B\).
Then, after a smaller
base ball, \(g\) descends
and extends holomorphically
through the base discriminant
for every time in the
given disc.

First fix any two points
of the cover above the
same \(x\). Their two
time functions agree near
\(A'\), by the assumed
anchor function. The identity
theorem in time makes
them agree on the
whole time disc.
If initially the equality
to the anchor function
is known on just one
open lift, the identity
theorem on the connected
base cover gives that
equality on its whole
anchor product first.
The descended function is
holomorphic on
\(\Delta\times(B\setminus H)\).

Here is the extension
through \(H\), with no
growth hypothesis.
Choose a complex coordinate
line on which the
first nonzero homogeneous
part of a defining
equation for \(H\)
does not vanish identically.
Write the coordinates
as \(x=(z,w)\).
Choose a small circle
\(|\zeta|=r\) on that
line which misses \(H\).
By compactness it still
misses \(H\) for all
small \(w\).
The finite-root preparation
and continuity used in
CF.B place all the
nearby intersections of
\(H\) strictly inside
that circle.
Write \(g_t(z,w)=g(t,z,w)\)
and define
\[
\begin{gathered}
\widehat g(t,z,w)\\
=\frac1{2\pi i}
 \int_{|\zeta|=r}
 \frac{g_t(\zeta,w)}{\zeta-z}\,d\zeta .
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.15}
\]
The integrand has a
fixed compact nonsingular
contour, so this is
jointly holomorphic for
\(|z|<r\).
Near \(t=A'\), the
ordinary Cauchy formula
for the anchor function
gives \(\widehat g=g\).
For every fixed \(x\)
outside \(H\), both
sides are holomorphic on
the whole time disc.
The identity theorem in
time gives equality there
for every \(t\).
Thus MC.15 is the
required extension.
For \(n=1\) this is
the same one-circle proof
without \(w\); for \(n=0\)
there is no discriminant
to remove.

#### MC.E. Relating the function quotient to a directional relation

Take finitely many functions
\(f_i\) continuing on
the cover of \(X\setminus S\),
and finitely many special
operators \(\mu_i\).
Their directional classes
are actual classes of
CF.A. Namely, the cofinal
future-convex supports in
CF.A and FD.C contain
the whole \(S\).
Each convex complement
\(I_Z\) is simply connected
and avoids \(S\).
Its path-class lift, fixed
by the reference branch
on \(W\), gives a
holomorphic representative
on that whole complement.
The same construction applies
to every \(T_\gamma f_i\).
On the reference negative
cone form
\[
H_\lambda=\sum_i\mathcal A_\lambda(\mu_i)f_i .
\tag{MC.16}
\]
The actual calibration
ISF.13, PM.D and CF.A
identifies its directional
class with
\(\sum_i\mu_i[f_i]\)
using the full kernel
action, not a formal
normal-order sum.

Assume that this directional
class is zero.
On a smaller negative
cone, \(H_\lambda\) then
agrees with an ordinary
holomorphic germ \(h_0\).
Indeed the zero has a
cofinal support witness;
that support misses every
fixed strict negative cone
after shrinking. Restriction
and the identity theorem
give the asserted equality
of holomorphic representatives.

The anchor can be moved
closer to zero inside
the domain of \(h_0\).
The difference is a
fixed past-path integral,
with input paths in the
negative cone.
All these input functions
are holomorphic near that
compact path for the
whole smaller base ball.
MC.11–MC.12 proves that
its full spatial sum
is holomorphic on a
full output time disc
and that smaller base.
Thus it changes \(h_0\)
only by an ordinary
holomorphic function.
This is the two-anchor
normalization, with all
spatial indices retained.

Choose the new anchor
inside a product where
this new holomorphic
representative is defined.
Shrink the base until
all fibre roots are
inside its normal disc.
First verify that the
anchor values over
the base cover agree
with one ordinary anchor
function. To verify this,
the anchor lift and
its short time neighbourhood
are inside the reference
negative cone on
\(X\setminus S\).
Every \(f_i\) is single
valued there. Base loops
in the anchor product
contract in \(X\setminus S\),
so their lifts do not
change those values.
The local derivative and
integral formulas have
that same property.
Equivalently apply the
identity theorem on a
connected restricted base
cover to its anchor
product.
On the ordinary anchor
product this function
equals the new holomorphic
representative, since they
already agree on its
nonempty negative-cone open.
Thus they agree at the
anchor of every lifted
fibre, on every restricted
base component.

In each such fibre,
all meridians can be
drawn inside the ordinary
holomorphic product.
Continuation of \(H_\lambda\)
around them returns the
same holomorphic function.
Since they generate the
whole fibre group, the
function descends and
extends across every root.
These extensions are
jointly holomorphic: near
the roots they are the
given ordinary representative,
and off the roots they
are the descended holomorphic
function on the cover.
They agree on overlaps
by the identity theorem.
Consequently
\[
H_\lambda\in\mathscr G .
\tag{MC.17}
\]
Changing back to the
old anchor adds only
the full-time holomorphic
past-path integral, so
MC.17 holds for it
as well.

Now take a loop in
\(\Gamma\), and lift it
to a loop in \(\Pi\)
using MC.A.
The functions \(T_\gamma f_i\)
still continue on
\(X\setminus S\).
Equations MC.14 and MC.17
give
\[
\sum_i\mathcal A_\lambda(\mu_i)T_\gamma f_i
\in\mathscr G .
\tag{MC.18}
\]
Near any sufficiently small
negative anchor its left
side is holomorphic on
the whole ordinary base
ball: use the short
anchor paths and the
ordinary branches of the
\(T_\gamma f_i\) on \(W\).
If the representative of
MC.18 uses a smaller
output disc, move the
anchor inside that disc;
the fixed past-path integral
is again ordinary holomorphic.
The cylinder-extension lemma
MC.D applies. Thus the
left side of MC.18
is an ordinary holomorphic
germ at zero.
Its directional class
is zero:
\[
\sum_i\mu_i[T_\gamma f_i]=0
\quad\text{in }\mathcal C_{p_0}.
\tag{MC.19}
\]
This proves the precise
continuation rule needed
for every presentation row.
It does not assert an
action of arbitrary finite
or full microlocal symbols
on \(\mathscr F/\mathscr G\).

#### MC.F. All actual relations and the monodromy group law

The bounded actual presentation
from
§5.31, L.4–L.6
and
§5.49, ISF.3–ISF.4
has finite matrices over
the spatial-polynomial coefficient
ring. That ring is
contained in the special
ring by ISF.9.
Its actual finite counterpart
has degree-zero cokernel
equal to the whole
\(M\).
No exactness over the
canonical coefficient ring
is needed here.

Theorem CF.1 supplies
one common continuation
domain for the finitely
many basis-generator values.
For every presentation row
and each basis vector,
the initial directional
relation is zero.
There are finitely many
such relations.
The two-anchor construction
in MC.E and a common
shrink give the product
\(X\) used above for
all of them.
Every continued row
has zero directional class
by MC.19.
The continued generator
classes thus define an
actual \(\mathscr E_{p_0}\)-linear
homomorphism from the
finite presentation of \(M\).
This establishes the asserted
map \(T_\gamma\Phi\in V\)
on the whole module.
Finite-ring linearity follows
from that actual cokernel,
including coefficients outside
the special ring.

The action is linear.
To check its group law,
write the generator values
of \(T_\delta\Phi_a\)
as the corresponding linear
combination of the fixed
basis-generator functions.
Their difference from
the functions \(T_\delta f_{ai}\)
has zero directional class.
Both sets of functions
continue on the whole
cover of \(X\setminus S\),
so that difference agrees
near zero with an ordinary
holomorphic germ, by the
same representative identity
used in MC.E.
MC.B makes its every
continuation return that
same germ.
Continuing once more
therefore gives exactly
the classes prescribed
by MC.7. Hence
\[
\begin{gathered}
\rho(\gamma\delta)
=\rho(\gamma)\rho(\delta),\\
\rho(1)=I .
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.20}
\]
The inverse loop gives
the inverse matrix.
This is a representation,
not only a family of
linear maps chosen separately
for different loops.

The same argument applies
to a change of continuing
representatives: their difference
is a continued holomorphic
germ, and MC.B makes
its directional class stay
zero. On a common
smaller admissible product,
the path-class restriction
and the same finite
presentation matrices commute
with all formulas. Its
representation is the pullback
along the inclusion-induced
map of fundamental groups.
No inverse for that
group map is presumed.

#### MC.G. One finite-determination ideal for the function representatives

Put \(A_\Gamma=\mathbf C[\Gamma]\),
let \(I\) be its augmentation
ideal, and set
\[
\begin{gathered}
\chi:A_\Gamma\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\mathbf C}(V),\\
\mathfrak c=\ker\chi,\\
\mathfrak a=I\mathfrak c .
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.21}
\]
Both ideals are two-sided.
The representation gives
\[
\dim_{\mathbf C}A_\Gamma/\mathfrak c
\le q^2 .
\tag{MC.22}
\]
For \(c\in\mathfrak c\),
every function \(c f_{ai}\)
has zero directional class
and is an ordinary
holomorphic germ near zero.
It continues on the whole
cover of \(X\setminus S\),
as a finite linear
combination of the fixed
continued functions.
MC.B therefore gives the
function equality
\[
\begin{gathered}
(\gamma-1)c f_{ai}=0\\
\text{for every }\gamma\in\Gamma.
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.23}
\]
By the identity theorem
the equality holds on
the whole connected cover.
Thus \(\mathfrak a\) annihilates
every \(f_{ai}\) as a
function, not only as
a directional quotient class.

Let \(g_1,\ldots,g_d\)
generate \(\Gamma\).
The word identity
\[
\begin{gathered}
ab-1\\
=(a-1)b+(b-1)
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.24}
\]
and
\(g_j^{-1}-1=-(g_j-1)g_j^{-1}\)
show that
\[
I=\sum_{j=1}^d(g_j-1)A_\Gamma .
\tag{MC.25}
\]
Since \(\mathfrak c\) is
two-sided,
\(I\mathfrak c=\sum_j(g_j-1)\mathfrak c\).
The linear map
\[
\begin{gathered}
(A_\Gamma/\mathfrak c)^d
\longrightarrow I/I\mathfrak c,\\
(\bar r_j)_j\longmapsto
 \sum_j(g_j-1)r_j
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.26}
\]
is well defined and
surjective. The quotient
by \(I\) has dimension
one, so
\[
\begin{gathered}
\dim A_\Gamma/\mathfrak a\\
=1+\dim I/I\mathfrak c\\
\le 1+dq^2 .
\end{gathered}
\tag{MC.27}
\]
This proves MC.3.
Each individual function
orbit is an image of
\(A_\Gamma/\mathfrak a\);
the same ideal works
for all the finitely
many chosen functions.
Zero functions and the
zero module are immediate;
one may take the whole
group algebra as annihilator
when there are no
nonzero inputs.

The theorem supplies the
actual monodromy representation
and a common finite
function determination.
The conversion to a
finite coherent D-type
module, with the full
infinite-order evaluation map,
still requires the algebraic
tensor witnesses of III.4.9
and the actual comparison
maps proved earlier.

### 5.86. A faithful D-type realization of the whole infinite extension

Let \(M\) be a coherent actual holonomic microlocal module in
generic position at \(p_0=(0;dt)\), and put
\[
\begin{gathered}
E=\mathscr E_{p_0},\qquad B=\mathscr E^\infty_{p_0},\\
R=\mathcal D^\infty_{X,0},\\
N=B\otimes_E M .
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.1}
\]
The action of \(R\) on \(N\) uses the actual inclusions
\(R\subset T\subset B\), where \(T\) is the chosen-fibration
special ring of ISF.1–ISF.5. Its ordinary part and its map to
the full microlocal ring are those actual kernel maps.
The hypersurface \(S\) is the ordinary projection of the whole
characteristic support. Keep the actual directional module \(\mathcal C\)
of §5.82, CF.A.
Write
\[
\begin{gathered}
V=\operatorname{Hom}_E(M,\mathcal C),\\
q=\dim_{\mathbf C}V .
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.2}
\]
Its finite dimension and its whole-module interpretation are
§5.83, FD.1.

**Theorem EV.1.** There are a finite D-type module \(L\) along exactly
\(S\), an embedded trivial connection \(\mathcal O_X^q\), and a coherent
holonomic finite-operator quotient
\[
\begin{gathered}
K=L/\mathcal O_X^q,\\
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal D_X}(\mathcal O_X,K)_0=0 .
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.3}
\]
There is an actual \(R\)-linear injection \(e:N\to K^\infty_0\), where
\(K^\infty=R\otimes_{\mathcal D_X}K\), such that
\[
\begin{gathered}
\Psi:N\longrightarrow B\otimes_R K^\infty_0\\
\simeq B\otimes_{\mathcal D_{X,0}}K_0,\\
\Psi(s)=1\otimes e(s)
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.4}
\]
is \(B\)-linear and injective. These are stalk maps of the actual
ordinary algebraic tensors. No finite-pole conclusion for \(M\) is
included in this assertion.

#### EV.A. Continuation of arbitrary infinite-extension sections

Choose the finitely many spanning ordinary fibrations \(F_j\) of
CF.C, with vertical vectors
\[
v_0,\ v_0-\lambda e_1,\ldots,v_0-\lambda e_n .
\tag{EV.5}
\]
They keep the time coordinate and its directional tangent condition.
The actual finite, infinite and real coordinate maps are
§5.56, BCT.5.3.
The entire transported module has a finite principal fibre in each
fibration, by CF.C. Thus the full Späth generation theorem
§5.49, ISR.2
applies in each of them.

For any \(s\in N\), it gives a finite expression
\[
\begin{gathered}
s=\sum_i a_{j,i}u_{j,i},\\
a_{j,i}\in A_j^\infty .
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.6}
\]
The generators \(u_{j,i}\) belong to the actual finite module in that
fibration. The time-only ring \(A_j^\infty\) is contained in its actual
special ring by ISF.9. Each expression is obtained in its own
coordinates; it is not obtained by transporting a finite spatial degree.

Fix finitely many such sections and finitely many functionals in \(V\).
CF.1 gives common full-complement continuations for their finitely many
generator values. Apply every \(a_{j,i}\) by its full ordinary head and
joint Volterra kernel. The arbitrary-input construction
§5.85, MC.C
produces holomorphic functions on the covers of
\[
\begin{gathered}
U_j\setminus(S\cup D_j),\\
D_j=F_j^{-1}(H_j).
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.7}
\]
All normal domains are chosen before the spatial epsilon; long lifted
contours cost their finite length. Both infinite coefficient tails and
all spatial indices are therefore retained.

On a common strict negative cone these functions represent the same
class \(\Phi^\infty(s)\). Their differences extend as ordinary
holomorphic germs by CF.8. Subtract these finitely many germs on a
common smaller ordinary ball. The functions then have exactly the same
initial scalar germ.

The bad cylinders have intersection of codimension at least two by
CF.13 and CF.F. That proof depends only on the spanning vertical
directions: a common hypersurface component would be tangent to all
of them at a regular point. The all-branch path argument of CF.F now
applies to EV.7. Its convex-ball detours arrange each overlap path
outside all cylinders, so the next fibration continues the branch
which has actually arrived there. CF.G then removes the remaining
codimension-two set: its small complement balls are connected and
simply connected, and the fixed-circle Cauchy extension identifies
the continued holomorphic functions. These arguments use no equation
for the resulting scalar function.

Consequently every prescribed finite list of values
\(\Phi^\infty(s)\), with \(s\) in the whole \(N\), has full multivalued
holomorphic representatives on one ordinary \(U\setminus S\).
The neighbourhood may depend on that finite list.

#### EV.B. A stable finite function algebra

Fix a product \(U_0\) carrying the basis-generator functions of MC.1
and its actual representation \(\rho_0\) on \(V\). Use a cofinal system
of smaller root-containing products \(U\), with the same reduced
Weierstrass degree \(m\). Base points and their comparison paths lie
in the fixed negative cone. Write
\[
\begin{gathered}
\Gamma_U=\pi_1(U\setminus S),\\
\rho_U:\Gamma_U\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(V).
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.8}
\]
Here \(\rho_U\) is the pullback of \(\rho_0\).

Every inclusion of two such products induces a surjective group map.
Indeed MC.A shows that the larger group is generated by the meridians
in any one generic fibre. Choose that fibre sufficiently close to zero
that all punctures lie in the smaller time disc. The same meridians
then lie in the smaller product. Its own negative anchor paths and
the larger anchor paths differ by a homotopy in the common convex
negative cone. Thus their images are precisely a generating set of
the larger group. An isomorphism of the groups is unnecessary.

For \(s\in N\), choose a full-complement representative \(f_s\) of
EV.A on a common such \(U\), and use the original fibration expression
\(s=\sum_i a_i u_i\) in EV.6. The relation
\[
\sum_i a_i[f_i]-[f_s]=0\quad\text{in }\mathcal C
\tag{EV.9}
\]
is a finite relation between globally continued inputs with special
coefficients. MC.E applies to this exact relation, including the
coefficient \(-1\) of \(f_s\). For every \(\gamma\in\Gamma_U\) it gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
{}[T_\gamma f_s]\\
=\sum_i a_i[T_\gamma f_i]\\
=(\rho_U(\gamma)\Phi)^\infty(s).
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.10}
\]
The last equality uses actual extension adjunction and ISR.2, not
continuation of an infinite normal-order sum.

Put
\[
\begin{gathered}
A_U=\mathbf C[\Gamma_U],\\
c_U=\ker(A_U\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbf C}V),\\
a_U=I_Uc_U ,
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.11}
\]
where \(I_U\) is the augmentation ideal. The proof MC.G applies with
EV.10. Each \(c f_s\), for \(c\in c_U\), is a globally continued
ordinary holomorphic germ at zero. MC.B makes all its continuations
unchanged. Hence \(a_U\) annihilates \(f_s\) as a function, on every
branch, and
\[
\dim_{\mathbf C}A_U/a_U\le 1+mq^2 .
\tag{EV.12}
\]
This ideal works for the whole finite list of sections and functionals.

There is one stabilized algebra for all further germs. For
\(U'\subset U\), the surjection \(h:A_{U'}\to A_U\) satisfies
\[
\begin{gathered}
c_{U'}=h^{-1}(c_U),\\
h(I_{U'})=I_U,\\
h(a_{U'})=a_U .
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.13}
\]
It therefore gives a surjective algebra map
\[
A_{U'}/a_{U'}\longrightarrow A_U/a_U .
\tag{EV.14}
\]
The finite dimensions are nondecreasing under shrinking and are
bounded by EV.12. Choose \(U_*\) at which their maximum is attained.
Every map EV.14 to this product, from a smaller admissible product,
is an isomorphism: it is surjective between spaces of the same
dimension. In particular \(a_{U'}\) is the inverse image of \(a_{U_*}\).

Thus
\[
A_*=A_{U_*}/a_{U_*}
\tag{EV.15}
\]
controls every value of every whole infinite-extension section,
on its own sufficiently small representative domain. This proves
stability of finite algebra quotients; it makes no assertion that
the underlying fundamental groups stabilize.

#### EV.C. The finite D-type quotient and its directional injection

Let \(a_*=a_{U_*}\). The cyclic dual construction PD.39–PD.44 and
the prescribed-complement theorem
§5.79, FB.D–FB.E
give an actual finite D-type module \(L_*\) along \(S\).
Its ordinary infinite extension is, by the actual all-parameter map
FB.39,
\[
\begin{gathered}
R\otimes_{\mathcal D_X}L_*
\simeq\mathscr F_{a_*},\\
\operatorname{rank}(L_*|_{X\setminus S})
=\dim_{\mathbf C}A_* .
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.16}
\]
Here \(\mathscr F_{a_*}\) consists of all jointly holomorphic branch
functions of that type, as germs on the fixed restricted covers.
EV.14 identifies this space with the corresponding local function
spaces on all further products.
Explicitly, if a small-complement loop maps to the identity in
\(\Gamma_{U_*}\), its difference from \(1\) lies in \(a_U\).
Every function of type \(a_U\) is invariant under that kernel,
so descends from the small universal cover to the restriction of
the fixed cover. The surjective group map makes this restricted
cover connected. Conversely, pullback of a function of type
\(a_*\) is annihilated by \(a_U\), since these ideals are exact
inverse images. The descents are holomorphic in the ordinary
covering charts.

Since \(a_*\subset I_{U_*}\), augmentation gives a nonzero invariant
functional on \(A_*\). Its invariant functional space has dimension
one:
\[
A_*/I_{U_*}A_*\simeq\mathbf C .
\tag{EV.17}
\]
Every horizontal germ in \(L_*\) restricts to an invariant vector
on a smaller complement. Its group surjects onto
\(\Gamma_{U_*}\), so this is the same one-dimensional invariant
space. A meromorphic section vanishing on that complement is
zero. Thus the horizontal germs of \(L_*\) are exactly the
constant multiples of this unit.
The corresponding horizontal section is the scalar function \(1\).
It embeds the trivial connection \(\mathcal O_X\) in \(L_*\).
Here is its finite-module extension. Apply FB.D also to the
trivial local system. Its normalized lattice is
\(\mathcal O_X\): this is the residue-zero logarithmic lattice on
the normalized locus, and the reflexive extension DT.E identifies
it everywhere. DT.21 therefore identifies that finite D-type
module with \(\mathcal O_X(*S)\).
The invariant local-system map extends uniquely to
\(\mathcal O_X(*S)\to L_*\) by DT.E.
Restrict to \(\mathcal O_X\).
The resulting map is injective, since its restriction off \(S\)
is injective and an ordinary holomorphic function vanishing on
that dense open is zero. Under FB.39 its map is precisely
the ordinary scalar-function inclusion.

Set \(K_*=L_*/\mathcal O_X\). It is coherent holonomic. It has no
horizontal germ. To see this directly, lift a horizontal germ of
\(K_*\) to \(l\in L_*\). In coordinates \(z_1,\ldots,z_{n+1}\),
write \(\partial_i l=b_i\in\mathcal O_X\).
Commuting derivatives gives \(\partial_i b_j=\partial_j b_i\).
The holomorphic function
\[
h(z)=\int_0^1\sum_i z_i b_i(\lambda z)\,d\lambda
\tag{EV.18}
\]
has \(\partial_i h=b_i\): differentiate the integrand and use the
closedness identity to obtain the derivative of
\(\lambda b_i(\lambda z)\). Thus \(l-h\) is horizontal in \(L_*\).
EV.17 makes it a constant multiple of the embedded unit, so its
quotient germ is zero.

Ordinary right flatness of \(R\) over \(\mathcal D_X\), proved in
§5.47, MF.6–MF.7,
and the empty-divisor case of SI give
\[
K_*^\infty\simeq\mathscr F_{a_*}/\mathcal O_X .
\tag{EV.19}
\]
Every function on the right gives an actual directional class by
the anchored lift on the convex complements of CF.A and FD.C.
This defines an \(R\)-linear map
\[
j:K_*^\infty\longrightarrow\mathcal C .
\tag{EV.20}
\]
Its ordinary infinite action is the actual action: FB.39 and ISF
use the same every-epsilon holomorphic heads on each larger
Cauchy product.

The map is injective. A class in its kernel has a branch agreeing
near zero with an ordinary holomorphic germ. MC.B fixes this
globally continued error under all meridians, and hence under
the whole complement group. Apply it on the universal cover
of a smaller representative product. Surjectivity to the fixed
group accounts for every branch of its restricted cover.
It is the same ordinary germ on
every branch of a smaller representative domain, so is zero
in EV.19.

For each \(\Phi\in V\), EV.A–EV.15 therefore define a unique map
\[
\begin{gathered}
e_\Phi:N\longrightarrow K_*^\infty,\\
j e_\Phi=\Phi^\infty .
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.21}
\]
Uniqueness also proves its linearity and its \(R\)-linearity:
apply the injective \(j\), use the actual \(R\)-action, and use
the \(B\)-linearity of \(\Phi^\infty\). This does not yet assert
linearity of the tensor-unit map over \(B\).

#### EV.D. The actual normal-parameter module

One independent parameter \(u\) suffices. Let \(X'\) have
coordinates \((u,s,x)\), let \(p'_0=(0;0,ds)\), and use finite
and full rings \(E',B'\) there. The original rings embed by
operators independent of \(u,D_u\). Put
\[
\begin{gathered}
H=E'/E'D_u,\\
M^{[u]}=H\otimes_E M,\\
N^{[u]}=B'\otimes_{E'}M^{[u]} .
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.22}
\]
These are actual algebraic quotients and tensors.

Here is the normal form needed for the first quotient. In the
chart \(\tau_s\ne0\), use \(\eta=\nu_u/\tau_s\).
For every homogeneous coefficient \(p_k(u,s,x,\xi/\tau_s,\eta)\),
Taylor division gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
p_k(\eta)-p_k(0)=\eta q_k(\eta),\\
q_k(\eta)=\int_0^1
                  \partial_\eta p_k(\lambda\eta)\,d\lambda .
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.23}
\]
Choose a larger covariable disc before all indices.
Cauchy's formula bounds \(q_k\) by the old coefficient norm
times its fixed inverse margin. Multiplying by \(\tau_s^{-1}\)
shifts the homogeneous order by one. A fixed exponential
enlargement absorbs the resulting negative factorial ratio;
for the positive every-epsilon head choose the input epsilon
smaller first. The same fixed-margin argument bounds every
prescribed further derivative. Thus the coefficient sums give
an actual operator \(Q\), in the finite class for a finite
upper order and in the full class otherwise, with
\[
P=P|_{\nu_u=0}+QD_u .
\tag{EV.24}
\]
Right multiplication by \(D_u\) is exactly multiplication by
\(\nu_u\) on these symbols. The remainder is unique.
For several parameters repeat this division in their ordered
covariables.

A finite presentation of \(M\), together with \(D_u\) on its
generators, is a finite presentation of EV.22 over \(E'\).
Finite-ring coherence makes \(M^{[u]}\) coherent. Its actual
finite-module support is contained in
\[
\operatorname{supp}M\times\{(u;\nu_u=0)\}.
\tag{EV.25}
\]
Use the actual finite support convention of
§5.32, J.1–J.2.
If \(\nu_u\ne0\), \(D_u\) is an actual elliptic unit, so its
relations kill every generator. If \(\nu_u=0\) and the old
cotangent point is outside \(\operatorname{supp}M\), the old
finite presentation has zero cokernel. Its finitely many
unit rows express all generators in its relation rows.
Their actual coefficient identities, extended independently
of \(u,\nu_u\), express every new generator as zero too.
This proves the stated containment without a scalar-flatness
or a principal base-change assertion.
The reverse support containment follows from EV.24.
At any fixed \(u=a\), evaluation of its remainder is a right
\(E\)-linear map \(H\to E\), split by constant operators.
Right \(E\)-linearity holds because an old operator differentiates
only \(s,x\), and its coefficients are independent of \(u\).
Tensor these two maps with \(M\). Wherever \(M\) is nonzero,
the resulting split copy is nonzero in the new stalk.
Thus the reduced support is exactly the product in EV.25.
The set in EV.25 is Lagrangian of the new base dimension.
Thus \(M^{[u]}\) is holonomic, with the zero object allowed.
Its fibre over the new origin is contained in the one ray
through \(p'_0\), so it is in generic position.

The map \(N\to N^{[u]}\), sending a finite tensor
\(b\otimes m\) to the same operator and generator, respects
every \(E\)-balance relation. Its image is killed by \(D_u\).
No injectivity of a parameter tensor is required below.

Its whole directional Hom is canonically \(V\). Pullback of
representatives gives one direction. Conversely, the images
of the original generators under a functional for \(M^{[u]}\)
satisfy \(D_u f=0\) in the new directional module.
Choose a common convex representative domain from CF.A;
its isotropic future majorant is preserved by \(u\mapsto\lambda u\),
for \(0\le\lambda\le1\).
The derivative \(\partial_u f\) is an ordinary holomorphic germ.
Subtract its holomorphic \(u\)-primitive based at zero.
The resulting representative is independent of \(u\).
Restriction to \(u=0\) then gives the original directional class.
The old finite relations hold there, and pullback restores all
classes. The universal property of \(H\otimes_E M\) verifies
the two inverse Hom maps. For several parameters use the
closed-form radial primitive EV.18.

The actual actions agree under these maps. Symbols independent
of the parameter act by their original full kernels, and
the removed \(D_u\)-terms act by zero on constant representatives.
The finite quotient EV.24 and the common Cauchy estimates verify
this with all tails retained.

The characteristic projection in EV.25 is exactly
the product of the parameter disc with \(S\).
Apply EV.A–EV.B to this actual module, restricting functions
to the complement of that product. Its group is \(\Gamma_U\),
by contraction of the parameter disc, and its Hom representation
is \(\rho_U\). The same stabilized algebra \(A_*\) therefore
applies, with no new dimension bound or stabilization choice.

The all-parameter comparison FB.39, followed by the ordinary
exact quotient by the trivial connection, gives an injective
map of the parameter version of \(K_*^\infty\) into its
directional module. Hence EV.21 has a canonical parameter
version
\[
e_\Phi^{[u]}:N^{[u]}\longrightarrow K_*^{\infty,[u]} .
\tag{EV.26}
\]
It is linear over the full ordinary
\(D^\infty_{u,s,x}\), by the same injective-action argument.
On the embedded \(N\) it is the constant-parameter pullback
of \(e_\Phi\). These statements concern actual ordinary tensors:
the inverse in FB.39 has the finite row witnesses PD.35–PD.36.
The finite parameter quotient is exact as well. In ST.13 its
transfer is \(\mathcal O_{X'}\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}\mathcal D_X\);
the coefficient projection is flat by the completion proof of
GL06, Lemma3.0c.1.
Explicitly, let \(A_0=\mathcal O_{X,0}\), and localize
\(A_0[u]\) at its origin maximal ideal. This is flat over \(A_0\).
Its Noetherian completion and that of \(\mathcal O_{X',0}\)
are the same formal power-series ring. Flatness of the first
completion and faithful flatness of the second are the
Noetherian completion theorem
Completion, Theorems3.1–3.2.
A kernel after tensor with \(\mathcal O_{X',0}\) would survive
its faithful completion, where flatness over \(A_0\) makes it
zero. This proves the stated coefficient flatness.
Thus its tensor sends \(L_*/\mathcal O_X\) to
\(L_*^{[u]}/\mathcal O_{X'}\). The ordinary infinite extension
is exact by MF.6–MF.7 in the new dimension. This gives precisely
the target in EV.26.

#### EV.E. A finite tensor witness from the normal primitive

Use the exact special quotient and external transfer of
§5.71, ST.A–ST.D.
Thus
\[
\begin{gathered}
T=\widetilde{\mathscr E}^{\,\infty}_{X,0},\\
A=D^\infty_{u,s,x},\\
C_{\mathrm{tr}}=A/AD_u,\\
J=T/R\\
\simeq C_{\mathrm{tr}}/D_sC_{\mathrm{tr}} .
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.27}
\]
Here \(C_{\mathrm{tr}}\) is the transfer quotient, distinct
from the directional function module \(\mathcal C\).
All variables \(u,s\) remain independent.

For the finite module \(K_*\), ST.13–ST.15 identifies
\[
C_{\mathrm{tr}}\otimes_R K_*^\infty
       \simeq K_*^{\infty,[u]} .
\tag{EV.28}
\]
There is also a direct map
\[
\begin{gathered}
\kappa:C_{\mathrm{tr}}\otimes_R N\longrightarrow N^{[u]},\\
c\otimes s\longmapsto c\,s^{[u]} .
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.29}
\]
It is well defined: \(D_u s^{[u]}=0\), so \(AD_u\) acts
by zero, and the right \(R\)-balance is the literal operator
action. It commutes with \(D_s\).

Take any element \(v\) of the source of EV.29. It is one
finite sum of elementary tensors. Since \(\tau_s(p'_0)=1\),
the actual operator \(D_s^{-1}\) exists in \(B'\). Form
\[
w=e_\Phi^{[u]}(D_s^{-1}\kappa(v)).
\tag{EV.30}
\]
This is an actual element of the right side of EV.28.
Using EV.26 and \(D_sD_s^{-1}=1\) gives the exact module
identity
\[
D_sw=(C_{\mathrm{tr}}\otimes e_\Phi)(v).
\tag{EV.31}
\]
The equality uses the constant-parameter compatibility of
EV.26 on each of the finitely many entries of \(v\).
It is not an equality only after applying a function map.

ST.12 and EV.31 imply \(J\otimes_R e_\Phi=0\).
The equivalent finite tensor criterion ST.16–ST.19 now gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{im}(T\otimes_R e_\Phi)\\
\subseteq
\operatorname{im}(K_*^\infty\to T\otimes_R K_*^\infty).
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.32}
\]
Specifically, EV.30 supplies the primitive in ST.18.
Represent it by the finite ordinary row supplied by FB.39.
Its equality EV.31 is a finite sum of tensor balancing
relations. Lift their finitely many coefficient factors
through ST.8, project to \(J\), and balance the remaining
ordinary factors into \(K_*^\infty\), exactly as in ST.19.
This produces a finite elementary-tensor equality for every
input in EV.32. No infinite sum of elementary tensors,
completed tensor, or closure of a relation space is involved.

#### EV.F. The full infinite-order linearity and faithfulness

For \(P\in T\) and \(s\in N\), EV.32 gives \(k\in K_*^\infty\)
with
\[
\begin{gathered}
P\otimes e_\Phi(s)=1\otimes k\\
\text{in }T\otimes_R K_*^\infty .
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.33}
\]
Apply the balanced map to the actual directional module,
\[
\begin{gathered}
T\otimes_R K_*^\infty\longrightarrow\mathcal C,\\
P\otimes k\longmapsto Pj(k).
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.34}
\]
Its right balance is precisely the \(R\)-linearity of \(j\).
The left side of EV.33 becomes
\(P\Phi^\infty(s)=\Phi^\infty(Ps)=j(e_\Phi(Ps))\).
The right side is \(j(k)\). Injectivity of \(j\) therefore
identifies \(k=e_\Phi(Ps)\). Consequently
\[
\begin{gathered}
s\longmapsto1\otimes e_\Phi(s)\\
N\longrightarrow T\otimes_R K_*^\infty
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.35}
\]
is \(T\)-linear.

The actual special balancing ISR.3, equations ISR.8–ISR.10, gives
\[
B\otimes_TN\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}N .
\tag{EV.36}
\]
For completeness, its earlier polynomial-coefficient tensor
is \(B\otimes_{R_{\mathrm{pol}}^\infty}N\).
The two inverse multiplication maps are ISR.4–ISR.7, and
\(R_{\mathrm{pol}}^\infty\subset T\) by ISF.9.
Quotient by the additional \(T\)-balance relations.
The inverse \(s\mapsto1\otimes s\) is \(B\)-linear before that
quotient, hence after it.
Multiplication and this map are inverse on every elementary
tensor. This proves EV.36 without an extension-flatness assertion.

Tensor EV.35 on the left by \(B\) over \(T\), then use EV.36
and finite tensor reassociation. The result
\[
\begin{gathered}
\Psi_\Phi(s)=1\otimes e_\Phi(s)\\
\text{in }B\otimes_R K_*^\infty
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.37}
\]
is \(B\)-linear.

Choose a basis \(\Phi_1,\ldots,\Phi_q\) of \(V\), and take
\[
\begin{gathered}
L=L_*^{\,q},\\
K=K_*^{\,q},\\
e=(e_{\Phi_1},\ldots,e_{\Phi_q}) .
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.38}
\]
The full \(B\)-action on \(\mathcal C\) gives a balanced contraction
\[
B\otimes_R K^\infty\longrightarrow\mathcal C^q .
\tag{EV.39}
\]
Its composite with \(\Psi=(\Psi_{\Phi_a})_a\) is exactly
\((\Phi_a^\infty)_a\).
This latter map is injective on the whole \(N\), including
its singular sections, by
§5.84, SE.1.
Thus both \(\Psi\) and \(e\) are injective.
The finite reassociation
\[
\begin{gathered}
B\otimes_R(R\otimes_{\mathcal D_X}K)\\
\simeq B\otimes_{\mathcal D_X}K,\\
b\otimes(r\otimes k)\\
\longmapsto br\otimes k
\end{gathered}
\tag{EV.40}
\]
has inverse \(b\otimes k\mapsto b\otimes(1\otimes k)\).
Both balance identities hold on each generator.
This proves every assertion of EV.1.
If \(q=0\), SE.1 gives \(N=0\), and the zero target proves
the theorem.

The theorem retains the original projected hypersurface,
the entire infinite extension and the actual finite D-type
quotient. Its finite-pole and intrinsic microlocal order
properties require the further regularity hypotheses and
arguments stated in Q.8.
